c10_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch01.scenario: Aarav skips breakfast and plays a full football match at school. By half-time his leg muscles are burning and feel heavy, and he is panting hard. His teammate tells him to just breathe faster for a minute and he will be fine.
c10_bio_ch01.prompt: What is actually happening in his muscles, and what will really help?

options.text: His muscles have outrun their oxygen supply and switched to anaerobic respiration, which releases little energy and produces lactic acid — that acid buildup is the burn. Rest, slow deep breathing, and some food help because the lactic acid must be carried to the liver and broken down using oxygen.
options.outcome: This matches how respiration and transport really work: oxygen delivery is limited by blood flow, not just breathing speed, and clearing lactic acid takes minutes of aerobic respiration.

options.text: The burn means his muscles ran out of oxygen completely, so breathing as fast as possible will instantly turn the lactic acid back into energy and he can sprint again.
options.outcome: Breathing faster cannot instantly raise oxygen delivery — that depends on the heart and circulation — and lactic acid still has to be processed biochemically, which takes time.

options.text: It is simple dehydration — a big glass of water and the burning will stop immediately.
options.outcome: Water helps hydration but does not remove the lactic acid or restore the glucose his muscles need.

c10_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch02.scenario: Meera snatches her hand back from a hot iron before she even feels the burn. A week later she notices her windowsill money plant has leaned sideways toward the light. She wonders how both 'knew' what to do.
c10_bio_ch02.prompt: How are these two responses coordinated differently?

options.text: Her hand used a nervous reflex arc — receptors in the skin fired a sensory neuron to the spinal cord, which fired a motor neuron to the muscle, all in a split second. The plant has no nerves; auxin hormone redistributed to the shaded side, making those cells elongate and slowly bend the stem toward light.
options.outcome: Both are real coordination: animals use fast electrochemical nerve impulses with receptor and effector, plants use slower chemical signals (hormones) that redirect growth.

options.text: The plant bent because sunlight physically pushed the stem over, the same way the heat pushed her hand away.
options.outcome: Nothing pushed either one — both are living responses to a stimulus, one through nerves and one through differential growth driven by a hormone.

options.text: Plants must have tiny nerves like ours, just slower ones, since both responses move a body part.
options.outcome: Plants coordinate without a nervous system — through hormones such as auxin and through electrical-chemical waves in cells, not neurons.

c10_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch03.scenario: Reema's grandmother fills the whole balcony with pots of money plant grown from cuttings of one parent. When a mealybug attack hits, every single plant suffers equally. She asks why the pests didn't spare at least a few.
c10_bio_ch03.prompt: What explains why the whole collection was hit equally hard?

options.text: Cuttings are asexual reproduction — every plant is genetically identical to the parent, so whatever made one plant vulnerable made all of them vulnerable. Plants grown from seeds carry mixed genes and usually vary in resistance.
options.outcome: This is exactly the trade-off of asexual reproduction: fast and faithful copies, but no variation — so one disease or pest can wipe out an entire clone population.

options.text: Cloned plants are actually stronger, so the attack must have been caused by over-watering rather than the mealybugs.
options.outcome: Cloning copies genes exactly — it cannot add resistance the parent did not have. The bugs spread easily precisely because no plant had a different genetic defence.

options.text: The pests attacked all plants equally because insects always spread uniformly through any group of pots.
options.outcome: Spread explains exposure, not equal damage — in a genetically varied population some individuals typically resist. Uniform collapse signals uniform genes.

c10_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch04.scenario: At a family dinner, an uncle learns that a child has blood group O while the parents are A and B. He jokes that the hospital must have mixed up the babies, since 'blood group always comes from the parents.'
c10_bio_ch04.prompt: Is the uncle right to be suspicious?

options.text: No mix-up is needed. If the mother is I-A-i and the father is I-B-i, each can pass the recessive i allele, and a child getting i from both is group O. Gametes carry only one allele each, so A and B parents can have an O child.
options.outcome: This is ordinary Mendelian inheritance — recessive alleles can hide in parents and reappear in children. ABO involves three alleles with codominance, so many combinations are possible.

options.text: He is right — a child's blood group must always match one of the parents, so an O child from A and B parents is impossible.
options.outcome: That ignores recessive alleles. Parents who each carry a hidden i allele produce an O child one time in four on average.

options.text: The child's group is just a blend of A and B, and O is what the blend looks like.
options.outcome: Blending inheritance is wrong — alleles stay discrete and separate into gametes; O is not a mixture but the result of inheriting two i alleles.

c10_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch01.scenario: For a school project, Kavya leaves an iron nail standing in blue copper sulphate solution overnight. In the morning the blue has faded to pale green and the nail has a reddish-brown coat. Her lab partner says the colour just 'soaked into the nail' like dye.
c10_chem_ch01.prompt: What actually happened, and how can she prove it was a chemical change?

options.text: Iron displaced copper from the solution — iron is more reactive, so it went into solution as iron sulphate (the green tint) while copper metal deposited on the nail (the reddish-brown coat). A new substance formed on the nail and the solution's composition changed — both signs of chemical change, plus the tube warms slightly.
options.outcome: The colour change, the deposited new metal, and the heat given off together confirm a displacement reaction, not staining.

options.text: Her partner is right — only colours moved around, which is a physical change like mixing paint.
options.outcome: A physical change makes no new substance; here copper metal actually left the solution and iron entered it, so the reaction is chemical.

options.text: The nail simply rusted in the water overnight, and the colour fading is a coincidence.
options.outcome: Rust is iron oxide, which needs oxygen and would not explain copper appearing on the nail or the solution turning green.

c10_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch02.scenario: A home garden's soil tests too acidic, and the rose plants are yellowing despite good watering. Grandfather suggests mixing in slaked lime. The neighbour instead recommends pouring vinegar into the beds, 'because sour things feed sour soil.'
c10_chem_ch02.prompt: Whose advice will actually fix the soil, and why?

options.text: Slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, is a base — it neutralises the excess acid in the soil and raises the pH back toward a level plants tolerate. Vinegar is acetic acid; adding it would push the pH even lower.
options.outcome: Neutralisation is the point: a base cancels acid. Gardeners really do treat acidic soil with lime for exactly this reason.

options.text: Vinegar is the better choice because acid added to acidic soil will balance it the way like dissolves like.
options.outcome: Like does not neutralise like — adding acid to acid only makes the soil more acidic and the plants worse.

options.text: Neither chemical is needed; the plants just need more water to dilute the acid away permanently.
options.outcome: Water dilutes temporarily but the acid remains in the soil and concentrates again as the soil dries; only a neutralising base removes it.

c10_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch03.scenario: At a jewellery shop, a family is choosing bangles. The salesman offers 24-carat pure gold at a higher price and 22-carat gold — gold mixed with copper — for everyday wear. A cousin insists pure gold must be better for everything because 'purer means stronger.'
c10_chem_ch03.prompt: Why does the jeweller actually recommend 22-carat for bangles worn daily?

options.text: Pure gold is extremely malleable but very soft — daily wear would bend and scratch it. Mixing in copper makes the alloy harder and more durable while keeping enough malleability to shape into ornaments.
options.outcome: Alloying deliberately trades a little purity for hardness — the foreign atoms disturb the metal's crystal layers so they do not slide as easily, which is exactly why 22-carat survives daily wear.

options.text: The cousin is right — 24-carat is best for bangles because the purest metal is always the strongest.
options.outcome: In metals, purity often means softness — pure gold's uniform atomic layers slide over each other easily, which is why it can be beaten thin but also dents easily.

options.text: 22-carat gold is recommended only because it is cheaper and the jeweller wants a quicker sale.
options.outcome: The price difference is real, but the functional reason is hardness — the copper alloy resists scratches and keeps its shape far better than soft pure gold.

c10_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch04.scenario: For a science exhibition, a student builds a simple conductivity tester — a bulb, a battery and two wires — and dips it into salt water, pure water, and a bottle of cooking spirit (ethanol). The bulb glows brightly only in the salt water. A classmate concludes the tester is broken 'because all clear liquids should behave the same.'
c10_chem_ch04.prompt: What explains why only the salt water lights the bulb?

options.text: Salt water contains free-moving ions — sodium and chloride — which carry charge through the liquid and complete the circuit. Pure water has almost no ions, and ethanol is a covalent compound that stays as neutral molecules in solution, so neither can conduct.
options.outcome: Conduction needs mobile charged particles. Ionic compounds supply them when dissolved; covalent molecules like ethanol do not ionise, so they stay non-conducting.

options.text: The classmate is right — any clear liquid conducts equally, so the tester must be faulty.
options.outcome: Clarity has nothing to do with it — conductivity depends on whether dissolved particles carry charge, and ethanol and pure water lack ions.

options.text: The salt water conducts because salt makes water thicker, and thicker liquids carry electricity better.
options.outcome: Thickness is irrelevant — it is the presence of free ions, not viscosity, that lets the liquid carry current.

c10_chem_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch05.scenario: For the school science quiz, a team is given three element cards — chlorine (35.5), bromine (80), iodine (127) — and told that early chemists grouped similar elements in threes. They must decide if these three really fit that old rule before the next round.
c10_chem_ch05.prompt: How can the team check whether these three elements genuinely form a triad?

options.text: Average the atomic masses of the lightest and heaviest: (35.5 + 127) / 2 = 81.25, which is close to bromine's 80. Chlorine, bromine and iodine also share chemical properties — coloured, reactive non-metals — so they genuinely form a Dobereiner-style triad.
options.outcome: The triad rule puts the middle element's mass near the mean of the other two, and all three must actually resemble each other chemically — both checks pass here.

options.text: They form a triad simply because there are three of them — any three elements make a triad.
options.outcome: Three elements are a triad only if their properties are similar and the middle atomic mass is approximately the average of the other two.

options.text: They cannot be a triad because the average, 81.25, does not equal 80 exactly, and the rule demands a perfect match.
options.outcome: The rule expects an approximate match, not a perfect one — bromine's 80 is close enough to 81.25, and the shared chemistry confirms the grouping.

c10_civ_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_civ_ch01.scenario: A new school has two large language groups among its students. The student council, dominated by the bigger group, proposes that all school announcements, the canteen menu vote and the annual-day language be decided by simple majority — meaning the larger group wins everything, every time.
c10_civ_ch01.prompt: What would a fairer arrangement, modelled on how Belgium handled its language divide, look like?

options.text: Guarantee both groups seats in the council, require decisions affecting each community to have that community's consent, and let each group run its own cultural affairs — Belgium's mix of equal representation, community governments and coalition rule shows how a minority can be protected instead of permanently overruled.
options.outcome: Belgium stayed stable because no group could rule alone: Dutch and French speakers share power at the centre, run their own community governments, and Brussels has special arrangements. The same logic stops a permanent majority at school.

options.text: Simple majority is the fairest system possible — if most students agree, the minority should accept whatever is decided.
options.outcome: Permanent majority rule in a divided group means one community never wins anything — exactly the resentment that majoritarianism created in Sri Lanka and that Belgium designed its constitution to avoid.

options.text: The only fair fix is to split the school into two separate schools, one for each language group.
options.outcome: Separation is not the only answer — Belgium kept one country intact while giving each community autonomy and shared power at the centre.

c10_civ_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_civ_ch02.scenario: During a dengue outbreak, the state government orders hospitals and municipalities to follow its own health protocol. An uncle at home insists the Prime Minister can simply take over every hospital in the state because 'health is a national matter, and the Centre outranks states on everything.'
c10_civ_ch02.prompt: Is the uncle right that the Centre can run health services in any state at will?

options.text: No — public health and public order are State List subjects, so the state government holds the primary power to legislate and run hospitals. The Centre can coordinate, advise and assist, but it cannot routinely legislate or administer on State subjects as if they were its own.
options.outcome: Indian federalism divides legislative power into Union, State and Concurrent lists. The Centre is supreme in its list and has special levers, but State List subjects belong to the states in normal times.

options.text: Yes — in India the Centre can legislate on any subject whenever it likes, since the Union government is superior to the states.
options.outcome: The division of powers is real: Parliament cannot casually take over State List subjects except in defined situations like a national emergency or a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest.

options.text: Neither level can act — health decisions must wait until both Centre and state pass identical laws.
options.outcome: Each level acts independently on its own list; there is no rule requiring identical laws before a state can run its hospitals.

c10_civ_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_civ_ch03.scenario: Both parents in a household work the same nine-hour day at their offices. Every evening the mother also cooks, cleans, and helps the children with homework while the father rests. Relatives praise her as a 'superwoman' who 'manages it all so well.'
c10_civ_ch03.prompt: What is this arrangement really showing, beyond one person's efficiency?

options.text: It is the sexual division of labour — paid work is shared but unpaid housework and childcare fall entirely on her, a 'double burden' of invisible work that is praised instead of shared. Equal office hours do not mean equal total work.
options.outcome: Calling it a division of labour names the pattern: society assigns domestic work to women as a duty, and that unpaid load — invisible in income statistics — limits their time and opportunities.

options.text: It is just efficient household management — she does the home tasks because she is naturally better at them, so everyone benefits.
options.outcome: Skill at cooking and cleaning is learned, not born — treating it as natural hides the unpaid hours she contributes and makes the unfair load look like talent.

options.text: Since she is praised and appreciated, no inequality exists — recognition makes the arrangement fair.
options.outcome: Praise does not reduce her hours or return her time; 'superwoman' compliments often mask the double burden rather than fix it.

c10_civ_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_civ_ch04.scenario: A neighbourhood's only park is crumbling, but residents disagree on the fix — some want a playground, some a walking track, some a parking lot. At the residents' meeting someone declares: 'We don't need any association or committee — every person should just fight for their own demand.'
c10_civ_ch04.prompt: Why would forming an organised group with a clear programme serve the residents better than everyone lobbying alone?

options.text: An organised body bundles many individual demands into one workable programme, contests for the authority to act, and can be held responsible if it fails — the same linkage function political parties perform between citizens and government. 200 lone voices cannot negotiate, but a committee with a platform can.
options.outcome: Parties and associations exist precisely to aggregate scattered preferences, mobilise support, and turn demands into policy — no single resident could do that alone.

options.text: The speaker is right — committees only add politics; if each resident pressures the municipality separately, the best demand will win on its own merit.
options.outcome: Without aggregation, conflicting demands cancel out and officials face a noise of voices with no one accountable for delivering anything.

options.text: The park question should be settled by whoever shouts loudest or donates most, since money and voice show real commitment.
options.outcome: That replaces aggregation with power — the richest or loudest resident wins regardless of what the community needs.

c10_civ_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_civ_ch05.scenario: At a family debate, a teenager argues that democracy is inefficient: 'Our colony's road took two years of meetings and complaints to get repaired. Under a dictator it would be fixed in a week — so democracy delivers less.'
c10_civ_ch05.prompt: How should the family judge democracy's actual outcomes?

options.text: Democracy should be judged by accountability, legitimacy and dignity, not only speed. The road was delayed because officials had to answer complaints, budgets were scrutinised and citizens could protest — those checks slow decisions but make them the people's own, and rulers who fail can be removed.
options.outcome: A dictator may pour tar faster, but no one can question where the money went or vote him out — democratic outcomes include answerable government and citizens' dignity, which speed alone cannot measure.

options.text: The teenager is right — the only fair test of a government is how fast it completes projects, so non-democratic rule wins.
options.outcome: Speed without accountability lets rulers act against citizens' wishes with no remedy — a fast road paired with silence, no elections and no right to complain is a poor outcome.

options.text: Democracy is clearly better because it guarantees every decision is made quickly and correctly.
options.outcome: Democracy does not guarantee quick or perfect decisions — it guarantees that decisions can be questioned and rulers changed, which is its real strength.

c10_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch01.scenario: A farming family is offered good money to sell their land to a factory. The son wants to sell — the salary looks big. The grandmother refuses — the land is security, food and their way of life. The daughter wants enough money only to fund her college seat.
c10_eco_ch01.prompt: Who is 'right' about what development means here?

options.text: Each is right about their own goal — development means different things to different people. The son seeks higher income, the grandmother seeks security and way of life, the daughter seeks education and opportunity. There is no single 'development' that fits all three.
options.outcome: This is the core lesson: development goals vary with a person's situation — income matters, but so do freedom, security and dignity. What is development for one may be a loss for another.

options.text: The son is objectively right — whoever brings the highest income defines development, so the family should sell.
options.outcome: Income is only one goal; for the grandmother the lost security and land may outweigh any salary, and income figures alone hide that trade-off.

options.text: The grandmother is right for everyone — development should always mean protecting land and tradition over money.
options.outcome: Her goals are legitimate for her, but imposing them on the son and daughter makes the same mistake — treating one person's goals as universal.

c10_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch02.scenario: For a school project, a student lists the jobs on her street: a grape farmer, a winery worker who turns grapes into wine, a trucker who delivers the wine, and a guide who shows tourists the vineyard. Her teammate marks them all 'agriculture' because 'it all starts with grapes.'
c10_eco_ch02.prompt: How should the four jobs actually be sorted into sectors?

options.text: Sort by the nature of the output, not the ingredient: the grape farmer is primary (grows a natural product), the winery worker is secondary (manufactures wine from grapes), and both the trucker and the guide are tertiary (they provide transport and tourism services).
options.outcome: The chain also shows interdependence — each sector depends on the one before it, but classification follows what each job produces: raw material, manufactured good, or service.

options.text: The teammate is right — anything connected to farming counts as the primary sector, so all four jobs are primary.
options.outcome: That erases the distinction the classification is built on — making wine is manufacturing and driving tourists is a service, whatever the original crop.

options.text: The trucker and guide belong in the secondary sector because they 'work on' the wine industry like the winery does.
options.outcome: They produce no physical good — moving and presenting things are services, which places them in the tertiary sector.

c10_eco_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch03.scenario: At lunch, Nikhil wants Aditi's paratha and offers his apple. Aditi wants Ravi's cookies instead, but Ravi wants Nikhil's apple. The three spend ten minutes failing to arrange a trade, and Nikhil sighs, 'This is why people invented money.'
c10_eco_ch03.prompt: What exact problem did the three friends hit, and how does money fix it?

options.text: They hit the double coincidence of wants — each pair wanted what the other did not have at that moment, so no direct swap worked. Money fixes it because everyone accepts it: Nikhil could sell his apple for money, then use the money to buy the paratha, without needing Aditi to want his apple.
options.outcome: Money acts as a medium of exchange — it splits one impossible three-way swap into two simple sales, which is precisely the function that made barter economies give way to money.

options.text: The problem was that they had no adult to referee the trades — a teacher could have matched them up, which is all money really does.
options.outcome: A referee only finds matches; money removes the need to find a matching partner at all, since anything can be sold for it and it can buy anything.

options.text: Barter failed only because food items are too cheap — for expensive items like phones, trading directly works fine.
options.outcome: Expensive items make barter worse, not better — the seller must find a buyer who both wants the phone and has exactly what the seller wants.

c10_eco_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch04.scenario: A student unboxes a new smartphone and reads the fine print: designed in California, processor from one country, display from another, assembled in India, sold worldwide. Her brother asks why the company doesn't just make the whole phone in one factory.
c10_eco_ch04.prompt: What explains the phone's multi-country production?

options.text: The company is an MNC spreading production across a global chain — each stage goes where it is most advantageous: advanced components where the technology and skilled engineers are, assembly where costs and skills balance, sales where the markets are. Interlinked production across borders is exactly what globalisation means.
options.outcome: No single location is best at everything, so the firm coordinates factories in several countries — cheaper labour, better technology and market access at different stages lower total cost.

options.text: It is mostly for the label — companies scatter production across countries so the box looks impressive, but one factory could do it all just as cheaply.
options.outcome: The spread is economic, not decorative — each stage really does cost less or perform better in its chosen location, which is why assembly plants, chip fabs and display makers sit in different countries.

options.text: Phones are made in many countries only because trade rules force companies to share production between nations.
options.outcome: Firms choose multi-country production to cut costs and access skills and markets — trade rules shape where they can go, but no rule forces them to split production.

c10_eco_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch05.scenario: A family buys a sealed packet of spices and finds it adulterated with filler. When they return to the shop, the trader shrugs: 'Once sold, goods are yours — no refunds.' Someone at home says nothing can be done for a ₹200 packet.
c10_eco_ch05.prompt: What can the family actually do?

options.text: Keep the bill and packet as proof, and file a complaint — the consumer courts set up under the Consumer Protection Act are designed for exactly this: low-cost redressal where a district commission can order refund or compensation without needing an expensive lawyer.
options.outcome: COPRA 1986 created a three-tier system precisely because individual complaints about small purchases used to cost more to fight than they were worth — the Act flipped that calculus.

options.text: Nothing — a shopkeeper's 'no refund' rule is final, and ₹200 is too small for any court.
options.outcome: Consumer forums exist for small claims too; 'sold goods are not taken back' is a shop rule, not law, and does not excuse selling adulterated goods.

options.text: The only real remedy is to warn neighbours and boycott the shop, since the law only handles big purchases.
options.outcome: Boycott helps socially but the law is not limited to big purchases — adulteration is a serious violation and consumer commissions routinely hear small claims.

c10_engl_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch01.scenario: After reading 'A Letter to God', a classmate laughs at Lencho: 'What an idiot — he wrote a letter to God, then got angry at the very people who helped him.' The class is asked to defend or challenge that verdict.
c10_engl_ch01.prompt: What is the fairest reading of Lencho's behaviour?

options.text: His faith was real and, in his position, almost rational — a hailstorm had destroyed his crop and a poor farmer had no other appeal left. But the same certainty became rigidity: so sure God had sent exactly one hundred pesos, he could only read the shortfall as theft by the post office staff who had actually collected the money for him.
options.outcome: This reads both sides of Lencho — faith as the strength that made him act, and as the flaw that made him misjudge the humans who quietly helped him.

options.text: The classmate is right — writing to God was simply irrational, and no sensible person would do it.
options.outcome: Within Lencho's world — an isolated farmer whose whole year's food was destroyed — appealing to God was the only channel he had; the letter is desperation expressed through faith, not stupidity.

options.text: Lencho's faith actually failed him, because God never delivered the full hundred pesos he asked for.
options.outcome: The story never shows the request failing — the money arrived through human hands; the failure was Lencho's inability to see goodness coming through people rather than directly from heaven.

c10_engl_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch02.scenario: In a class discussion on Mandela's 'Long Walk to Freedom', a student shrugs: 'Apartheid just meant separate buses and schools — unfair but not that evil. Laws are laws.' The teacher asks the class to respond.
c10_engl_ch02.prompt: What is the strongest reply to that student?

options.text: Apartheid was not a few separate queues — it was a legal system that defined your race at birth, dictated where you could live and travel, and decided what work and future were open to you. Mandela's point is deeper still: such a system cages the oppressors too, so freedom means dismantling the unjust laws themselves, not just swapping who sits where.
options.outcome: Laws like race classification, the pass system and segregated areas made discrimination the structure of the state itself — 'legal' and 'just' are not the same thing.

options.text: The student is basically right — separation was the real harm, and once separate facilities ended, nothing else about apartheid mattered.
options.outcome: That misses how deep it went: apartheid legally fixed identity, movement, residence and opportunity from birth — ending separate benches alone would not undo it.

options.text: Mandela's story shows the opposite — that unjust laws should simply be obeyed patiently until rulers change their minds.
options.outcome: Mandela resisted unjust law and went to prison for it; the chapter's whole arc is that freedom had to be fought for, not waited for.

c10_engl_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch03.scenario: A junior student has memorised her lines for the school play but freezes at every rehearsal, terrified of the stage. Her older brother, who just read the story of the young seagull's first flight, says: 'I know exactly what's going on with you.'
c10_engl_ch03.prompt: What does the seagull's story actually suggest about her fear?

options.text: That the fear is self-doubt, not inability — the seagull could fly perfectly well but was paralysed by the unknown, and only hunger pushed him over the edge, where instinct took over. For the student, the fix is not more skill but the first leap — one pushed step, and the capability she already has will carry her.
options.outcome: The story's point is that fear of the unknown outlives itself in one moment of action — the seagull discovered wings only after falling into air, and stage fright works the same way.

options.text: It proves she should wait until she feels zero fear — the seagull only flew once he was calm and ready.
options.outcome: The seagull was never calm — he flew because hunger forced the leap while he was still terrified; waiting for fear to disappear first would have left him on the ledge forever.

options.text: It proves her fear means she is genuinely not ready, since instincts warn us away from things we cannot do.
options.outcome: The seagull's fear was false alarm — his wings were ready while his mind was not; a prepared student's fright is the same kind of false signal.

c10_engl_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch04.scenario: A student finishes Anne Frank's diary and says, 'Honestly, the family was safe in hiding — Anne complained a lot for someone who wasn't in a camp.' His teacher asks him to rethink before writing his exam answer.
c10_engl_ch04.prompt: What is wrong with the student's reading?

options.text: It ignores the lens every entry must be read through — the family hid because anti-Jewish decrees had already stripped their freedom, and discovery meant deportation. And calling Anne only a victim misses her agency: she studied, wrote, argued and planned a future inside two years of confinement. The diary records resistance by a mind, not just suffering by a body.
options.outcome: Reading her complaints without the historical context flattens the diary; 'safe' hiding was really a shrinking cage under constant threat, and her writing itself was an act of defiance.

options.text: The student is right — since the family was never caught during the diary years, Anne's fears were exaggerated and her complaints immature.
options.outcome: The threat was real and eventually did find them; the diary's value is that it records, in real time, what persecution felt like before anyone knew how it would end.

options.text: The student is right because Anne's diary is just a teenage journal — it cannot be treated as evidence of anything larger.
options.outcome: Precisely because it is a real-time account without hindsight, it is a valuable historical source — it shows ordinary life under extraordinary persecution.

c10_engl_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch05.scenario: A grandmother describes how, in her childhood, the neighbourhood baker came each morning with a jingling basket and kept every family's monthly account in pencil on the wall. Her grandson scoffs: 'Old trades like that died out because delivery apps are just better.'
c10_engl_ch05.prompt: What does the Goan 'pader' tradition in the chapter suggest about what would actually be lost?

options.text: The pader was not just a bread-seller — he was a daily ritual, a trusted figure whose jingling staff woke the village, and his pencil-on-the-wall accounts ran on relationship rather than apps. When such a trade disappears, what is lost is a sensory rhythm, human trust and a living piece of Goa's Portuguese-era culture — not merely a delivery channel.
options.outcome: The chapter treats the pader as a living link to the past: the loaves, the morning routine and the informal credit all carry cultural memory that an app notification cannot replace.

options.text: The grandson is right — trades survive only if they are efficient, so the pader's disappearance would just prove he was inferior.
options.outcome: Survival is not a verdict on worth — the pader endured because he was woven into community life, and his loss would be cultural, not just commercial.

options.text: Grandmother's memory proves the pader was mainly about nostalgia — the actual bread and accounts were incidental.
options.outcome: The text shows the opposite — the bread was a daily necessity and the monthly pencil accounts a real trust-based economy; nostalgia is how it is remembered, not what it was.

c10_engl_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch06.scenario: A friend's beloved dog dies, and within a week he is browsing exotic-pet ads, saying he just wants 'something unusual to stop feeling sad.' He asks whether he should order the most interesting animal he can find.
c10_engl_ch06.prompt: What does Maxwell's story of getting Mijbil the otter suggest about doing this well?

options.text: A new animal can genuinely heal grief — Maxwell was 'too sad to think of another dog,' and the otter filled that emptiness — but he chose a creature that suited his watery Camusfearna home and then learned its needs. Healing through a pet works when the choice fits the animal's nature and your life, not just your mood.
options.outcome: Maxwell's decision joined emotion with suitability: the otter thrived because the environment and the owner's commitment matched what an otter actually is.

options.text: He should buy whatever animal looks cutest right away — Maxwell's story proves replacing a pet quickly is always the best cure for grief.
options.outcome: Maxwell did not pick at random — the otter fit his surroundings and habits; an impulse purchase of an unsuited animal would harm both the pet and the grieving owner.

options.text: He should never get another pet, since getting a new animal means betraying the one he lost.
options.outcome: The story treats the new companion as healing, not betrayal — Maxwell's love for Mijbil did not erase his dog; it gave his affection somewhere to go.

c10_engl_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch07.scenario: An eight-year-old neighbour girl has saved every coin for months, memorised bus timings from watching the stop, and can tell you the fare to town to the last paisa — all for a solo ride she has been quietly planning. Her mother laughs it off as 'naughty scheming.'
c10_engl_ch07.prompt: Reading Valli in 'Madam Rides the Bus', how should we see this child's behaviour?

options.text: As intelligence at work, not mere disobedience — like Valli, the girl's 'overwhelming' curiosity drove her to observe, ask questions, save resources and plan carefully. The same drive that adults call nosiness is what lets a child turn a wish into a workable plan.
options.outcome: The chapter portrays Valli's curiosity as a thinking faculty — she gathered details, calculated fares and waited for the right moment. Curiosity plus preparation is exactly how independent action becomes possible.

options.text: It is simply disobedience — a child plotting anything in secret is doing wrong and the savings should be confiscated.
options.outcome: The story complicates that verdict — Valli's secret trip showed planning, restraint (she refused treats to save her return fare) and self-reliance; the behaviour deserves guidance, not just blame.

options.text: It is harmless daydreaming — children who plan such things never actually carry them out.
options.outcome: Valli did carry hers out — she boarded the bus alone and managed the whole journey; underestimating a determined child is how adults get surprised.

c10_engl_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch08.scenario: A classmate's grandfather dies, and weeks later she is still inconsolable, saying, 'Why did this happen to my family? It's not fair.' Friends have run out of comforting words.
c10_engl_ch08.prompt: What does the Buddha's teaching in 'The Sermon at Benares' offer her?

options.text: The lesson Kisa Gotami learned when told to fetch mustard seed from a house untouched by death: grief feels uniquely unjust until you discover that every household has buried someone. Mortality is the one certainty all living beings share — accepting that does not erase love, but it loosens the feeling of being singled out, which is what keeps grief stuck.
options.outcome: The sermon does not say 'do not grieve' — it says sorrow only multiplies when we fight the fact of death itself; peace begins with accepting what cannot be changed.

options.text: That she should hide her grief completely, because mourning openly is a weakness the Buddha condemned.
options.outcome: The sermon never calls grief weakness — Kisa Gotami's grief was honoured; what the Buddha addressed was the refusal to accept death's universality.

options.text: That death only feels unfair because her family was unlucky — most families never actually face it.
options.outcome: The sermon's whole point is the opposite: there is no house where death has not entered; believing one's own loss is unique is precisely the illusion the teaching removes.

c10_engl_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch09.scenario: The school drama club rehearses 'The Proposal'. The lead actors play it as a tender love scene — soft voices, shy glances — and the show falls flat. A junior watching rehearsal blurts out, 'Shouldn't they be yelling about meadows and dogs instead?'
c10_engl_ch09.prompt: What has the club misunderstood about the play?

options.text: They are playing a farce as a romance. The play's comedy lives in three proud, irritable neighbours who quarrel hysterically over land and dogs while the actual proposal keeps getting lost — the shouting, interruptions and absurd priorities ARE the scene, not an obstacle to it.
options.outcome: Recognising the genre fixes the performance: Chekhov wrote a pressure-cooker farce where trivial disputes drown the marriage question, which is why the junior's instinct was right.

options.text: The club is right — since Lomov and Natalya get engaged at the end, the play is a romance and should be played gently.
options.outcome: An engagement alone does not make a romance — here it is the punchline of a farce, squeezed in between shouting matches about Oxen Meadows and the dogs.

options.text: The play is really a tragedy about property disputes, so the actors should perform it with heavy seriousness.
options.outcome: The disputes are deliberately trivial and exaggerated for laughter — playing them as tragedy would miss the farce just as much as playing them as romance.

c10_engl_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch10.scenario: A family adores their dog so much that they feed him sweets, fried snacks and extra helpings all day. He grows fat, listless and refuses walks. An aunt insists, 'He just needs more treats — food is how we show love.'
c10_engl_ch10.prompt: What does 'A Triumph of Surgery' say is really going on?

options.text: The dog is being loved to death — exactly like Tricki, whose real illness was Mrs. Pumphrey's indulgence, not any disease. What cured Tricki was not medicine but a stern cut in food and normal exercise; the 'treatment' the family needs is to stop mistaking feeding for caring.
options.outcome: The story's irony is that the cure was discipline, not surgery — the vet's job was managing the owner's love, and this family needs the same prescription.

options.text: The aunt is right — a well-fed, fat pet is a healthy and happy one, so more treats will fix the listlessness.
options.outcome: Overfeeding caused the listlessness; Tricki's bloated misery lifted only when the extras stopped and he had to run with other dogs.

options.text: The dog needs immediate surgery or strong medicine, since only medical intervention can fix a pet this sick.
options.outcome: The story's title is ironic — no surgery happened; rest, diet and play cured Tricki, and this dog most likely needs the same ordinary discipline.

c10_engl_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch11.scenario: A neighbourhood teenager is caught shoplifting. Most residents want him banned from their doors; one shopkeeper instead offers him small paid errands and teaches him to keep accounts. People call the shopkeeper a fool for trusting a thief.
c10_engl_ch11.prompt: In light of 'The Thief', what is the wisest reading of the shopkeeper's gamble?

options.text: It is the Anil approach — Hari Singh stole from a man who trusted him, taught him to cook and write, and paid him with respect; it was precisely that trust, and the glimpse of what an educated life could bring, that pulled Hari back to return the money. Trust is not naivety here; it is the only thing in the story that changes anyone.
options.outcome: The chapter argues that reform comes from being treated as worth trusting — punishment alone would have made Hari merely a more careful thief.

options.text: The shopkeeper is indeed a fool — once a thief, always a thief, and trust just gives the boy easier targets.
options.outcome: Hari literally returned under the weight of the trust he was shown; writing off every young offender guarantees the prediction comes true.

options.text: Trust only works if combined with a strict warning and watching his every move for months.
options.outcome: Anil never watched or warned — it was his deliberate, open-handed trust and the gift of education that did the work; surveillance would have taught the boy only to hide better.

c10_engl_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch12.scenario: Casting a spy skit for the school function, the class picks the tallest, fittest boy for the agent role because 'a spy has to look like James Bond.' The teacher quietly suggests the quick-witted boy with the ordinary face instead.
c10_engl_ch12.prompt: What does 'The Midnight Visitor' say the teacher knows?

options.text: That real cleverness wears no uniform — Ausable is fat, sloppy and accented, yet he survives a gunman purely by inventing a balcony and a knock at the door, talking Max into his own doom. A spy's weapon is presence of mind, not physique — the unremarkable-looking boy is the truer casting.
options.outcome: The story builds its whole joke on the gap between the romantic spy image and the real thing — Ausable wins because Max, like the class, trusted appearances.

options.text: The class is right — audiences need a spy who looks the part, and quick thinking cannot be acted anyway.
options.outcome: The entire play IS quick thinking — Ausable's escape is a dialogue performance of wit under pressure, which an actor of any build can carry off.

options.text: Neither matters — a spy skit succeeds only if there are gadgets and fight scenes, not talking.
options.outcome: The story contains no gadgets or fights at all — its suspense comes entirely from words and a believable lie, which is what makes it dramatic.

c10_engl_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch13.scenario: A student copies homework daily but insists, 'I'm basically honest — I only copy because I have no time, and I'd never actually steal anything.' His friend is reminded of Horace Danby, the respectable locksmith who robbed one safe a year to buy rare books.
c10_engl_ch13.prompt: What does 'A Question of Trust' suggest about this kind of self-image?

options.text: That 'not completely honest' is still dishonest — Horace too saw himself as good and respectable, stealing only for books he loved, yet the story strips that excuse: he is outwitted by someone even less honest and ends up in prison. A good reason for a dishonest act does not make it honest.
options.outcome: The chapter's irony is aimed exactly at this self-deception — Horace's hobby-theft felt civilised to him, but the law and a cleverer criminal treated it as plain theft.

options.text: The student's self-image is accurate — copying homework is nothing like real theft, so the comparison fails completely.
options.outcome: The scale differs but the pattern is identical — both excuse a small dishonesty with a reasonable-sounding story, which is precisely the habit the story warns about.

options.text: Horace was actually honest, since he stole only to buy books rather than for greed.
options.outcome: The purpose of a theft does not change the act — he took what was not his, and his taste for books made the irony sharper, not the crime cleaner.

c10_engl_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch14.scenario: At a sleepover, the group debates which superpower they'd want. Most pick invisibility — 'imagine what you could get away with!' One quiet kid who just read 'Footprints without Feet' says the story changed his mind.
c10_engl_ch14.prompt: What caution does Griffin's story actually offer?

options.text: That a great power without character becomes a crime spree — Griffin was a brilliant scientist who made his body transparent like glass, but instead of serving science he used invisibility to steal, assault and terrorise. The story shows the discovery was not the problem; the man misusing it was. A power only amplifies what the person already is.
options.outcome: Griffin could have been celebrated for one of the great discoveries; because he chose selfish ends, invisibility turned a promising scientist into a hunted lawbreaker.

options.text: The story proves science itself is dangerous — discoveries like invisibility should simply never be made.
options.outcome: The science was neutral — the harm came from Griffin's choices; a discovery's danger lies in its misuse, not its existence.

options.text: It proves invisibility is the best power to have, since Griffin got away with everything thanks to it.
options.outcome: He did not get away — he was chased, freezing, forced to bandage himself visible again, and finally cornered; the power gave him no peace at all.

c10_engl_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch15.scenario: A classmate loses at the zonal science fair — his neat butterfly display wins nothing — and announces he is 'obviously not a science person' and will quit entering fairs.
c10_engl_ch15.prompt: What would Ebright's story in 'The Making of a Scientist' tell him?

options.text: That the loss is the lesson — Ebright also lost at his first county fair, realised a fancy display of slides was not real science, and responded by doing actual experiments, starting with why the monarch butterfly's gold spots mattered. Failing once showed him the difference between showing off and doing research; quitting is the one move that guarantees no discovery.
options.outcome: The chapter traces a scientist made, not born — curiosity plus the discipline to convert a defeat into real experiments is what produced his later work.

options.text: He is right to quit — losing a fair once is proof a person lacks scientific talent.
options.outcome: Ebright's own first fair ended in exactly that failure; the difference between him and a quitter was that he asked what real science required instead of walking away.

options.text: He should keep entering but with flashier posters and displays, since presentation is what wins science fairs.
options.outcome: The story holds the opposite — Ebright learned that real work, experiments answering real questions, beats impressive display; polish without inquiry is what lost him that first fair.

c10_engl_ch16.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch16.scenario: A student is invited to a rich friend's birthday party and is miserable — not because she lacks a dress, but because hers isn't expensive-looking enough. She pressures her parents to borrow jewellery she cannot afford to replace.
c10_engl_ch16.prompt: What warning does 'The Necklace' give about this frame of mind?

options.text: Matilda suffered the same ache — 'born for all the delicacies and all the luxuries,' she felt humiliated by an ordinary but adequate life, and one evening of borrowed splendour cost her ten years of real poverty. The story shows the sickness was the craving to appear rich, not the actual want — and borrowing to sustain appearances is exactly how her trap shut.
options.outcome: Her unhappiness was psychological before it was economic — envy of a life she imagined made the decent one she had feel like suffering, and the necklace's fake glitter made the irony complete.

options.text: She is right to want more — Matilda's story shows ambition is healthy and she deserved the better life she dreamed of.
options.outcome: Matilda's longing was not ambition to become something but envy to appear something — and it is that hunger for appearances, not aspiration, that the story punishes.

options.text: The real moral is to simply never borrow anything, since objects themselves are dangerous.
options.outcome: The necklace was not cursed — the danger was Matilda's deception about losing it and her need to pose as wealthy; borrowing was just where the pretence became payable.

c10_engl_ch17.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch17.scenario: A new girl joins the class and stammers when nervous. Within a week she has a mocking nickname, classmates finish her sentences for her, and she has stopped raising her hand. Some say the teasing is 'just harmless fun.'
c10_engl_ch17.prompt: What does 'Bholi' reveal about what is happening to this girl?

options.text: The nickname is doing real damage — Sulekha was renamed 'Bholi' until even she accepted the label, and her family's neglect hurt her as much as her stammer did. The story shows that mockery and low expectation are choices people make, and that respect plus education — the teacher who treated her as capable — is what lets a labelled child reclaim her real name.
options.outcome: Bholi's arc is about identity stolen by a label and recovered through dignity and learning — the classmates finishing the new girl's sentences are replaying her family's mistake.

options.text: The teasing is harmless — every kid gets a nickname, and it does not affect who she really is.
options.outcome: The whole story disagrees — 'Bholi' swallowed 'Sulekha'; a label repeated by everyone becomes the identity a child believes she deserves.

options.text: The girl's stammer is the real problem — once it is fixed the teasing and self-doubt will vanish on their own.
options.outcome: Bholi's suffering came as much from being treated as a burden as from her stammer — speech improved only after a teacher first treated her with respect.

c10_engl_ch18.title: Use it in the wild
c10_engl_ch18.scenario: A classmate skims a poem for two minutes, then announces to the class that it's obviously a coded protest anthem — 'the poem mentions a river, and rivers always mean rebellion.' He is completely confident and completely wrong.
c10_engl_ch18.prompt: Which character from 'The Book That Saved the Earth' is he imitating, and what is the lesson?

options.text: He is doing a Think-Tank — the Martian commander who confidently 'decoded' a book of nursery rhymes as military secrets and surrendered to Earth over 'Humpty Dumpty.' The play satirises exactly this: arrogant misreading, where supreme confidence replaces actual understanding, and the reader's ego, not the text, supplies the meaning.
options.outcome: The comedy works because Think-Tank never doubts himself — and the classmate's confident nonsense about rivers shows the same error the play skewers.

options.text: His confident reading is fine — a poem means whatever the reader first thinks it means, so he cannot be wrong.
options.outcome: Think-Tank is a warning against precisely this — his confident misreading of 'Mistress Mary' as explosives nearly caused a war; interpretation has to answer to the text.

options.text: He is right that nursery rhymes and poems are too trivial to matter — only the Martians were foolish enough to take a book seriously.
options.outcome: The joke cuts the other way — the 'trivial' book saved an entire planet; the play insists the written word is more powerful than invading fleets.

c10_geo_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch01.scenario: For a school chart on 'Resources of India', a student sorts pictures into two columns — 'from living things' and 'from non-living things'. She places coal and petroleum under living things 'because they are made of dead forests and sea creatures.' Her partner disagrees.
c10_geo_ch01.prompt: Which column do coal and petroleum actually belong in, and why?

options.text: The non-living column — the biotic/abiotic classification follows what the resource is now, not what it was millions of years ago. Petroleum and coal are minerals extracted from rock; biotic resources are obtained from the living biosphere — forests, animals, fisheries. Their biological ancestry does not make them biotic.
options.outcome: This is exactly the trap the classification guards against: 'comes from dead organisms' describes origin, but the resource itself is abiotic — a mineral obtained from the lithosphere.

options.text: She is right — anything made of once-living matter counts as a biotic resource forever.
options.outcome: That rule would make every fossil fuel and limestone deposit 'biotic'; classification looks at the resource's present form and where it is obtained from, not its deep ancestry.

options.text: Both are wrong — coal and petroleum belong in a third 'fuel' column, since fuels are a separate class.
options.outcome: Use-based grouping exists too, but for the biotic/abiotic question they are still abiotic — the chart's two columns already have a correct answer.

c10_geo_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch02.scenario: The school eco-club spots a rare migratory bird at the local pond and excitedly proposes declaring it a 'biodiversity hotspot' in their annual report. Their teacher asks them to check what the term actually requires before printing it.
c10_geo_ch02.prompt: What should the eco-club's checklist look like?

options.text: A hotspot is defined by exceptional species richness — especially species found nowhere else — combined with serious threat or habitat loss. One rare bird sighting, however exciting, proves neither richness nor endemism, so the pond cannot claim the label — the same reason even the famous Sundarbans are not a separate hotspot just because tigers live there.
options.outcome: The criteria are about how many unique species a place holds and how endangered the habitat is — fame or a single charismatic animal is not on the list.

options.text: One rare species is enough — any place hosting something endangered qualifies as a hotspot automatically.
options.outcome: That would make every zoo and park a hotspot; the term is reserved for regions with extraordinary overall diversity and endemism under threat.

options.text: Any green area counts as a biodiversity hotspot as long as students formally declare it one.
options.outcome: Hotspot status is a scientific designation based on measured diversity and threat, not a title a school club can confer.

c10_geo_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch03.scenario: A family in a hill city that gets generous monsoon rain faces strict water rationing every May and June. A visiting cousin laughs: 'You people get more rain than we do — how can you have a water shortage?'
c10_geo_ch03.prompt: How can heavy annual rainfall and real water scarcity coexist?

options.text: Rainfall volume is not the same as usable supply — the rain arrives in a few months while demand runs all year, and if the city depends on springs and has too little storage, the water simply isn't there in summer. Scarcity can be seasonal, infrastructural or caused by polluted sources, not just by low rain — the same reason a humid coastal district can suffer shortage if its groundwater is contaminated.
options.outcome: This is the chapter's core distinction: scarcity is about water being available, storable and safe when needed — not just how much falls from the sky.

options.text: The cousin is right — shortage in a high-rainfall city is impossible, so the rationing must be a billing error.
options.outcome: High rainfall with poor storage and seasonal sources is a textbook scarcity pattern — cities like Shimla face exactly this every summer.

options.text: The only real cause is people wasting water — rain amount is irrelevant either way.
options.outcome: Overuse worsens scarcity but is not the only cause — seasonal timing, storage gaps and water quality create scarcity even where rain is abundant.

c10_geo_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch04.scenario: A teenager reads two headlines on the same day: 'Country records highest-ever foodgrain harvest' and 'Farmers in several districts protest rising debt.' She asks her family how both can be true at once.
c10_geo_ch04.prompt: What explains record production alongside farmer distress?

options.text: Output and income are different things — a record harvest can still leave farmers behind if input costs (seed, fertiliser, diesel, borewell water) rise faster than crop prices, if small holdings keep earnings thin, or if water-intensive cropping quietly eats the groundwater that future farming depends on. Indian agriculture can be a victim of its own success.
options.outcome: The chapter's point exactly: production statistics measure grain, not the grower's prosperity — distress and bumper harvests can genuinely coexist.

options.text: They cannot both be true — a record harvest means every farmer earned more, so the protests must be exaggerated.
options.outcome: Higher national output says nothing about per-farmer income; most farmers work tiny plots, and costs can outrun prices even in a bumper year.

options.text: The protests must be about something else entirely — agriculture that produces record food cannot have problems.
options.outcome: Rising debt, groundwater depletion and volatile prices are precisely the problems that record production can mask rather than solve.

c10_geo_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch05.scenario: On a school trip, students learn that gold was once panned from the sands of one river but is blasted out of deep rock at a famous goldfield nearby. A student asks why the same metal needs such different ways of getting it.
c10_geo_ch05.prompt: What decides how a mineral is extracted?

options.text: Its mode of occurrence — where the mineral sits in the earth. In river sands the metal is a placer deposit: rock eroded long ago left heavy grains concentrated in the sediment, so simple panning works. In the goldfield it lies in veins and lodes inside rock, so shafts and blasting are needed. The same mineral, two different geological settings, two different methods.
options.outcome: The chapter's key idea: minerals occur as veins and lodes in cracks, as layers or beds, as residual masses, or as alluvial placers — and the occurrence dictates the mining technique and its cost.

options.text: It is just the company's preference — any mineral can be panned or mined either way depending on budget.
options.outcome: You cannot pan metal still locked inside solid rock, and digging shafts for loose river sand would be absurd — geology fixes the menu of methods.

options.text: River gold and mine gold must be different minerals, since they are found so differently.
options.outcome: Same metal, different occurrence — rivers merely collect and concentrate gold eroded from rock elsewhere.

c10_geo_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch06.scenario: For a class project, students propose relocating the district's sugar mill from the cane belt to a plot beside the city's biggest mall 'so more customers can reach it.' Their economics teacher asks them to reconsider what a sugar mill really needs to be near.
c10_geo_ch06.prompt: Why do sugar mills sit next to cane fields rather than next to customers?

options.text: Sugarcane is a weight-losing, perishable raw material — only a small fraction of its weight becomes sugar, and it must be crushed quickly after harvest. Hauling heavy cane to a city mill would cost more than the sugar is worth and let the cane go stale, so the mill stays near the fields and only the light, shippable sugar travels to market.
options.outcome: This is the classic raw-material location rule: when inputs are bulky, perishable and lose weight in processing, the industry is pulled to the input, not the consumer.

options.text: The students are right — being next to the biggest market always matters most, so the city site wins.
options.outcome: Market pull wins only when transport of the finished product is the costly or risky leg; here the costly leg is moving heavy perishable cane, so raw material wins.

options.text: Mills locate near fields only because city land is expensive — raw material has nothing to do with it.
options.outcome: Land cost helps, but the decisive factor is the cane itself — its weight, bulk and perishability make long haulage ruinous regardless of land prices.

c10_geo_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c10_geo_ch07.scenario: A family's small farm business must send two consignments to a distant city: crates of ripe mangoes that spoil in two days, and a large load of cheap building stone that can take a week. A cousin advises sending 'everything by truck — road is always best.'
c10_geo_ch07.prompt: How should the family actually choose between road, rail, coastal shipping and air?

options.text: Match the mode to the cargo — the mangoes are perishable and high-value, so speed justifies the dearer option: refrigerated trucking or air gets them there inside the spoiling window. The stone is bulky, heavy and cheap, where cost per tonne matters far more than speed — rail or coastal shipping, the cheapest per tonne-kilometre for long hauls, is the right fit.
options.outcome: Transport choice trades cost against time and cargo character: road gives door-to-door flexibility, rail and waterways win on bulk, air wins on urgency — no single mode is 'always best.'

options.text: The cousin is right — road is always best because only trucks offer door-to-door delivery.
options.outcome: Door-to-door convenience does not beat cost for a week's-worth of cheap stone, and may be too slow for mangoes on a very long haul — the cargo decides, not the convenience.

options.text: They should send both by air — fastest is always safest for business.
options.outcome: Flying cheap building stone would cost more than the stone earns — speed matters only when the cargo's value or perishability demands it.

c10_hist_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_hist_ch01.scenario: In a history debate, a student argues: 'A nation is just a group of people who share the same ancestors and language — nothing more.' His opponent counters with what changed in France in 1789.
c10_hist_ch01.prompt: What did the French Revolution add to the meaning of 'nation'?

options.text: It turned subjects into citizens — the nation became a community of people bound by equal laws and shared sovereignty, where authority flows from the people themselves rather than from a king or a common bloodline. After 1789, belonging to France meant holding rights and a say in sovereignty, not merely sharing origins.
options.outcome: This is the modern meaning the Revolution created: the Declaration of the Rights of Man placed sovereignty in the nation, so the people — not the monarch — became the source of legitimate rule.

options.text: The first student is right — nations have always meant shared descent and language, and 1789 changed nothing about that.
options.outcome: That was the older meaning; the Revolution redefined the nation politically — as citizens under common laws and sovereignty — which is exactly why multi-language states can still be nations.

options.text: 1789 only changed who ruled France — 'nation' stayed a cultural word with no political meaning.
options.outcome: The Revolution fused the two: the nation became the very source of political authority, so the word carried a new legal and political force.

c10_hist_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_hist_ch02.scenario: At a family discussion on the freedom struggle, an elder claims: 'India sent soldiers and money to help Britain in the First World War, and Britain rewarded that loyalty fairly — nationalism after 1918 was ungratefulness.'
c10_hist_ch02.prompt: What does the record of 1914–18 actually show?

options.text: The war deepened colonial extraction, not partnership — over a million Indian soldiers, huge war loans and massive food exports drained the country while taxes and prices rose at home, and the influenza of 1918 killed millions. Indians gave so much precisely because they were promised a say in return; when self-rule did not follow, the sacrifice itself became fuel for nationalism.
options.outcome: The war years turned contribution into a claim: leaders argued India had bled for the Empire and earned the promised reforms — and the gap between sacrifice and reward is what swelled the movement.

options.text: The elder is right — wartime help created goodwill, and the postwar nationalist surge had nothing to do with the war.
options.outcome: The surge was inseparable from the war — the economic hardship and the broken expectation of self-government after such sacrifice are precisely what historians link to the post-1918 mass movement.

options.text: India actually refused to help in the war, which is why Britain cracked down afterwards.
options.outcome: India contributed enormously — soldiers, loans and food — the grievance was that this help was extracted under colonial rule and repaid with too little reform.

c10_hist_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_hist_ch03.scenario: At dinner, a child insists that aloo tikki and chilli paneer are 'purely Indian, they've always been here.' An uncle who teaches history smiles and asks where the potato and the chilli actually came from.
c10_hist_ch03.prompt: What does the plate reveal about the making of a global world?

options.text: That global exchange shaped even 'traditional' food — potatoes, chillies, tomatoes and maize all reached India from the Americas through trade routes after the Columbian exchange, and noodles and pasta themselves travelled along older routes. A dish can be authentically Indian today and still be built from global travellers.
options.outcome: The chapter's point lands on the dinner table: pre-modern routes like the Silk Routes and later ocean trade moved crops, foods and ideas as surely as silk and silver — globalisation has a long prehistory.

options.text: The child is right — if a food is traditional in a place, it must have originated there.
options.outcome: Tradition describes how long we've cooked something, not where it began — the humble potato reached every Indian kitchen only after crossing an ocean.

options.text: Foods never really travelled before modern shipping — old trade routes carried only luxuries like silk and spices.
options.outcome: The routes carried far more than luxuries — crops, techniques, religions and even diseases moved along them, reshaping diets and societies at both ends.

c10_hist_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_hist_ch04.scenario: An aunt runs a small clothing business: she supplies cloth and designs to neighbourhood women who embroider at home around their other work, then collects the finished pieces and sells them in the city. A cousin scoffs, 'That's not real industry — there's no factory.'
c10_hist_ch04.prompt: What does the history of industrialisation say about the aunt's business?

options.text: It closely resembles the putting-out system that industrialised Europe before factories — a merchant supplies raw material and takes the finished product, workers keep flexible hours at home yet depend on the merchant's prices and orders. Industry did not begin with factory chimneys; this countryside network was proto-industrialisation, the stage before mechanised production.
options.outcome: The women hold real autonomy over their time but real dependence on the merchant — the same double character the putting-out weavers of England had, which is why the system expanded before factories existed.

options.text: The cousin is right — industry means machines and factory buildings, so home-based work was never industry.
options.outcome: Factories were the later chapter — for over a century before them, merchant-directed household production was Europe's growing industrial system.

options.text: The aunt's workers are independent artisans, since working from home means they control their own production.
options.outcome: Home work hid the dependence — like the putting-out weavers, they did not own the material or choose the price, which made them workers for the merchant rather than free artisans.

c10_hist_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_hist_ch05.scenario: Clearing out the school library, a student says printed books were always just 'slow internet' — they never changed anything that speeches couldn't. The librarian asks him to think about what print made possible for the first time.
c10_hist_ch05.prompt: What did print actually change that speeches never could?

options.text: Scale and permanence — one speech reaches whoever stands in the crowd and vanishes, but one printed text reaches thousands of strangers identically, survives to be reread, debated and answered. That is how ideas built movements: cheap printed matter created reading publics, spread reform and criticism, and let arguments travel far beyond the speaker's voice.
options.outcome: From woodblock editions meant for free distribution to the pamphlet wars of later centuries, print turned private thought into a public force — the effect speeches could never sustain alone.

options.text: The student is right — print is just speech on paper and changed nothing fundamental.
options.outcome: Print multiplied an idea a thousandfold and froze it in checkable form — creating shared debates and publics that no sequence of speeches could produce.

options.text: Print mattered only for religion — printing sacred texts for merit — and played no role in political or social change.
options.outcome: Early printing did serve devotion, like the Diamond Sutra distributed freely for merit, but print quickly escaped the temple — pamphlets, books and newspapers reshaped politics and society.

c10_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch01.scenario: For sports day, 72 students must be split into identical teams. A classmate writes '72 = 8 × 9' on the board and declares that the prime factorisation is done, so teams of 8 or 9 are the 'prime' options.
c10_math_ch01.prompt: Has he actually found the prime factorisation, and what does it tell the organisers?

options.text: No — 8 and 9 are factors but neither is prime (8 = 2×2×2, 9 = 3×3). The prime factorisation is 72 = 2³ × 3², and it is the only one — the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees every number breaks into primes in exactly one way. Prime-sized teams must come from those primes: only 2 or 3 students per team.
options.outcome: Checking that every factor is prime, and knowing the answer is unique, is what makes prime factorisation a tool rather than just any multiplication that works.

options.text: He is right — any two numbers that multiply to 72 count as its prime factorisation.
options.outcome: A factorisation is only 'prime' if every factor is itself prime; 8 × 9 hides the real primes inside composite numbers.

options.text: There is no single prime factorisation — different people can break 72 into different primes.
options.outcome: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic rules this out: the list of primes is unique, only the order of writing can differ.

c10_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch02.scenario: A student sells handmade diyas, and her profit in rupees works out to P(x) = -2x² + 24x - 40 for x diyas sold. She graphs it, sees the curve cross the x-axis twice, and a friend says, 'Those crossing points just mean zero profit — useless information.'
c10_math_ch02.prompt: What do the x-intercepts actually tell her?

options.text: They are the break-even sales numbers — the zeros of the polynomial, where P(x) = 0. Solving -2x² + 24x - 40 = 0 gives x = 2 and x = 10: selling fewer than 2 or more than 10 diyas loses money, and between them she is in profit. The x-intercepts of a polynomial's graph are precisely its zeros — the most useful points on the whole curve for her.
options.outcome: Zeros are where the graph meets the x-axis — geometrically a crossing, economically the break-even points. The 'useless' points are actually the ones that answer her question.

options.text: The friend is right — zeros of a polynomial are just where profit is zero and carry no business meaning.
options.outcome: Zero profit is exactly the break-even threshold — the zeros mark where she crosses from loss to profit and back, which is crucial information.

options.text: The two crossings mean the equation has no real solution, since a real profit curve shouldn't dip below zero.
options.outcome: Crossing the axis twice means the quadratic has two real zeros — the dips below zero are the loss zones, which is why the curve dips at all.

c10_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch03.scenario: Two siblings compare receipts from the same shop: one paid ₹65 for 5 pens and 3 pencils, the other paid ₹50 for 2 pens and 4 pencils. A cousin claims each item's price is 'obviously' the total divided by the count — about ₹8 each.
c10_math_ch03.prompt: How do you actually recover the two prices?

options.text: Set up two equations — 5p + 3q = 65 and 2p + 4q = 50 — and solve them together: elimination gives p = 10 and q = 5, so a pen costs ₹10 and a pencil ₹5. Graphically, the two lines intersect at that single point, which is the only price pair satisfying both bills.
options.outcome: Two unknowns need two independent equations — the pair of receipts supplies exactly that, and the solution is the point both conditions share.

options.text: The cousin's method works — dividing each total by the number of items gives the price of each thing.
options.outcome: Dividing the total by item count mixes two different prices into one average; ₹8 each predicts a bill of ₹64 for 8 items yet the receipts disagree, showing the two prices differ.

options.text: The prices cannot be found — one shop visit's totals are not enough information to separate two items.
options.outcome: Two different purchases give two equations in the same two unknowns, which is exactly enough to pin down both prices.

c10_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch04.scenario: A family buys a rectangular plot: the length is 3 metres more than the breadth and the area is 180 m². Father guesses 'just divide 180 by 3 to get the length' and starts measuring 60 metres along the ground.
c10_math_ch04.prompt: How should the dimensions actually be found?

options.text: Let the breadth be x, so length is x + 3 and x(x + 3) = 180 gives the quadratic x² + 3x - 180 = 0, which factorises as (x + 15)(x - 12) = 0 — so breadth is 12 m and length 15 m. The '3 more' relationship multiplies through the whole equation; it cannot be handled by dividing the area by 3.
options.outcome: Translating 'length is 3 more than breadth' into x and x + 3, then solving the quadratic, is the correct route — and 12 × 15 = 180 checks.

options.text: Father's shortcut works — 180 divided by 3 gives the 60 m length because the difference between the sides is 3.
options.outcome: The 3 is a difference between the sides, not a divisor of the area; 60 × 57 would give 3420 m², not 180.

options.text: The problem is unsolvable as stated — you would need the perimeter as well to find two unknowns.
options.outcome: The area relation x(x+3) = 180 already pins down x — one quadratic equation in one unknown is enough.

c10_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch05.scenario: A student tracks her savings account: ₹5000, ₹5500, ₹6050, ₹6655 at the end of four years. She tells her brother, 'It goes up every year, so it's an arithmetic progression — I can predict any year by adding.'
c10_math_ch05.prompt: Is she right that this is an AP?

options.text: No — an AP needs a constant common difference, but here the gaps are 500, 550 and 605: they grow each year because the balance increases by a percentage, not a fixed amount. It is actually a geometric pattern (each term is 1.1 times the last), so predicting requires multiplying, not adding.
options.outcome: Checking the differences — not just whether terms rise — is the test for an AP. Equal growth in amount is additive; equal growth in rate is multiplicative.

options.text: She is right — any sequence that keeps increasing is an arithmetic progression.
options.outcome: Increasing is not the test — the increase itself must be the same each time; here it changes from 500 to 550 to 605.

options.text: It is an AP as long as the differences are positive — they do not need to be equal.
