options.outcome: Equal differences are the definition of an AP; positive but unequal gaps make it some other progression entirely.

c10_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch06.scenario: A student enlarges a 4 cm × 6 cm photo to 8 cm × 12 cm for a poster. His friend says, 'Same picture, same shape — the two photos are congruent, just one is bigger.'
c10_math_ch06.prompt: What is the precise relationship between the two photos?

options.text: They are similar, not congruent — corresponding angles are equal and every side doubled, so the shape is preserved at scale factor 2. Congruence demands corresponding sides be equal in length, which fails the moment the enlargement happens; 'same shape' alone gives similarity, and 'same shape and same size' is what congruence requires.
options.outcome: This is the classic trap: equal angles and proportional sides define similarity; congruence additionally demands the sides actually match — no scaling allowed.

options.text: The friend is right — same shape is exactly what congruent means, so the photos are congruent.
options.outcome: Same shape with different size is similarity; congruence also requires equal corresponding sides — an enlargement can never be congruent to the original.

options.text: The photos are neither similar nor congruent, since changing the size changes the figure completely.
options.outcome: Doubling every side keeps all angles and all ratios — the very definition of similar figures.

c10_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch07.scenario: On the school's gridded sports field, a student must run straight from a flag post at one grid point to a water cooler 3 squares east and 4 squares north. He calculates the distance as '3 + 4 = 7 squares' and wonders why the straight path looks shorter.
c10_math_ch07.prompt: What is the actual straight-line distance, and why isn't it 7?

options.text: Five squares — the run is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are 3 and 4, so the distance formula gives √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. Adding the legs counts the corner-cutting walk along the grid edges, which is always longer than the direct diagonal — that is why the formula squares and roots instead of adding.
options.outcome: The distance formula is Pythagoras on a grid: horizontal and vertical gaps combine as squares because the direct path is the hypotenuse, never the sum of the legs.

options.text: He is right — distance is just total horizontal plus total vertical, so 3 + 4 = 7 squares.
options.outcome: That sum describes a path that walks right then up, not the straight line — the diagonal of a 3-4-5 triangle is 5, which is visibly shorter.

options.text: The distance is 3 × 4 = 12 squares, since distance equals area covered.
options.outcome: Multiplying the legs gives the rectangle's area, not the length of the diagonal — the distance formula uses squares added under a root, not the product.

c10_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch08.scenario: A hospital must build a wheelchair ramp rising 1.5 m, and safety rules cap the incline at 15°. The contractor has a 6-metre ramp plank and says, 'Six metres is plenty long, so it will definitely be gentle enough.' A student is asked to verify.
c10_math_ch08.prompt: Does the 6 m ramp satisfy the 15° limit?

options.text: Check the angle, not just the length — sin θ = rise ÷ ramp = 1.5/6 = 0.25, so θ is about 14.5°, which is under the 15° limit, so the ramp is acceptable. The inclination depends on the ratio of rise to ramp length, which is exactly what sine measures.
options.outcome: Trigonometry turns 'seems long enough' into a checkable number — the angle follows from opposite over hypotenuse, and 14.5° clears the rule.

options.text: The contractor is right — a longer ramp always means a safer angle, so measuring the angle is unnecessary.
options.outcome: Length alone does not fix the angle — the same 6 m plank would exceed 15° on a rise above about 1.55 m; the rise-to-ramp ratio is what must be checked.

options.text: The ramp fails automatically — to be safe, a ramp must be at least 15 metres long whenever the rise is over a metre.
options.outcome: There is no fixed length rule — safety is about the angle, and a 6 m ramp for a 1.5 m rise gives roughly 14.5°, inside the limit.

c10_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch09.scenario: The school wants the flagpole's height painted on the new noticeboard, but nobody can climb it and the pole is too tall for a ladder. A student claims the height simply cannot be found without going up.
c10_math_ch09.prompt: How can trigonometry measure the pole from the ground?

options.text: Stand a known distance from the base — say 10 m — and measure the angle of elevation to the top. Then tan θ = height ÷ distance, so height = 10 tan θ, plus the observer's eye height. The line of sight, the ground and the pole form a right triangle, so one angle and one side give the unreachable side.
options.outcome: This is the everyday power of angles of elevation: any tall object — tower, tree, building — becomes measurable with a tape and an angle, no climbing needed.

options.text: The student is right — a vertical height can only be measured by going to the top with a tape.
options.outcome: Angles let you measure what you cannot reach — a right triangle forms between you, the base and the top, and trigonometry solves for the pole.

options.text: You can only estimate by comparing shadows — exact height from the ground is impossible.
options.outcome: Shadow comparison is one valid trick, but measuring the angle of elevation with a clinometer gives an exact answer too — ground measurement is quite possible.

c10_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch10.scenario: A circular garden has a straight walking path that just grazes its edge at one point. For a geometry display, a student claims: 'Through that touching point you could draw infinitely many tangent lines, since infinitely many lines pass through any point.'
c10_math_ch10.prompt: How many tangent lines can actually touch the circle at that point?

options.text: Exactly one — a tangent must touch the circle without cutting into it, and at a given point only the line perpendicular to the radius at that point does so. Every other line through the point either misses the garden or slices through it as a secant, so 'many lines through a point' does not mean many tangents.
options.outcome: The radius-to-tangent perpendicularity is the key theorem: it both defines the unique tangent and explains why rotating the line even slightly makes it cut the circle.

options.text: The student is right — since infinitely many lines pass through any point, infinitely many tangents are possible there.
options.outcome: Infinitely many lines pass through the point but only one touches without crossing — every tilted line becomes a secant entering the circle.

options.text: Zero — a straight line can never touch a curve at only one point.
options.outcome: A tangent does exactly that — it grazes the circle at one point while lying perpendicular to the radius drawn there.

c10_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch11.scenario: A circular pond of diameter 10 m gets a 2 m wide tiled path built all around it. The contractor calculates the path's area as 'the circumference times the width' and orders tiles on that basis. A student checks the estimate.
c10_math_ch11.prompt: How should the path's area be computed?

options.text: As a ring — the outer circle has radius 7 m and the pond has radius 5 m, so the path's area is π(7² − 5²) = π × 24 ≈ 75.4 m². Circumference × width uses the inner circle's edge and misses that the outer edge is longer, so the contractor's shortcut underestimates the real area.
options.outcome: The ring area is always the difference of two circle areas — π(R² − r²) — because the path is the gap between two circles, not a rectangle of circumference by width.

options.text: The contractor's method is fine — a path of uniform width is just a rectangle whose length is the pond's circumference.
options.outcome: Unrolling a ring into a rectangle understates it — the outer boundary is longer than the inner one, so the true area is π(R² − r²).

options.text: The path area is π(7 − 5)² = about 12.6 m², since the width is the only new radius.
options.outcome: Squaring the width alone gives a small disc, not a ring — the path surrounds the whole pond, so it is the outer circle minus the inner one.

c10_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch12.scenario: For a craft fair, a student builds a toy by gluing a cone on top of a hemisphere, base to base. To order paint, her partner adds the full surface areas of both solids — 'every face needs paint.'
c10_math_ch12.prompt: What is wrong with adding the two complete surface areas?

options.text: The joined faces are not exposed — the cone's flat base and the hemisphere's flat face are glued together inside the toy, so no paint can reach them. The surface to paint is only the cone's curved part (πrl) plus the hemisphere's curved part (2πr²); the shared circular base must be left out entirely.
options.outcome: For combined solids, surface area means only what is visible from outside — faces glued together vanish from the surface, so each must be excluded once.

options.text: The partner is right — you paint the toy the same way you'd paint each solid separately, so add both total surface areas.
options.outcome: That double-counts the joined circle — once as the cone's base and once as the hemisphere's face — inflating the paint estimate for a surface that no longer exists outside.

options.text: Subtract the cone's base but keep the hemisphere's flat face, since it is the 'bottom' of the toy.
options.outcome: The hemisphere's flat face is exactly the circle glued to the cone — it is internal too, so both sides of the join must be excluded.

c10_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch13.scenario: At a school health camp, the mean weight of 100 children comes out as 38.2 kg — then someone discovers the scale read 0.5 kg too low for every child. A volunteer says the whole table must be re-entered and the mean recalculated from scratch.
c10_math_ch13.prompt: Is a full recalculation really needed?

options.text: No — adding a fixed amount to every single data value shifts the mean by exactly that amount, so the corrected mean is simply 38.2 + 0.5 = 38.7 kg. The same shortcut works in reverse for any uniform error: the mean moves with the data.
options.outcome: Because the mean is the total divided by the count, bumping every entry by 0.5 adds 0.5 to the total's per-child share — one addition replaces a hundred corrections.

options.text: The volunteer is right — any measurement error means every entry must be corrected before the mean can be trusted.
options.outcome: Individual entries do need the +0.5, but the mean needs no rebuild — a uniform shift in all values produces the identical shift in the average.

options.text: The mean stays 38.2 kg anyway, since a constant error cancels out across so many children.
options.outcome: A constant offset does not average away — it shifts every value the same direction, so it shifts the mean by the full 0.5 kg, not by zero.

c10_math_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch14.scenario: At a school fair, a game stall offers: draw one marble blindfolded from a bag of 20 — 8 green, 7 yellow, 5 blue — and win a prize only on blue. The stallholder calls it 'a fair game, one-in-three colours.'

options.text: No — probability counts marbles, not colour names. P(blue) = 5/20 = 1/4, so a player wins only one draw in four while the stall keeps the other three quarters. 'Three colours' does not mean three equal chances — the counts of each colour decide the odds.
options.outcome: This is the core of probability: each marble is equally likely, so uneven counts make the colours uneven — a classic way 'fair-looking' games are tilted.

options.text: The stallholder is right — with three colours the chance of any one is one in three, so the game is fair.
options.outcome: Colours are not outcomes — marbles are. With only 5 blue among 20, blue's chance is 1/4, not 1/3, and the stall quietly profits from the difference.

options.text: The game is unfair only if marbles are removed mid-game — with a fixed bag the stated odds must be true.
options.outcome: A fixed bag still hides uneven counts; the fairness depends on how many blue marbles there are, not on whether the bag changes.

c10_phy_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_phy_ch01.scenario: A student builds a simple circuit — battery, switch, one long wire, a bulb. She adds a second ammeter far from the battery and predicts it will read lower, 'because some of the current gets used up travelling along the long wire.'
c10_phy_ch01.prompt: Will the far ammeter really read lower?

options.text: No — current is the rate of flow of charge, and charge is neither created nor used up in the wire. In a single loop the same charge per second must pass every point, so both ammeters read the same; the wire's resistance affects how much current flows, but not 'how much survives' the journey.
options.outcome: The bulb is dimmer or brighter because the whole circuit's current changed — not because current leaks away along the path. What enters the wire must leave it.

options.text: She is right — the farther ammeter reads lower since current is consumed by the wire on the way.
options.outcome: Current is not a substance that gets spent — it is the flow of charge itself, and charge conservation forces the same reading at every point in one loop.

options.text: The second ammeter will read higher, because charge piles up waiting to get through the long wire.
options.outcome: Charge cannot accumulate in a steady circuit — it flows through continuously at the same rate everywhere, so neither end can read higher.

c10_phy_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_phy_ch02.scenario: For a physics chart, a student draws a bar magnet's field lines: eight lines emerging from the north pole but only five curving back into the south pole. 'Three lines get used up in the middle,' he explains.
c10_phy_ch02.prompt: What is wrong with his diagram?

options.text: Field lines are continuous closed loops — every line that leaves the north pole returns to the south pole (and continues inside the magnet), so the counts must match. Lines also crowd near the poles, which is what shows the field is strongest there; lines cannot end, cross or vanish midway.
options.outcome: Correcting the drawing to equal lines in and out captures two real rules: field lines form closed curves and their density — not their survival — tells the field's strength.

options.text: He is right — some field lines dissipate in the air between the poles, so fewer reach the south end.
options.outcome: Field lines do not wear out or dissipate — each one is a closed loop, so the number leaving north always equals the number entering south.

options.text: The error is the opposite — more lines should enter the south pole than leave the north, because south 'pulls harder.'
options.outcome: Neither pole outranks the other — the lines are shared closed loops, so the counts at both poles are always equal.

c10_phy_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_phy_ch03.scenario: A family is deciding fuel for a small food stall. One member argues for the fuel with the highest calorific value 'since more heat per kilo always means cheaper cooking.' Another wants to compare what a kilo of each actually buys.
c10_phy_ch03.prompt: How should they really choose a fuel?

options.text: Compare cost per unit of useful energy, not energy per kilo alone — a fuel with high calorific value can still lose if each kilo is much costlier, and a lower-value fuel can win if it is cheap enough per megajoule. Convenience also matters: a liquid like LPG lights easily, stores compactly and leaves little ash, which a solid fuel does not.
options.outcome: The chapter's lesson is that 'good fuel' is a package — calorific value, cost per unit energy, ease of handling and cleanliness all count, not one number.

options.text: The first member is right — whichever fuel releases the most heat per kilo is automatically the cheapest choice.
options.outcome: Cost per kilo can overwhelm heat per kilo — divide the price by the energy each fuel delivers and the 'stronger' fuel often loses.

options.text: They should simply pick whichever fuel the shop sells — all fuels deliver the same energy anyway.
options.outcome: Fuels differ enormously in energy per kilo and in handling — treating them as identical wastes money or heat.

c10_phy_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_phy_ch04.scenario: Checking reflection laws on the back of a shiny steel spoon, a student draws the 'normal' as a line straight down, perpendicular to the spoon's handle axis. Her measured angles of incidence and refusal don't match, and she blames the spoon for being curved.

options.text: In the normal — on a curved mirror the normal at any point is the line from that point to the mirror's centre of curvature, not a fixed vertical. The laws of reflection hold perfectly on curved surfaces point by point: measure the incident and reflected angles against that radial normal and they will be equal.
options.outcome: Curved mirrors follow the same laws as flat ones — the normal just changes direction with the surface, which is exactly what makes concave and convex mirrors focus and spread light.

options.text: The spoon is at fault — the laws of reflection only work on perfectly flat mirrors, so curved surfaces cannot obey them.
options.outcome: Reflection laws apply to every smooth surface — the mirror's curvature only changes where the normal points, not whether angle in equals angle out.

options.text: Her normal is right — on any mirror the normal must stay perpendicular to the object's longest axis.
options.outcome: The normal is defined by the surface at the point of incidence — for a spherical mirror it always runs through the centre of curvature, not along any external axis.

c6_biology_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c6_biology_ch06.scenario: In the Class 6 photo, three friends who all turned twelve this year look wildly different — one looks fifteen, one looks twelve, one still looks ten. A visiting relative whispers that somebody must be lying about their age.

options.text: Nothing is wrong — adolescence and its growth spurt start on each body's own schedule, somewhere in the early teens, so same-age classmates can look years apart. Bodies are not products off an assembly line with a fixed finish date; each has its own timetable.
options.outcome: The chapter's key idea: adolescence is a window, not a birthday — entering it at eleven or thirteen are both normal, and the height differences even out over time.

options.text: The relative is right — children of the same age should look the same, so someone is lying.
options.outcome: Same age does not mean same stage — growth spurts begin at different ages for different children, which is exactly what the photo shows.

options.text: The shorter children must be sick or underfed, since healthy children always grow at the same rate.
options.outcome: A later growth spurt is not illness — healthy children simply enter adolescence at different ages within the normal window.

c6_biology_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c6_biology_ch09.scenario: During a school lunch conversation, a student asks why the digestive system is a long, winding tube that takes food on a whole journey — 'wouldn't a short, wide pouch be a simpler design?'
c6_biology_ch09.prompt: What does the long tube actually accomplish that a pouch could not?

options.text: Digestion is a staged process, and the length buys both time and surface — food is broken down step by step (mouth, stomach, then the long intestine), and the intestine's huge surface area is what lets digested nutrients actually pass into the blood. A short wide pouch would dump food through before it was fully digested or absorbed.
options.outcome: The tube's shape is the function: each section does a different job, and the intestine's length exists for absorption — a pouch would leave nutrients unharvested.

options.text: The student has a point — the tube is long mainly to store more food so we can go days between meals.
options.outcome: The gut is a processing line, not a storage tank — its length exists for the stages of digestion and the surface area needed to absorb nutrients.

options.text: The pouch design would work equally well — length is just leftover anatomy with no purpose.
options.outcome: Every part of the tract has a role — churning, acid breakdown, enzyme action and absorption happen in sequence along the length.

c6_biology_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c6_biology_ch10.scenario: A child sprouts a bean seed on a wet paper towel on the windowsill — no soil at all — and shows it proudly. Her grandmother objects: 'Impossible. Plants need soil; that sprout must be fake.'
c6_biology_ch10.prompt: What does the sprouting seed really prove?

options.text: That germination needs water, air and warmth — not soil. The seed drank the moisture, swelled, and the embryo inside woke up and began growing on the food stored inside the seed itself. Soil matters later for minerals and support, but the first sprout runs entirely on the seed's own provisions.
options.outcome: The paper-towel sprout is real biology: a seed is a baby plant packed with its own lunchbox, and water is the trigger that starts it growing.

options.text: Grandmother is right — without soil's nutrients no seed can germinate, so the sprout must have been faked.
options.outcome: Seeds carry stored food precisely so they can sprout before roots reach soil — moisture alone is enough to start germination.

options.text: It sprouted only because of sunlight — the paper towel's dampness had nothing to do with it.
options.outcome: Seeds can germinate in a dark cupboard if kept moist — water is the trigger; light becomes important once the shoot needs to make its own food.

c6_chemistry_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_chemistry_ch04.scenario: Sorting classroom objects for a 'properties of materials' display, a student declares a rule: 'Anything hard is automatically opaque — you can tell both properties at once.'
c6_chemistry_ch04.prompt: Does one property really predict the other?

options.text: No — a glass pane or a diamond is hard yet transparent, and butter paper is soft but translucent. Hardness and transparency are independent properties, which is the whole point of classifying materials: each property must be tested on its own, and one tells you nothing about the other.
options.outcome: The glass counterexample breaks the rule instantly — materials are grouped by separate, measurable properties, and assuming they travel together misleads the sorting.

options.text: The student is right — hard things block light and soft things let it through, so the properties always agree.
options.outcome: Glass is the standing counterexample — hard enough to scratch many materials yet perfectly transparent, so the two properties clearly vary independently.

options.text: It is actually the reverse — transparent things are always hard and opaque things are always soft.
options.outcome: Neither pairing holds — rubber is opaque and soft, glass is transparent and hard; each property stands alone.

c6_chemistry_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_chemistry_ch05.scenario: At a bonfire, a student insists that the burning paper is only a physical change: 'Look, the paper is still there — it just became smaller grey ash.' His friend is asked to check the claim.
c6_chemistry_ch05.prompt: Is burning paper a physical or chemical change?

options.text: Chemical — the paper did not just get smaller; it turned into new substances (ash, smoke and gases) that cannot be gathered up and turned back into paper. Compare grinding chalk: the powder is still chalk, so that is physical even though you cannot rebuild the stick. The test is whether a new substance formed, not whether something remains.
options.outcome: The 'still there' argument fails because what remains is no longer paper — irreversibility and a new material are the marks of a chemical change.

options.text: The student is right — as long as some material survives, the change is physical.
options.outcome: Survival of material is not the test — ash is a different substance from paper, and the change cannot be undone, which makes it chemical.

options.text: It is physical because fire only makes things smaller, like cutting or tearing.
options.outcome: Burning is not cutting — it rearranges the paper's substance into gases and ash; no amount of reassembling gives back paper.

c6_civics_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch10.scenario: A parent tells a child, 'I give you the right to go to school — so behave and I won't take it back.' Down the street, a shopkeeper refuses to sell milk to a family because of their religion, saying, 'My shop, my rules.'
c6_civics_ch10.prompt: What is wrong with both statements?

options.text: Rights are not gifts — the child's schooling is a right she holds simply by being a person, so a parent cannot 'grant' or withdraw it. And the shopkeeper breaks the right to equality: refusing a customer on grounds of religion is discrimination, and owning the shop does not exempt him from it.
options.outcome: Rights are inherent — they belong to everyone equally and no private person may hand them out or take them away; that is what separates a right from a favour.

options.text: The parent is right — rights are permissions given by whoever is in charge, at home or in a shop.
options.outcome: A permission can be granted and withdrawn by the granter; a right belongs to the person herself, which is why it cannot be gifted or revoked.

options.text: The shopkeeper is within his rights — private property owners may choose customers however they like.
options.outcome: Running a shop does not suspend equality — refusing service purely on religion is exactly the discrimination the right against discrimination forbids.

c6_civics_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch11.scenario: At a family dinner, an uncle grumbles: 'Why must I pay tax for the city bus and the government school? I use neither — tax should be optional for people who don't use the service.'
c6_civics_ch11.prompt: Why do governments in a democracy get to collect taxes even from people who object?

options.text: Because shared services can only exist if everyone contributes — no one person could fund a road network, a water supply or schools alone, and the system works only if paying in does not depend on personally using each service. In a democracy the law obliges everyone precisely because the government that makes it was chosen by the people themselves.
options.outcome: Government's coercive power is legitimate here because it funds public goods and is answerable to voters — taxes are the membership fee of a shared system, not a shop bill.

options.text: The uncle is right — taxes are like purchases, so people should pay only for the services they personally use.
options.outcome: Public services are not private purchases — clean water, roads and schools exist only because everyone funds the common pool whether or not they use each part.

options.text: He has a point that taxes are unfair — but at least the services would survive if only willing people paid.
options.outcome: Voluntary payment collapses public services — too few would pay, and prices for the rest would soar; that is why the law makes contribution universal.

c6_civics_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch12.scenario: A village full of children has no playground. At the weekly meeting, one elder suggests writing a petition to the state government in the distant capital, 'since real power sits up there.'
c6_civics_ch12.prompt: Is the state capital the right address for this problem?

options.text: No — this is exactly what the Gram Panchayat is for. A local body knows the village's children, the available land and the budget needed, and can act quickly because the decision sits with the people affected. The three-tier system deliberately keeps village-sized problems in the village, reserving bigger issues for higher levels.
options.outcome: Local problems are solved best locally — a playground needs no state machinery, only the village institution designed to handle exactly such community needs.

options.text: The elder is right — only the state government has real authority, so every decision should travel up to the capital.
options.outcome: That would bury a small local fix in distant bureaucracy — grassroots democracy exists precisely so villages decide their own everyday matters.

options.text: Neither should act — a playground is a private want, and government at any level has no role in children's recreation.
options.outcome: Common village needs like play spaces, water and paths are exactly what local self-government exists to provide — a playground is a public good, not a private luxury.

c6_civics_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch13.scenario: A city council has a fixed sum of money and two urgent demands — repairing a crumbling park and cleaning a blocked drain. One councillor says, 'Just do a bit of both and announce everything is funded.'
c6_civics_ch13.prompt: How does a budget change this conversation?

options.text: A budget forces the council to put income and expenses on paper, match them, and choose openly what to fund first — you cannot promise both if the money covers only one. It turns a vague argument into a stated priority that citizens can see and question.
options.outcome: That is the budget's job: it makes trade-offs explicit and public, so the choice between park and drain is argued with numbers instead of promised away with words.

options.text: The councillor's approach works — a government can spend on everything and sort out the money later.
options.outcome: Spending beyond income creates a deficit — money must come from borrowing or new taxes, so 'do a bit of both' just hides a bill rather than paying it.

options.text: A budget is just an accounts formality — the real decision is made the same way whether or not one is published.
options.outcome: Publishing the budget is what lets citizens see and challenge the priorities — without it, choices are made in the dark.

c6_civics_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch14.scenario: On the class video call with a partner school abroad, a classmate is embarrassed: 'India has so many languages and foods and festivals — honestly, are we even one country?'
c6_civics_ch14.prompt: How would you answer her using the idea of unity in diversity?

options.text: One country does not mean one culture — India's diversity is held together by shared things: harvest festivals celebrated under different names across regions, stories like the Panchatantra that travelled every language, one constitution and common institutions. Many voices, one conversation — the variety is the unity, not a crack in it.
options.outcome: Unity in diversity means the bond is shared life — festivals, stories, institutions and citizenship — not sameness of language or custom.

options.text: She is right — a real country needs everyone to speak one language and follow one custom.
options.outcome: That confuses uniformity with unity — India is one nation precisely through its many languages and traditions being woven into shared institutions and festivals.

options.text: India is actually many separate countries that only share a border on the map.
options.outcome: Shared citizenship, one constitution, common markets and festivals celebrated across states make it one nation — a map line is the least of what holds it together.

c6_civics_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch15.scenario: The municipal council quietly approves a highway that will cut through the city's oldest public park. Most residents don't know yet. A young reporter at the local paper gets hold of the plan.
c6_civics_ch15.prompt: What can the newspaper actually do here?

options.text: Inform the public before the decision is final — once residents read about the plan they can protest, question their councillors and demand hearings. The media acts as democracy's watchdog: it carries information from the government to the people, and public pressure back to the government, which is exactly why it is called a pillar alongside the courts.
options.outcome: Without the report, the highway would be discovered only when the trees fell — media turns a closed decision into a public debate while change is still possible.

options.text: Nothing much — newspapers only report events after they happen, so the park is already lost.
options.outcome: Reporting plans before execution is precisely the watchdog role — early information is what lets citizens intervene rather than merely grieve.

options.text: The paper should stay out of it — reporting a government plan would be interfering in governance.
options.outcome: Informing citizens about public decisions is the media's democratic function, not interference — a government answerable to people needs the people to know.

c6_civics_ch16.title: Use it in the wild
c6_civics_ch16.scenario: A student spends a weekend building a bookshelf for his own room. The next weekend he builds an identical one for a neighbour, who pays him for the work. He asks, 'Same effort both times — so both were economic activity, right?'
c6_civics_ch16.prompt: Which of the two weekends counts as an economic activity?

options.text: Only the paid one — economic activity is work done for payment or income. The identical labour becomes 'economic' the moment money changes hands; building his own shelf stays a non-economic activity, though it is still real, valuable work — just like volunteering, which society values even without a price tag.
options.outcome: The dividing line is payment, not effort — the same hands doing the same work cross from non-economic to economic depending on whether it earns.

options.text: He is right — identical effort means identical classification, so both weekends were economic activity.
options.outcome: Effort does not decide the category — payment does; unpaid work for oneself is non-economic even when it is hard, skilled work.

options.text: Neither weekend counts — building furniture only counts as economic work if done in a factory.
options.outcome: Location does not matter — a paid bookshelf built at home is economic activity just as much as factory carpentry.

c6_economics_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c6_economics_ch07.scenario: A hill village grows superb apples, but half the harvest rots before reaching city markets. The farmers ask the government for 'development' — and what arrives is not money, but a proper road and a cold-storage point.
c6_economics_ch07.prompt: Why are a road and a cold store 'development' for the village?

options.text: Because they are infrastructure — the supporting system that lets every economic activity work. The road connects the orchard to distant markets before the fruit spoils; the cold store holds produce until prices are right. Like a factory that cannot run without power and water, farming cannot reach its value without the invisible framework beneath it.
options.outcome: Infrastructure multiplies what producers already do — the same apples now reach buyers in Delhi, which no amount of extra farming effort alone could achieve.

options.text: The farmers were shortchanged — real development aid would have been cash, not concrete and wires.
options.outcome: Cash is spent once; a road keeps paying every season by connecting the village's produce to markets — infrastructure is the durable kind of help.

options.text: A road helps only drivers — for farmers, 'development' would mean new seeds and fertiliser.
options.outcome: Better seeds raise yield, but without transport the extra apples rot in the same village — infrastructure is what converts production into income.

c6_economics_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c6_economics_ch08.scenario: A villager keeps his savings in a tin box under the bed 'where no bank can touch it.' Meanwhile, a neighbour needs exactly that amount for a sewing machine but cannot find anyone to lend it.
c6_economics_ch08.prompt: What does the bank do that the tin box cannot?

options.text: It connects the saver to the borrower — deposits from people with spare money become loans for people who need it, so the saver earns interest and the neighbour gets her sewing machine. Money under a bed funds nothing; the same sum in a bank quietly finances someone's livelihood while staying safer than any tin box.
options.outcome: The bank's 'magic' is intermediation — idle savings are recycled into working capital, which is why a village that banks its money can grow businesses.

options.text: The tin box is wiser — money you can see is safer than money in an institution.
options.outcome: A box can be stolen, lost or eaten by inflation, and it earns nothing — a bank both safeguards the deposit and puts it to work for someone else.

options.text: The bank's only real job is storing money — lending to neighbours is a separate business altogether.
options.outcome: Lending deposits out is the core of banking — a bank is not a locker; the pool of savings is exactly what loans are made from.

c6_economics_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c6_economics_ch11.scenario: At a village barter fair, a cobbler wants bread, but the farmer who has bread wants cloth, and the weaver who has cloth wants shoes. They circle each other all morning and nobody trades. 'We're just unlucky today,' the cobbler sighs.
c6_economics_ch11.prompt: Was it bad luck, and how would money fix it?

options.text: It was not luck but the double coincidence of wants — barter needs each partner to want exactly what the other offers, and their three-way mismatch makes that nearly impossible. Money fixes it because everyone accepts it: the cobbler sells shoes for money, then buys bread with it — no need to find a farmer who happens to want shoes.
options.outcome: One universally accepted item splits an impossible matching puzzle into two simple trades — which is why growing villages moved from barter to money.

options.text: It was just a bad day — barter always works eventually if people keep asking around.
options.outcome: Searching harder does not remove the mismatch — the bigger the village, the worse the coincidence problem; money removes the need for matching altogether.

options.text: The fix is to barter bigger items — valuable goods like a bicycle trade easily for anything.
options.outcome: Value does not help if the other person does not want that item — a bicycle cannot buy a phone unless the phone-owner happens to want a bicycle.

c6_economics_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c6_economics_ch12.scenario: A student orders a textbook online from a seller in another city. Her grandfather snorts: 'Ordering on a screen isn't a market — a market is a place with stalls and shouting, like our weekly haat.'
c6_economics_ch12.prompt: Who is right about what a market is?

options.text: The student — a market is any arrangement where buyers and sellers exchange goods for money; a physical place is optional. The online order has both parties, a good and a price, so it is as much a market as the haat. The real test is the exchange — a shop standing empty with no buyers for a month is a building, not a functioning market.
options.outcome: The haat and the app share the same essence — a buyer, a seller and a price agreed between them; the weekly gathering and the website are just two shapes of the same thing.

options.text: Grandfather is right — if there is no physical place where people gather, it cannot be a market.
options.outcome: Markets are defined by exchange, not geography — buyers and sellers who never meet still complete a market transaction.

options.text: Neither is fully right — only shops open daily count; both the haat and the app are something else.
options.outcome: Frequency is irrelevant — a weekly haat and an online order are both markets because both are exchanges; 'every day' is not in the definition.

c6_english_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c6_english_ch01.scenario: A student is writing a story about a girl who finally decides to ask to go to school. Her draft just says 'then she decided.' Her teacher suggests she look at how the river in Jahnavi's story marked the turning point without naming it.
c6_english_ch01.prompt: How can a writer show a turning point instead of announcing it?

options.text: Let the setting carry the moment — in the story, the river seems to speak to Jahnavi exactly when she is poised between staying and daring, so the place itself voices her inner turn. The student can do the same: have something in the scene — a road stretching past the house, a school bell carrying over fields — 'answer' the girl at the instant her decision forms.
options.outcome: Setting does more than decorate a story: a living detail of place can mirror and mark the character's inner change, making the turning point felt rather than stated.

options.text: She should simply write 'this was the turning point' — clarity is always better than hints.
options.outcome: Announcing it flattens the moment — the river works because readers feel Jahnavi's decision through the scene instead of being told about it.

options.text: The setting is irrelevant — turning points belong inside the character's head, so the background should be ignored.
options.outcome: The story uses the riverbank deliberately — the turning point is written through the setting, and a writer who ignores the scene loses that tool.

c6_english_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c6_english_ch02.scenario: The class comedy team is writing a sketch about animals discussing a human patient. Their first draft just makes the animals trip over furniture and fall down. 'It's not landing,' the director admits.
c6_english_ch02.prompt: What actually makes the Dr. Dolittle scenes funny, and how can the team copy that?

options.text: The humour is a role reversal — animals speak with calm, human-like insight while the humans are the confused ones; the parrot Polynesia even teaches the doctor his gift, so the 'wise' figure is a bird. The sketch should let the animals observe the human's strange habits shrewdly — comedy from flipped roles, not from clumsy falls.
options.outcome: Wit in the chapter comes from intelligence placed where nobody expects it — the joke is that animals understand humans better than humans understand animals.

options.text: The sketch just needs more slapstick — humour means characters looking foolish, so the animals should fall over more.
options.outcome: Falling over is noise without wit — the chapter's humour lives in clever reversal and surprising wisdom, not in making anyone look stupid.

options.text: Animals cannot be the source of wit — the sketch should give the clever lines back to a human character.
options.outcome: That reverses the reversal — Polynesia the parrot is the story's source of success precisely because the unexpected character holds the knowledge.

c6_english_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c6_english_ch03.scenario: A student is writing her own 'crazy inventor' story for the school magazine. She plans to save the invention's disastrous failure for the very last line, 'to surprise the reader.'
c6_english_ch03.prompt: What does Anand's story suggest about where a comic disaster should go?

options.text: Early — the story soaks the father first, establishing a pattern: Anand's inventions always backfire, and each new scheme repeats the comedy. Showing the disaster early turns it into the story's engine — every later invention is funnier because readers already know how it will end. Saving one failure for the end would just be a surprise, not a pattern.
options.outcome: Comic sequence is the craft here — an early failure sets the rule of the world (inventions fail), and the reader's anticipation of the next flop is what drives the humour.

options.text: Her plan is right — a disaster works best as a final shock, so it should stay at the end.
options.outcome: A last-line failure is a twist, not a pattern — the story's comedy comes from watching failure repeat, which requires the first failure to happen early.

options.text: She should cut the failure entirely — a perfect successful machine would make a stronger ending.
options.outcome: A perfect machine would break the story's whole comic purpose — the fun is that the inventions never work, and the pattern of flops is the plot.

c6_english_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_english_ch04.scenario: A student is writing a suspense scene about a boy who must cross into unknown territory. She sets it in a busy, noisy market 'because lots is happening there.' A friend suggests a narrow, dark tunnel instead.
c6_english_ch04.prompt: Why does the tunnel make a stronger setting for this kind of scene?

options.text: Because the danger is concentrated in the unknown — a tunnel is dark, enclosed and hides what lies ahead, so the tracks 'disappearing into' it create dread before anything even happens. A crowded market spreads attention thin; danger there must come from people or events, while the tunnel itself is the threat.
options.outcome: The chapter shows setting building suspense — confinement and invisibility of what's ahead make the reader lean forward, which scattered marketplace bustle cannot do.

options.text: Setting does not matter much — a scary plot is scary in any place, so the market is fine.
options.outcome: Place shapes the fear — the tunnel works because darkness and enclosure do half the storytelling; the same plot in a loud crowd loses that built-in menace.

options.text: The market is actually scarier — more people means more danger, always.
options.outcome: Crowds bring distraction, not necessarily dread — the tunnel's power is that the character cannot see what is coming, and uncertainty frightens more than noise.

c6_english_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_english_ch05.scenario: After visiting a war memorial on a school trip, a student must write about it twice — once for the noticeboard report and once as a letter to her grandmother. She asks whether she can submit the same paragraph for both.
c6_english_ch05.prompt: What should change between the report and the letter?

options.text: Everything in the voice — the report states facts ('the memorial was built in 2019'), while the letter carries her personal experience ('I felt like I was travelling back in time'). The letter form exists to hold feeling: it is how the writer turns names on a wall into a personal act of homage, which is why the chapter uses letters to honour the soldiers.
options.outcome: Format is meaning here — the intimate letter lets respect and grief be spoken directly, while the report's distance would make the homage sound like statistics.

options.text: The same paragraph works for both — writing is writing, and the facts matter more than the format.
options.outcome: The two forms do different work — a report informs, a letter connects; 'I felt moved' belongs in the letter, and 'it was built in 2019' belongs in the report.

options.text: The letter should be more formal than the report, since it is addressed to an elder.
options.outcome: Addressing an elder does not freeze the voice — the letter's warmth is the point; it lets her speak to her grandmother about what the visit felt like.

c6_geography_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c6_geography_ch01.scenario: A cousin visiting from abroad wants to see snow AND a desert on the same India trip, and laughs when told both are possible. 'One country can't have everything,' she says.
c6_geography_ch01.prompt: Can one trip really include snow and desert?

options.text: Yes — India's sheer size packs many worlds into one country: the Himalayas in the north hold snow, the Thar in the west holds desert, and coasts, plateaus and rainy forests lie between them. That range is exactly why 'diversity' is the right word for India's geography — and it exists because the country is huge.
options.outcome: Shrink India to a small island and most of that variety would vanish — it is the vastness that lets snow, sand dunes and sea beaches share one flag.

options.text: She is right — a single country has a single landscape, so snow and desert cannot both be in India.
options.outcome: Countries are not uniform — a large one can span mountains, deserts and coasts; India is the textbook example.

options.text: Both exist but only barely — the snow is on a few peaks and the desert is just a sandy patch.
options.outcome: These are full regions, not curiosities — the Thar is a vast desert and the Himalayan snow fields stretch for thousands of kilometres.

c6_geography_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c6_geography_ch02.scenario: A city gets an unusually cold day in the middle of summer. Two students argue: 'See, the climate has changed!' versus 'That's just today being weird.' Meanwhile a farmer nearby decides whether to plant rice based on last night's rain.

options.text: The second student — weather is what happens today or this week, while climate is the pattern built over about thirty years, so one cold day cannot change a climate. And the farmer should not plant on yesterday's rain — crops must match the region's long-term climate, not one evening's shower.
options.outcome: The words are not interchangeable: windy today is weather, windy every monsoon for decades is climate — decisions about crops and houses follow the second.

options.text: The first student is right — any unusual day is proof the climate has shifted.
options.outcome: Climate is an average over decades — a single odd day is weather noise, not a climate signal.

options.text: The farmer is right to plant on last night's rain — rain is rain, whenever it comes.
options.outcome: Planting must follow the season's expected pattern — a stray shower today says nothing about whether the rains will last.

c6_geography_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c6_geography_ch03.scenario: A family argues over a holiday: hill station or beach city. Dad insists the beach city must be cooler 'because sea breeze,' while the daughter claims the hills will be cooler even though they are far from the sea.
c6_geography_ch03.prompt: Who is closer to right, and why?

options.text: The daughter — altitude cools the air, so a hill station is usually cooler than a low coastal city even though the sea is far away. But Dad's sea logic has truth in it: coastal places stay mild with small swings between day and season, while inland cities swing between very hot days and cold ones — the sea moderates rather than simply chills.
options.outcome: Two climate rules are at play: height lowers temperature, and the sea softens extremes — hill stations win on coolness, coastal cities on evenness.

options.text: Dad is right — anything near the sea is always colder than anywhere inland.
options.outcome: The sea moderates swings but does not make coasts the coldest — a high hill station far inland beats a beach city on coolness.

options.text: Neither — distance from the sea and height do not affect temperature, only the season does.
options.outcome: Season matters, but geography rewrites it — altitude and the sea's moderating pull are exactly why Ooty and Chennai feel so different in the same month.

c6_geography_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_geography_ch04.scenario: In a history strategy game, a player must place a farming village on the map. The options: dry upland, dense forest, or a riverbank. 'Any flat spot works,' the player shrugs, and picks the upland.
c6_geography_ch04.prompt: What did early farmers actually look for, and why?

options.text: The riverbank — farming needs reliable water and fertile soil, and rivers supply both: they water crops and renew the floodplain's soil every year. A well-placed field grows more than the village eats, and that surplus is what later lets some people stop farming and become potters, weavers and rulers — the seed of a city.
options.outcome: The first farming villages clustered along rivers for exactly this reason — water and fertile flood soil came first, and surplus food came from them.

options.text: The player is right — any flat land can grow crops, so location is a detail.
options.outcome: Flatness is not fertility — dry upland starves crops without irrigation, and the river's yearly silt is what kept early fields productive.

options.text: The forest was the best pick — trees provide all the food a village needs.
options.outcome: Wild food feeds foragers, not farmers — a farming village needs cleared, watered, fertile land, which the riverbank offers and dense forest does not.

c6_geography_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_geography_ch05.scenario: In a map quiz, a student lists India's neighbours and is corrected for including Sri Lanka and the Maldives. 'They don't share a land border,' his teammate insists, 'so they aren't neighbours.'
c6_geography_ch05.prompt: Do island nations count as neighbours?

options.text: Yes — a neighbour is any country lying close, whether across land or across water. A ship sailing south from Kochi reaches an island nation directly, so Sri Lanka and the Maldives are India's neighbours just as the land-border countries are; the sea is a connection, not a wall.
options.outcome: India's neighbourhood has two kinds — countries sharing land borders and island nations across the sea — and both count on the map and in trade.

options.text: The teammate is right — neighbours are defined by shared land borders, so islands are out.
options.outcome: Borders across water are still borders — a short sea crossing makes countries neighbours, which is why Sri Lanka sits on India's neighbour list.

options.text: Only the biggest nearby countries count — small island nations are too minor to be called neighbours.
options.outcome: Size does not decide neighbourship — proximity does, and the Maldives is close enough to reach by sea.

c6_history_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch04.scenario: In a classroom simulation, a team runs a village that produces exactly as much grain as it eats. 'Let's grow into a city,' they decide, 'we'll just build bigger houses.'
c6_history_ch04.prompt: What is missing before any village can become a city?

options.text: A food surplus — a city means people who do not farm: potters, tool-makers, builders, rulers. They can exist only if farmers grow more than the farmers themselves need. A village producing exactly its own needs has nothing to feed specialists with — no surplus, no city, however big the houses get.
options.outcome: This is why the first cities grew on fertile river land — extra grain freed part of the population for crafts, trade and government.

options.text: The team is right — a city is just a village with bigger buildings and more people.
options.outcome: More people still need feeding — without surplus food, a bigger settlement just means more hungry mouths, not a city.

options.text: What is missing is walls — early settlements became cities the moment they built walls around themselves.
options.outcome: Walls are a feature, not the cause — the food surplus that pays for wall-builders has to come first.

c6_history_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch05.scenario: In a debate on how empires grow, one side declares: 'Empires are built by war, period — kings win territory or they don't.' The other side has just read about Chandragupta's empire and the small kingdoms around it.
c6_history_ch05.prompt: What does the Mauryan story say about how empires actually grow?

options.text: By war and diplomacy together — Chandragupta conquered some kingdoms but others joined through alliances, and a small kingdom often preferred joining willingly for protection over being crushed in battle. The empire covered most of the subcontinent because smaller states were absorbed by both force and negotiation — and even that needed a strategist like Chanakya, not just soldiers.
options.outcome: Empires were assembled through mixed tools — battles, treaties, advisors and voluntary unions — which is also why 'a great leader' is really a great team.

options.text: The first side is right — territory only changes hands through conquest, so alliances are just decoration.
options.outcome: Alliances moved borders too — kingdoms that joined willingly became part of the empire without a single battle.

options.text: Neither — empires grew mainly by trade, with armies and diplomacy playing only minor roles.
options.outcome: Trade enriched kingdoms but did not annex them — conquest and alliance did the absorbing, and trade followed the flag.

c6_history_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch06.scenario: A student cataloguing a museum coin argues with the curator. The coin is dated around 1000 CE, and the student wants a verdict: 'Ancient or medieval — pick one. There must be an exact year the ancient period ended.'
c6_history_ch06.prompt: Is there a precise border between the ancient and medieval periods?

options.text: No — the labels are rough shelves historians built after the fact, not real walls. Change happened gradually: ancient empires faded and new regional kingdoms, languages and building styles grew over centuries. The coin can be called early-medieval because of its era's features, but nobody woke up one January morning in a 'new period.'
options.outcome: Periods are tools for organising slow change — what makes an artifact 'medieval' is the world around it, not a date ticking over.

options.text: The student is right — historians must have fixed an exact day when ancient ended and medieval began.
options.outcome: No such day exists — period boundaries mark gradual transitions; pretending 700 CE flipped a switch misreads how history changes.

options.text: The coin is unclassifiable — without an exact boundary, no artifact can ever be assigned a period.
options.outcome: Approximate labels still work — 'medieval' usefully describes the era of regional kingdoms even though its edges are fuzzy.

c6_history_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch07.scenario: Making a timeline of Delhi's rulers for a school exhibition, a student marks the year 1206 with a big star. His partner asks, 'Why that year — kings came and went all the time, so why is this one a turning point?'

options.text: It is when the Delhi Sultanate began — Qutbuddin Aibak, who had served as a general under Muhammad of Ghur, took the throne and started a new ruling line based in Delhi that would last about three centuries and five dynasties. A 'turning point' marks the birth of a new order, not just a new king — and a historian would look for evidence like new coinage and inscriptions in the new dynasty's name.
options.outcome: The star marks a change in who ruled and how — a fresh dynasty with its own capital and institutions, not just another name on a list.

options.text: The partner is right — 1206 was just another succession, and calling it a turning point is exaggeration.
options.outcome: It began a durable new political order — the Sultanate reshaped northern India for centuries, which is what separates a turning point from a routine handover.

options.text: The year only matters because Delhi got a new ruler — any new king would deserve the same star.
options.outcome: New kings were routine; what made 1206 different was that a new dynasty and form of rule began, which is the kind of change worth marking.

c6_history_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch08.scenario: On a family trip to Hampi, a child kicks at the broken stones and asks why anyone flies across the country to look at 'a pile of ruins' when the empire is long gone.
c6_history_ch08.prompt: What do ruins like Hampi's actually give historians?

options.text: Evidence books cannot — the layout, temples, tanks and bazaars of the ruined city let historians reconstruct the empire's size, wealth, planning and daily life. When texts are lost or silent, stones speak: Hampi's remains are how we know the 'City of Victory' — a name reflecting its founders' ambitions — was real and grand.
options.outcome: A ruin is a primary source in stone — it tells us what was built, how people lived and what the kingdom valued, long after the writers are gone.

options.text: The child is right — once an empire ends, its ruins are just old rocks with nothing to say.
options.outcome: Ruins are evidence, not rubble — archaeologists read city plans, water systems and art from them that no chronicle preserved.

options.text: Hampi matters only because it is pretty — historians study it for the architecture's beauty, not its history.
options.outcome: Beauty is a bonus — historians read the ruins for information about the empire's scale, economy and life, not for decoration.

c6_history_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch09.scenario: At a museum, a sword labelled 'Panipat, 1526' sits in a glass case. A student reads the card and protests: 'Babur was a foreigner who invaded — how did an outsider end up founding an Indian empire?'
c6_history_ch09.prompt: How can a conqueror from outside found a genuinely Indian empire?

options.text: Because the dynasty he founded made India its home — Babur arrived from Central Asia and won at Panipat in 1526, but his successors ruled from India, built its cities, collected its taxes and patronised its culture for centuries. The empire was foreign in its founder's origin and Indian in where it lived, ruled and was remembered — both things are true at once.
options.outcome: 1526 is a turning point precisely because an outsider's victory began a dynasty that became part of India's own history — origin and identity are not the same thing.

options.text: The student's doubt stands — an empire founded by an invader can never be called Indian.
options.outcome: Dynasties take on the character of where they rule — the Mughals governed India, shaped its art and administration, and are studied as an Indian empire.

options.text: Babur was not really an outsider — the Mughals had always ruled in India before 1526.
options.outcome: Babur came from beyond India and won his empire by conquest — that is exactly why calling the empire he founded 'Indian' is the interesting fact.

c6_history_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch10.scenario: A class timeline project on Europeans in India hits an argument: 'All the Europeans arrived at once and immediately started ruling.' A student who has read about trading 'factories' at Surat disagrees.
c6_history_ch10.prompt: What does the timeline of arrivals and 'factories' actually show?

options.text: That rule came slowly and trade came first — the Portuguese reached India in 1498 by sea, and the English came later, building trading posts called factories at ports like Surat. A factory's founding date marks when a European company got a foothold to trade — decades before any of them ruled territory. Conquest was the last chapter of a story that began with commerce.
options.outcome: Reading the dates in order dissolves the myth: arrivals were staggered over a century, and each power spent generations as a trader before it became a ruler.

options.text: The first claim is right — European powers arrived together and began governing immediately.
options.outcome: The timeline contradicts it — arrivals were decades apart, and trading posts preceded political control by generations.

options.text: A 'factory' was a manufacturing plant, so the English industrialised India before ruling it.
options.outcome: These factories were trading warehouses, not mills — the word marks a commercial base, which is why their dates track trade, not industry.

c6_history_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch11.scenario: A student argues in class: 'The British built railways and spread English only to help themselves — so it's absurd to say those things helped the freedom movement.'
c6_history_ch11.prompt: Can something built for colonial profit still feed nationalism?

options.text: Yes — whatever the motive, trains let Indians from distant regions travel, meet and organise, and English gave them a shared language to exchange grievances. A merchant in Madras and a farmer in Bengal could discover they faced the same unfairness precisely because these tools connected them — an unintended 'positive' cause of nationalism alongside the 'negative' ones like heavy taxes.
options.outcome: The nationalist movement needed both the shared complaint and the means to share it — colonial networks of travel and language accidentally supplied the second.

options.text: The student is right — since the intent was selfish, the effects could only ever harm Indians.
options.outcome: Intent and effect are different — the railways and English were built for empire but ended up binding Indians together into a national conversation.

options.text: Railways helped only by carrying troops — they had no role in spreading nationalist ideas at all.
options.outcome: They carried ideas too — delegates, newspapers and speakers moved on those trains, turning scattered resentment into a coordinated movement.

c6_history_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c6_history_ch12.scenario: A student asks a fair question: 'The British ruled us for two centuries — why didn't they just leave us a ready-made constitution instead of us spending years writing one?'
c6_history_ch12.prompt: Why did independent India have to write its own Constitution?

options.text: Because a constitution is a nation's own rulebook — it had to express what Indians chose for themselves: equality, rights, self-government. So an elected Constituent Assembly debated and drafted it, with members from different regions and communities; a document written by departing colonisers could never carry that legitimacy, and an assembly missing women or whole regions would have produced a rulebook that didn't speak for everyone.
options.outcome: The years of debate were the point — a constitution is legitimate because the people's representatives argued it into existence, not because it arrived quickly.

options.text: A ready-made constitution would have been better — any complete rulebook works, and writing one wasted years.
options.outcome: Rules imposed by a departing power carry no consent — the Constituent Assembly's long debates are what made the document belong to Indians.

options.text: India wrote one only because other nations did — the content hardly mattered as long as a document existed.
options.outcome: It was not imitation — the Assembly chose specific rights and structures for India's own needs, which is why the drafting took years of real argument.

c6_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch01.scenario: At the stationery shop, a student holds a ₹200 note and wants 4 pens at ₹15 each plus 2 notebooks at ₹30 each. The queue behind is growing and the shopkeeper is waiting.
c6_math_ch01.prompt: How can she quickly know whether ₹200 is enough?

options.text: Estimate — 4 pens cost about 4 × 15 = ₹60 and the notebooks about 2 × 30 = ₹60, so roughly ₹120, comfortably inside ₹200. Estimation is not guessing: it is a quick, close-enough calculation that answers the actual question — 'can I afford this' — without needing the exact figure.
options.outcome: Mental rounding gives the answer in seconds, and ₹120 versus ₹200 leaves no doubt — the right tool for a decision that needs a fast approximate answer.

options.text: She cannot know until the shopkeeper computes the exact total — estimation is just guessing.
options.outcome: Estimation is structured arithmetic with rounded numbers, not a guess — 4 × 15 and 2 × 30 are already easy, and the rough total settles the question.

options.text: She should just hand over the ₹200 and trust the change will be roughly right.
options.outcome: Skipping the estimate means she cannot catch a billing error — the quick mental total is exactly what protects her change.

c6_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch02.scenario: A cold-storage display shows the temperature falling below zero, and a student compares two accounts: one is ₹200 in debt, the other ₹100 in debt. He claims, 'minus 200 is bigger than minus 100, since 200 beats 100.'

options.text: No — on the number line, more negative means further left, which means smaller: -200 sits far below -100, so -200 is the smaller number and the bigger debt. The sign reverses the comparison: with negatives, the larger-looking number is actually worth less.
options.outcome: Distance from zero still tells size — -200 is 200 below zero while -100 is only 100 below, so the first position is lower on the line.

options.text: He is right — 200 is bigger than 100, and the minus sign does not change the comparison.
options.outcome: The minus changes everything — it measures debt or depth below zero, so -200 is lower than -100 on the number line, not higher.

options.text: Neither is bigger — negative numbers cannot be compared at all.
options.outcome: They compare perfectly well on the number line — the one further left of zero is smaller, so -200 < -100.

c6_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch03.scenario: Two friends split a chocolate bar. One offers a trade: 'Give me your half — I'll give you two of my four pieces. Two is more than one, so you win!'
c6_math_ch03.prompt: Is the trade actually a good deal?

options.text: No — 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount cut differently: two quarter-pieces exactly equal one half. Counting pieces without looking at piece size is the trap; drawing the bar shows both offers cover the identical area of chocolate.
options.outcome: Equivalent fractions look different but weigh the same — the number of pieces means nothing until you know how big each piece is.

options.text: Yes — two pieces is always more than one piece, so the trade is a win.
options.outcome: More pieces only means finer cutting — four quarters make one whole just as two halves do, so 2/4 = 1/2 and nobody wins.

options.text: No — halves are always bigger than quarters, so 1/2 must be worth more than 2/4.
options.outcome: Halves are bigger pieces but there are only two of them — one half and two quarters cover the same chocolate exactly.

c6_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch04.scenario: Two bottles sit on the table — one holds 0.5 litres, the other 0.45 litres. A little brother grabs the second bottle saying, '45 is bigger than 5, so this one holds more.'

options.text: The 0.5 litre bottle — decimals are not whole numbers, and place value settles it: 0.5 is 0.50, which is more than 0.45. The digit after the point is tenths, the next is hundredths, so comparing '5 versus 45' mixes up the places and flips the answer.
options.outcome: Writing both to the same number of places — 0.50 versus 0.45 — makes the comparison as easy as 50 versus 45.

options.text: The brother is right — 45 beats 5, so 0.45 litres is more.
options.outcome: The digits after the point are tenths and hundredths, not whole numbers — 0.45 is forty-five hundredths while 0.5 is fifty hundredths.

options.text: The bottles hold the same amount, since both numbers start with zero point something.
options.outcome: The leading zero only says 'less than one' — the tenths digit decides the size, and 0.5 beats 0.45.

c6_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch05.scenario: A milkman charges ₹40 per litre plus a fixed ₹15 delivery fee per order. A student writes the cost formula as '55 × L' — forty plus fifteen, times the litres. Her mother spots the mistake on the bill.
c6_math_ch05.prompt: What is the right expression for the cost of L litres?

options.text: 40 × L + 15 — the ₹40 multiplies with every litre because it repeats per litre, while the ₹15 is charged once per order no matter how many litres. Lumping them into 55 × L wrongly charges the delivery fee again for every litre; keeping the constant separate is exactly what the expression is for.
options.outcome: Variables and constants behave differently — L can change order to order, the per-litre rate multiplies it, and the flat fee just sits at the end.

options.text: The student's 55 × L is right — all the charges combine into one rate per litre.
options.outcome: That bills the ₹15 fee once per litre — a 3-litre order would wrongly include three delivery fees.

options.text: The cost cannot be written as an expression at all, since the litres keep changing.
options.outcome: Changing quantity is exactly why a letter is used — L stands for whatever the order is, and the formula works for every order.

c6_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch06.scenario: A juice recipe mixes 500 ml of water with 200 ml of concentrate. Making a bigger batch, a cousin pours 1.5 litres of water but says 'a big batch needs a different ratio, so I'll just add a whole extra bottle of concentrate.'
c6_math_ch06.prompt: Will the bigger batch taste the same?

options.text: Only if the ratio is preserved — 500:200 simplifies to 5:2, and 1500:600 simplifies to the same 5:2, so the larger pitcher needs 600 ml of concentrate, not a random 'extra bottle.' Taste lives in the proportion: multiply both parts by the same number and the flavour survives; change one part alone and it does not.
options.outcome: Equal ratios are what 'the same taste' means mathematically — scaling both quantities by three keeps the drink identical, just more of it.

options.text: The cousin is right — a bigger batch needs a new, stronger ratio to taste the same.
options.outcome: Same taste means same ratio — adding extra concentrate without matching the water makes the batch stronger, not identical.

options.text: Any amount of concentrate works since it is just flavouring — the water quantity decides the taste.
options.outcome: The ratio of the two parts IS the taste — too little concentrate makes it watery, too much makes it overpowering.

c6_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch07.scenario: A student planning a toy-car track wants the shortest route from point A to point B. She also writes in her notebook: 'A line is just a very long line segment.'
c6_math_ch07.prompt: What should the path be — and is her definition right?

options.text: The shortest route is the line segment AB — straight between two endpoints. And the definition is wrong: a segment ends at both ends, while a line runs forever in both directions with no endpoints at all. No amount of length turns a segment into a line — the difference is in the endpoints, not the length.
options.outcome: Naming matters in geometry: ray, line and segment are different objects, and the endpoint count — not size — is what separates them.

options.text: She is right on both — any path works for the car, and a long enough segment becomes a line.
options.outcome: Only the straight segment is shortest, and no finite segment can become a line — a line has no endpoints by definition.

options.text: The shortest route is a curve, because curves can bend around and reach faster.
options.outcome: Any bend adds length — the straight segment between two points is always the shortest path.

c6_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch08.scenario: Two students each get 12 equal sticks. One lays out a square; the other lays out a long, flat rectangle. 'My shape is longer,' says the second, 'so my perimeter must be bigger.'
c6_math_ch08.prompt: Which shape really has the bigger perimeter?

options.text: Neither — both use the same 12 sticks, so both perimeters total the same length. Perimeter is just the total boundary, and reshaping the same material cannot stretch it. What actually changed is the area: the square encloses more space than the flat rectangle, even though the fences match.
options.outcome: Perimeter tracks the edge's length, not the shape's look — the same sticks always make the same perimeter, while the area inside can differ a lot.

options.text: The rectangle has the bigger perimeter — a longer shape always has a longer boundary.
options.outcome: Looking longer is not being longer — both boundaries are built from the same 12 sticks, so both perimeters are equal.

options.text: The square has the bigger perimeter — a balanced shape always has more edge.
options.outcome: Balance affects area, not perimeter — equal sticks mean equal boundaries either way.

c6_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch09.scenario: A student runs a favourite-colour survey of 20 classmates and proudly shows her table: 10 chose red, 8 chose blue. Her teacher frowns: 'Your table says 18. You surveyed 20. What do you do first?'
c6_math_ch09.prompt: What is the right first move?

options.text: Go back to the raw list — totals in the table must add up to the number surveyed, so the gap of 2 means two responses were never recorded or were miscounted, and the fix is to find them, not to write '2 other' and move on. This is exactly why tidy tables beat paragraphs: the mismatch is visible at a glance.
options.outcome: A frequency table is a check on itself — when the counts do not reach the sample size, the data has a hole that has to be found in the original list.

options.text: Just add a row labelled 'unknown, 2' — every survey has a few who forgot to answer.
options.outcome: Assuming abstention invents data — the two responses may exist on the list but were never tallied, and inventing a category hides the real answer.

options.text: Redo the entire survey — once a table has a gap, the whole dataset is useless.
options.outcome: Only the missing two are in doubt — the eighteen recorded responses are still valid, so checking the raw list fixes it without resurveying.

c6_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch10.scenario: For a greeting-card contest, a student draws a house: door in the centre, window on the left side only. 'It's roughly balanced,' she says, 'so it has a line of symmetry.'
c6_math_ch10.prompt: Does the drawing have a line of symmetry?

options.text: No — a line of symmetry must make both halves mirror each other exactly. The centred door would mirror fine, but the window sits only on the left; folding the card puts it over blank wall, so no fold line works. 'Roughly balanced' fails the mirror test — symmetry is exact or it is not symmetry.
options.outcome: The test is folding, not eyeballing — every feature on one side needs its twin on the other, and one unmatched window breaks it.

options.text: She is right — if a design looks balanced overall, that is close enough to count as symmetric.
options.outcome: Symmetry is a precise mirror match, not an overall impression — one unmatched window is enough to eliminate every possible fold line.

options.text: The drawing has two lines of symmetry, since the house shape itself is symmetric even if the window is not.
options.outcome: Symmetry applies to the whole drawing — the window is part of it, so its unmatched position removes all lines of symmetry.

c6_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch11.scenario: A student must measure an angle drawn in a tiny diagram — its arms are too short for the protractor to reach. Meanwhile a classmate claims the 40° angle on her small notebook is 'smaller' than the 40° angle on the classroom chart.
c6_math_ch11.prompt: How do you measure the short-armed angle — and is the classmate right?

options.text: Extend the arms with a ruler — an angle is the amount of rotation between its arms, not their length, so making the arms longer changes nothing about the opening and lets the protractor sit properly. That is also why the classmate is wrong: a 40° angle is 40° whether drawn on a stamp or a wall.
