options.outcome: Arm length is decoration; rotation is the angle. Extending the arms is the standard fix and it cannot alter the measurement.

options.text: Nothing can be done — short arms make the angle unmeasurable, so she should just guess.
options.outcome: The arms can always be extended with a straightedge — the opening between them stays identical while the arms grow.

options.text: The classmate is right — a bigger drawing means a bigger angle, since the arms cover more paper.
options.outcome: Angles measure rotation, not reach — two 40° angles are identical however long their arms are drawn.

c6_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch12.scenario: A child saves pocket money on a doubling plan: ₹5 on day one, ₹10 on day two, ₹20 on day three. A sibling predicts day five will be ₹25, 'because the numbers are going up by fives.'
c6_math_ch12.prompt: What will day five actually bring, and where did the sibling go wrong?

options.text: ₹80 — the rule is doubling, not adding five: 5, 10, 20, 40, 80. The sibling saw the first jump (+5) and assumed it repeats, but patterns are found by checking the rule against every step — 5 to 10 is also 'add 5', yet 10 to 20 breaks it while doubling survives every step.
options.outcome: The lesson of patterns: one jump suggests a rule, but the rule must explain all the steps — 'add 5' dies at day three, doubling holds to the end.

options.text: The sibling is right — the pattern adds five each time, so day five gives ₹25.
options.outcome: Adding five fails at the second step already — 10 to 20 is a jump of ten; the rule must fit every transition, not just the first.

options.text: Day five cannot be predicted — three numbers are never enough to continue a pattern.
options.outcome: Three terms are enough when one simple rule explains all of them — doubling accounts for both jumps and cleanly predicts 40 and 80.

c6_physics_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch01.scenario: Two brands of paper towels are in the kitchen, and the family argues about which absorbs more. One kid says, 'Let's just ask the shopkeeper.' Another reaches for a notebook and two bowls.
c6_physics_ch01.prompt: What does doing science here actually look like?

options.text: Test it fairly — cut equal-sized squares of each towel, dip them in equal amounts of water for the same time, weigh or measure what each holds, and write down the results. Science is a method — observe, predict, test with everything equal except the one thing being compared, record — and anyone can do it, whatever their maths marks.
options.outcome: The notebook kid is doing real science: a controlled test plus recorded data answers the question better than any opinion, including the shopkeeper's.

options.text: Asking the shopkeeper is faster and just as reliable — science is mainly about knowing facts from experts.
options.outcome: An opinion is not a measurement — the method exists so claims can be checked, and the towel test is doable at home in minutes.

options.text: Whichever towel feels thicker will absorb more, so no test is needed.
options.outcome: Thickness is a prediction, not a result — the point of the experiment is to check whether the hunch survives a fair test.

c6_physics_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch02.scenario: A courtyard puddle vanishes by evening, and a student wants to prove the sun did it. His plan: 'Just watch one puddle disappear — that proves the sun evaporated it.'
c6_physics_ch02.prompt: How should he actually test whether the sun matters?

options.text: Compare two matched puddles — pour equal water in two identical spots, shade one and leave one in the sun, then measure how much each loses. If only the sunny one shrinks faster, the sun's role is shown; and every step must be written down, because memory forgets numbers that a notebook keeps.
options.outcome: The single-puddle watch proves only that water disappears — the paired test isolates the sun as the one difference, which is what turns an observation into evidence.

options.text: His plan works — watching one puddle vanish while the sun is out already proves the sun caused it.
options.outcome: Correlation is not cause — the puddle might have drained into the ground or dried by wind; only a shaded twin puddle separates the sun's effect.

options.text: The test is impossible at home — questions like this need a laboratory to answer.
options.outcome: Two cups of water, one shaded and one sunny, is the whole experiment — science at home is how this chapter is meant to be used.

c6_physics_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch03.scenario: A torch stops working. A student checks: the battery is new, the bulb is fine, but inside the compartment the metal spring has rusted and one battery sits backwards. 'The battery must just be dead,' he concludes, and reaches for another.
c6_physics_ch03.prompt: What is actually stopping the torch?

options.text: The circuit is broken in two ways — the rusted spring no longer conducts well and the reversed battery breaks the proper direction of the path. A torch needs a complete loop of conducting material: current must leave one end of the battery, pass through the bulb, and return to the other end. Any gap, insulator or reversed cell interrupts the loop and the light dies.
options.outcome: Checking a circuit means checking the path, not just the parts — a good battery cannot push current through rust, plastic or a wrong-way cell.

options.text: He is right — when a torch fails, the battery is always to blame, so just swap in another.
options.outcome: A new battery in a broken path changes nothing — the fault here is in the connections, not the power source.

options.text: The bulb is at fault — if the battery and wires are fine, the filament must have burnt out.
options.outcome: The bulb was already checked — the remaining suspects are the conducting path itself: the rusty spring and the reversed battery.

c6_physics_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch07.scenario: Standing a few metres from a bonfire on a cold evening, a student feels her face grow hot even though the air around her stays chilly. 'The hot air must be reaching my face,' she says — but the wind is blowing sideways, away from her.
c6_physics_ch07.prompt: How is the heat actually reaching her?

options.text: By radiation — the fire sends heat directly through the air like light rays, no air current needed. Conduction needs touching and convection needs moving warm air, but her face warms across open space with the breeze blowing the wrong way, which is the signature of radiant heat.
options.outcome: The three modes carry heat differently — through solids by conduction, through fluids by convection, and straight through empty air by radiation, which is the bonfire-to-face route.

options.text: She is right — heat always travels through air, so the wind direction doesn't matter.
options.outcome: Moving air is convection — with the wind carrying warmth sideways, the heat reaching her face must be travelling without air, which is radiation.

options.text: Her face warms because the fire is big — distance and wind cannot affect heat.
options.outcome: Fire size affects intensity, not the mode — the interesting fact is that the heat crosses cool air at all, which only radiation explains.

c6_physics_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch08.scenario: The school garden club builds a sundial to time their plants' watering schedule. It works beautifully — until a cloudy week and an early-evening session leave them staring at a shadowless dial. 'The sundial is broken,' someone says.
c6_physics_ch08.prompt: Is the sundial broken — and why did people invent water clocks at all?

options.text: It is working exactly as designed — a sundial can only read time while the sun shines on it, so clouds and nights blind it completely. That is precisely why ancient civilisations added water clocks and sand clocks: those keep ticking in the dark, indoors, and in any weather. The sundial's limits, not its failure, are on display.
options.outcome: Each timekeeping tool covers the others' gaps — the sundial's dependence on sunlight is the reason other clocks were invented to work without the sky.

options.text: The sundial is broken — a properly built sundial works at any hour in any weather.
options.outcome: No sundial works without a shadow — sunlight is its input, so cloud cover and night are not malfunctions but the design's limit.

options.text: They should have built a bigger sundial — a larger shadow works even without much sun.
options.outcome: Size does not create light — with no sun there is no shadow at any scale, which is why the ancients switched to dripping water or falling sand.

c6_physics_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch11.scenario: On a terrace at night, a friend points at the bright moon and says, 'The Moon is a light source — look how it lights up the whole garden.' You have a ball and a lamp to prove otherwise.
c6_physics_ch11.prompt: How does the ball-and-lamp test settle it?

options.text: Switch the lamp on in a dark room and the ball glows — yet switch the lamp off and the ball makes no light of its own. The Moon is the same: it shines only because sunlight bounces off it, so it is a reflector, not a source. A true source — a star, a flame, a torch — produces its own light.
options.outcome: The test separates 'gives out light' from 'gives back light' — anything visible by reflected light, like the ball or the Moon, fails the lamp-off check.

options.text: The friend is right — anything that lights up your garden is by definition a light source.
options.outcome: Brightness is not proof of production — the ball glows under the lamp too, but goes dark the instant the lamp is off, showing it only reflects.

options.text: The Moon is half a source — it makes some light and reflects the rest.
options.outcome: It makes none — its entire glow is borrowed sunlight, which the ball-and-lamp demonstration mimics exactly.

c6_physics_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c6_physics_ch12.scenario: Video-calling a pen-pal abroad, a student is confused: it's bright afternoon at home but her friend's window is pitch dark. 'Maybe their Sun is off today,' her little brother offers.
c6_physics_ch12.prompt: What explains day in one place and night in another at the same moment?

options.text: The Earth is a spinning ball — at any moment, the Sun lights only half of it, and the line between light and dark keeps moving as Earth rotates. Her home sits on the lit side while her friend's sits on the dark side; in a few hours they will swap. If Earth were flat, everyone would share day and night at the same time — which is not what the call shows.
options.outcome: Day and night are just the two halves of a turning sphere — the moving edge between them is the terminator, and time zones are the same idea sliced by longitude.

options.text: The brother might be right — night could mean the Sun has dimmed or switched off over there.
options.outcome: The Sun never switches — the friend's side of the planet has simply rotated out of the sunlight, while the lit side enjoys afternoon.

options.text: Different countries have different suns — that is why their days differ.
options.outcome: There is one Sun — the spherical Earth's rotation makes it light different halves at different times, which the video call demonstrates directly.

c7_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_bio_ch01.scenario: At home, a teenager recovers from a sprained ankle in days while her grandfather's similar strain lingers for weeks. Meanwhile a growth chart shows she shot up fastest in her first year of life and again just now at thirteen — with slow years in between.
c7_bio_ch01.prompt: Why doesn't the body grow and repair at one steady rate?

options.text: Because life runs in stages, not on one fixed dial — growth surges in infancy and again at adolescence, while repair slows with age, so the teenager heals faster than the grandfather. Metabolic rate, nutrition needs and physical capability all shift across stages — infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age each run the body differently.
options.outcome: The two growth peaks and the slow grandparent recovery are the same principle: each life stage has its own biological settings for building and mending tissue.

options.text: The differences are just luck — the body grows and repairs at one steady pace, and the peaks on the chart are measurement errors.
options.outcome: The double peak is real biology — infancy and adolescence are programmed growth windows, and declining repair rate in old age is a life-stage effect, not noise.

options.text: The grandfather's slow healing means he is seriously ill — recovery speed should not vary with age at all.
options.outcome: Slower tissue repair is normal ageing, not necessarily disease — life stages change recovery rates as surely as they change growth rates.

c7_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_bio_ch02.scenario: In a classroom debate on 'which life process matters most,' a student argues: 'Eating is obviously first — an animal can skip breathing hard or going to the toilet for a while, but without food it dies.'
c7_bio_ch02.prompt: Which life process failure is actually the fastest killer?

options.text: Excretion and respiration can kill faster than hunger — a mouse sealed away from releasing carbon dioxide and wastes is poisoned within hours even with food and oxygen, because used-up products accumulate and turn toxic. The processes are a chain: nutrition brings material in, respiration extracts energy, and excretion throws the waste out — break any link and the whole animal fails.
options.outcome: The debate's premise is wrong — life processes are interdependent, and waste removal is as urgent as intake; the fastest deaths come from blocked exits, not empty stomachs.

options.text: The student is right — food is the foundation, so failing to eat is always the quickest way an animal dies.
options.outcome: Animals survive days without food but only hours to days without excreting waste — blocked removal lets toxins build to lethal levels first.

options.text: None of them kill quickly — an animal can pause any single life process indefinitely since the others compensate.
options.outcome: No process can fully cover for another — sealed excretion kills despite perfect food and oxygen, because nothing else removes the accumulating waste.

c7_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_bio_ch03.scenario: A gardener moves a row of potted plants behind a tall wall for decoration. Weeks later, watered and fertilised exactly like the others, the shaded plants are pale and stunted. 'More fertiliser will fix it,' the gardener decides.
c7_bio_ch03.prompt: Will extra fertiliser rescue the shaded plants?

options.text: No — the missing input is light, not nutrients. Photosynthesis makes the plant's food using light energy, so shaded plants starve even in rich, well-watered soil; paleness shows they cannot build enough chlorophyll and sugar. Moving them into the light fixes what fertiliser cannot — a nutrient cannot substitute for the energy source.
options.outcome: This is the farmer's shaded-wheat problem: same water, same feed, weaker plants — because the wall stole the sunlight that powers food-making.

options.text: Yes — fertiliser is plant food, so extra food compensates for the missing sunlight.
options.outcome: Fertiliser supplies minerals, not energy — the plant still needs light to convert carbon dioxide and water into its actual food.

options.text: The plants are stunted because the wall blocks their water, so deeper watering is the fix.
options.outcome: The scenario says watering was identical — the wall blocks light, and that is the input photosynthesis cannot do without.

c7_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_chem_ch01.scenario: In a science lab quiz, a student holds a grey, shiny pencil 'lead' (graphite) and declares: 'It shines AND conducts electricity — it must be a metal.'

options.text: No — classification needs several properties, not two convenient ones. Graphite is carbon: it shines and conducts, but it is brittle rather than malleable and lacks the metallic bond structure, so it stays a non-metal. Exceptions like this are exactly why scientists check a whole list of properties before labelling an element.
options.outcome: The pencil lead is the famous counterexample — one or two 'metal-like' traits cannot overrule the rest; malleability and metallic bonding are absent.

options.text: The student is right — shininess plus conductivity are the metal test, so graphite qualifies.
options.outcome: Those two properties are necessary but not sufficient — graphite fails malleability and ductility, keeping it in the non-metal column.

options.text: Graphite is neither metal nor non-metal — exceptions fall outside the classification entirely.
options.outcome: Every element classifies — graphite is a non-metal with unusual properties, not a classless anomaly.

c7_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_chem_ch02.scenario: Two mysteries at home: the camphor in the wardrobe has vanished completely over the month, and the copper vessel in the courtyard has grown a dull green coat. A student calls both 'chemical changes — stuff reacting and disappearing.'
c7_chem_ch02.prompt: Are the two changes really the same type?

options.text: No — the camphor simply sublimed: solid turned to vapour and drifted away with no new substance, a physical change. The green copper is different — the metal reacted with moist air over months into a new compound, which is chemical. Vanishing is not the test; whether a new substance formed is.
options.outcome: The contrast teaches the real criterion — the wardrobe lost its camphor to the air unchanged chemically, while the copper gained a genuinely new material on its surface.

options.text: The student is right — both are chemical because both changed over time without anyone touching them.
options.outcome: Time and disappearance do not decide the type — camphor subliming makes no new substance, while copper's green coat does.

options.text: Both are physical — nothing 'new' is ever created by air or time alone.
options.outcome: The green layer is a genuinely new compound formed by copper reacting with moist air — air and time together are quite capable of chemistry.

c7_civ_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_civ_ch01.scenario: At a dinner debate, an uncle argues: 'We barely need government — a billionaire could fund schools and fix roads if he wanted. Rich people could run everything better anyway.'
c7_civ_ch01.prompt: What can a government do that a billionaire simply cannot?

options.text: Govern — law and order, courts and defence apply to everyone equally and are backed by the authority to enforce them; a billionaire's money buys services only for those he chooses, binds nobody, and answers to no one. Governments exist because shared rules and public goods must cover the whole society, not just the funder's favourites — when a government collapses, markets and safety collapse with it, which shows the difference.
options.outcome: The state's job is universal and enforceable — no private fortune can make law apply to everyone or defend a whole country's borders.

options.text: The uncle is right — enough private money could replace the government entirely.
options.outcome: Money cannot create legitimate, enforceable law for everyone — a private funder answers to himself, serves whom he likes, and cannot bind a whole society.

options.text: Government's only real job is guarding the borders — everything else, like disaster relief, should be left to people themselves.
options.outcome: Defence is one function among many — citizens depend on government for relief, public services and dispute settlement that no individual can supply alone.

c7_civ_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_civ_ch02.scenario: A newly elected school council wins 80% of the seats. Their first announcement: 'We now have the right to ban the school newspaper that criticised us, and to remove all opposing voices from debates.'
c7_civ_ch02.prompt: Does a landslide victory really grant that power?

options.text: No — a constitution limits what any government may do, however big its majority. Rights like free expression and the existence of opposition sit above ordinary majority decisions, so the council can pass rules but cannot silence criticism. A constitution exists precisely to bind the winners — without it, every election would hand one group unlimited power.
options.outcome: Winning big grants the power to govern, not the power to abolish the rules of the game — constitutional limits are what keep a majority democratic.

options.text: Yes — whoever wins the most seats may make any rule, since the majority's choice is final.
options.outcome: Majority rule operates inside constitutional limits — dissolving criticism and opposition would break the very framework that made the election legitimate.

options.text: The council can ban the paper only if it wins 100% of the seats — any lower and the limits apply.
options.outcome: No percentage unlocks unlimited power — constitutional protections hold at 51%, 80% or 100%, because they guard the system itself.

c7_civ_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_civ_ch03.scenario: After a national election, a new party takes power and the old one steps down. A student watching the news asks: 'So did our country just end and a new one begin? Do all the police and clerks lose their jobs too?'
c7_civ_ch03.prompt: What actually changed — the state or the government?

options.text: Only the government — the state is the permanent framework: its people, territory, sovereignty and institutions outlast any party. Governments are its temporary managers, swapped at elections, while the state itself, and the officers who serve it, carry on regardless of who holds office.
options.outcome: This is the key distinction — Prime Ministers and cabinets come and go; the Republic, its courts and its services remain, which is why daily life continues through every transfer of power.

options.text: The whole country effectively restarts — a new ruling party means a new state, and officials serve at the party's pleasure.
options.outcome: Parties change; the state endures — police and civil servants serve the state, not the party, which is why they keep their jobs across elections.

options.text: Neither changes — elections are ceremonial, and the same people effectively keep running things.
options.outcome: The government genuinely changes hands — that is what elections decide — while the state's population, territory and sovereignty remain untouched.

c7_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_eco_ch01.scenario: At a barter market, two merchants argue over a bronze idol. One insists it's worth 5 bags of grain; the other says 3, because grain is scarce this season. With no money, there's no price tag to settle it.
c7_eco_ch01.prompt: Why can't the argument be resolved — and what does that reveal about barter?

options.text: Because barter has no common measure of value — the idol's 'worth' exists only as a negotiated ratio against whatever it is traded for, and that ratio shifts with scarcity: in a lean season, grain commands more. Money fixes exactly this by giving every good a single common measure — a price — instead of a different bargain for each pair of goods.
options.outcome: Both merchants are partly right — value in barter is situational, and the disagreement itself is the flaw that money was invented to remove.

options.text: The first merchant is right — valuable items keep a fixed worth, so 5 bags is the idol's true price.
options.outcome: Barter has no 'true price' — value is set per trade, and a scarce harvest legitimately makes grain dearer against everything.

options.text: The dispute is just about honesty — one of them is lying, and a truthful trader would end it.
options.outcome: Both may be honest — without a shared measure, two reasonable people can hold different valuations, which is the structural problem, not dishonesty.

c7_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_eco_ch02.scenario: A farmer harvests 100 kg of tomatoes — 20 kg feed his family, and the remaining 80 kg are carted to the wholesale market and sold. At dinner, his son declares, 'The whole harvest was market activity.'
c7_eco_ch02.prompt: Which part of the 100 kg actually counts as market activity?

options.text: Only the 80 kg sold — a market transaction needs a buyer, a seller, a good and an agreed price changing hands. The 20 kg eaten at home never met a buyer, so it is production and consumption but not market activity; the son's claim erases the line that defines what a market is.
options.outcome: The split matters economically — what a household consumes itself never enters the market, while what it sells becomes revenue and trade.

options.text: The son is right — everything produced is part of the market whether it is sold or eaten.
options.outcome: Production is not exchange — the eaten portion never met a buyer or a price, so it stays outside the market entirely.

options.text: None of it counts — real market activity requires a permanent shop, and a farmer's cart is not one.
options.outcome: Markets need buyers, sellers and exchange, not buildings — the wholesale sale of 80 kg is a market transaction however it was carried there.

c7_eco_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_eco_ch03.scenario: A district has one crore rupees to spend. Proposal A: five air-conditioned guest houses for visiting officials. Proposal B: a water pipeline and a paved road connecting three farming villages. A junior official argues for A — 'visible buildings show development.'
c7_eco_ch03.prompt: Which proposal is real infrastructure investment?

options.text: Proposal B — the road slashes transport costs and spoilage so crops reach market profitably, and the pipeline returns hours of daily labour to households; both keep generating economic gains year after year. The guest houses serve a few officials and generate nothing comparable — infrastructure earns its name by enabling everyone else's work.
options.outcome: The difference is multiplication: roads, water and power raise the productivity of a whole district, while a luxury building's benefit stops at its own walls.

options.text: Proposal A is equally good infrastructure — any government building counts as development spending.
options.outcome: Buildings alone are not infrastructure — the term means the enabling backbone (roads, water, power) that lifts all activity, not just any construction.

options.text: Neither — one crore is too small to matter, so the choice hardly makes a difference.
options.outcome: The road-pipeline package transforms trade and labour for three villages — infrastructure gains are about what they unlock, not just the amount spent.

c7_eco_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_eco_ch04.scenario: A mountain district has fertile land, hardworking farmers and eager shopkeepers — but no bank branch for miles. Savings sit in cash at home, a trader who wants to expand can't borrow, and a visitor wonders why such an industrious place stays poor.

options.text: Financial infrastructure — cash under a mattress earns nothing and funds nothing, while the same rupees in a bank would earn interest and become loans for the trader's expansion. Without banks, credit and payment networks, hard work cannot convert into investment — effort is trapped in place, which is exactly how a lack of banks keeps a capable region poor.
options.outcome: The chapter's core: saving and borrowing need institutions to connect them — no bank means no bridge from spare money to working capital.

options.text: Nothing is missing — hardworking people with resources always prosper eventually, banks or not.
options.outcome: Effort alone cannot scale — expansion needs borrowed capital, and idle cash savings never become anyone's loan without a bank between saver and borrower.

options.text: The district needs charity, not banks — donations from outside would fix the poverty faster.
options.outcome: Charity flows once; a bank keeps recycling local savings into local loans every year — the district needs the mechanism, not a one-time gift.

c7_engl_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_engl_ch01.scenario: A student adapts 'The Day the River Spoke' for a school anthology, but moves the whole story from the coastal river village to a dry desert plateau 'for variety' — keeping every scene otherwise identical.

options.text: Almost everything — the river is not scenery but the story's machinery: it shapes the villagers' commute, the isolation, and the voice that speaks to the protagonist. In a desert the same scenes lose their logic — no water to cross, no river to listen — so the character's relationship with her environment, and the imagery carrying it, must be rebuilt from scratch.
options.outcome: Setting in this story is causal, not decorative — change it and the plot's reasons evaporate, which is why 'same story, new backdrop' never survives the move.

options.text: Nothing breaks — settings are interchangeable backdrops, so the story works identically on a plateau.
options.outcome: The river drives the plot — the crossing, the isolation, the speaking water — so swapping it for desert deletes the story's causes, not just its look.

options.text: Only the descriptions need rewriting — the river's role is just pretty imagery.
options.outcome: The river does narrative work — it isolates the village and literally speaks to the protagonist — so it is plot machinery, not ornament.

c7_engl_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_engl_ch02.scenario: A family friend gives up a high-paying city clinic to run a free shelter for injured street animals. Relatives call it a waste of a medical degree — 'he had everything, and he chose dogs.'
c7_engl_ch02.prompt: How would Dr. Dolittle's story judge the friend's choice?

options.text: As success, not failure — Dolittle was called foolish for the same reason: he preferred animals and meaningful work over wealthy patients and status, and the story shows his devotion made him better at healing, not worse. The friend's choice mirrors that — the townspeople's verdict measures money, but the chapter measures purpose.
options.outcome: The chapter quietly redefines success: Dolittle's 'failure' by society's ledger was a life aligned with what he loved, which is exactly what the friend has chosen.

options.text: The relatives are right — success is income and status, and the friend traded both away.
options.outcome: That is the townspeople's measure in the story — and the story's whole point is that it misjudges Dolittle, whose real achievement was a life of purpose.

options.text: It is admirable but doomed — anyone choosing animals over human patients must fail in the end.
options.outcome: Dolittle's life contradicts that — his choice made him uniquely effective and fulfilled; the story predicts flourishing, not failure.

c7_engl_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_engl_ch03.scenario: A classmate's science project has failed three times — the circuit fizzles, the model collapses, the demo won't start. She tears up the plans and says, 'Three failures mean I should stop. Inventors don't wreck things this often.'
c7_engl_ch03.prompt: What would Anand, the story's tireless inventor, make of her three failures?

options.text: That three failures are the job, not the verdict — Anand's inventions keep failing too, and he keeps building anyway, eyes sparkling at sparking wires while everyone shouts. His character is defined by persistence and curiosity; the flops are the steps. Stopping after three is the only outcome where the failures win.
options.outcome: The chapter presents resilience as the inventor's real trait — Anand's chaos and cheerfulness after disasters are what keep him, and the story, moving.

options.text: She is right — real inventors rarely fail, so three flops prove she is not cut out for it.
options.outcome: Anand fails constantly and keeps inventing — the story treats repeated failure as the inventor's normal life, not a disqualification.

options.text: She should keep going but hide the failures — success is only meaningful if the flops stay secret.
options.outcome: Anand's failures are open and even funny — the chapter treats them as part of the work, not as shameful secrets to bury.

c7_engl_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_engl_ch04.scenario: Writing an adventure scene for the school magazine, a student sets her hero in a thick jungle. Her editor asks which element is the true 'frontier' — the wild jungle, the open railway track, or the dark tunnel mouth ahead.
c7_engl_ch04.prompt: Which element should carry the sense of stepping into the unknown?

options.text: The tunnel — the jungle is wild but sunlit and knowable, the track is a thin man-made line through it, and the tunnel is where the human path disappears into darkness: a brick-lined doorway into what cannot be seen. That juxtaposition — civilization's line ending at an unlit hole in the hill — is what turns the walk into an adventure's frontier.
options.outcome: The chapter's atmosphere is built exactly this way: isolation and heat in the jungle, then the tunnel mouth concentrating all the uncertainty into one dark opening.

options.text: The jungle is the real frontier — wildness always beats anything man-made for danger.
options.outcome: The jungle frames the scene but the tunnel is the threshold — the story places the unknown specifically inside the dark passage, not in the visible wild around it.

options.text: The railway track is the frontier — it is the boundary line itself.
options.outcome: The track leads to the frontier but is not it — the open line is known and lit; the tunnel's hidden interior is where anticipation actually lives.

c7_engl_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c7_engl_ch05.scenario: A student wants to answer a soldier's published letter that ends: 'Do not worry about the cold nights here; the warmth of serving our nation keeps every soldier going.' Her first draft begins by listing facts about the glacier's weather.
c7_engl_ch05.prompt: What is the soldier doing in that line — and how should her reply meet it?

options.text: He is using contrast to manage his family's worry — 'cold nights' named honestly, then answered by 'the warmth of serving,' turning hardship into reassurance rather than hiding it. Her reply should meet that tone: acknowledge the sacrifice, return warmth for warmth — a respectful, personal letter, not a weather report, because the letter form exists to carry feeling across the distance.
options.outcome: The line works because the letter lets him balance truth and comfort — and a reply that honours the theme of sacrifice in the same personal register completes the exchange.

options.text: He is simply reporting conditions — so her factual reply about the glacier's weather is the right register.
options.outcome: The line is emotional craft, not a weather report — it sets hardship against purpose to reassure readers, and a facts-only reply would miss the letter entirely.

options.text: He is complaining indirectly — 'cold nights' is a coded plea for help that should be answered with alarm.
options.outcome: The contrast does the opposite — he names the cold only to dissolve the worry in the warmth of duty; reading it as complaint inverts the reassurance.

c7_geo_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_geo_ch01.scenario: Meera in Ahmedabad video-calls her cousin in Arunachal Pradesh at 6 PM. Her cousin says it has been dark for nearly two hours, while Meera's street is still bright. Both clocks show the exact same Indian Standard Time.
c7_geo_ch01.prompt: How should Meera explain the mismatch between the sun and the clock?

options.text: India spans about 30 degrees of longitude, and since Earth rotates 1 degree in roughly 4 minutes, the sun rises and sets almost two hours earlier in the east. One standard meridian keeps both clocks on the same time, but it cannot move the sun.
options.outcome: This applies the 4-minutes-per-degree rule correctly: longitude governs solar time, while IST only standardises the clock.

options.text: Her cousin's clocks and watches must all be running two hours fast — she should ask him to reset them.
options.outcome: Both clocks read the same standard time by design; the difference is in solar time, not faulty clocks.

options.text: It is because Arunachal is at a higher latitude, and latitude is what controls the time of sunrise and sunset.
options.outcome: Latitude shapes climate and day-length, but east-to-west differences in solar time come from longitude as Earth rotates.

c7_geo_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_geo_ch02.scenario: During a school weather-diary project, Ravi looks outside on a calm, clear winter morning in Punjab and writes 'no weather today' because nothing dramatic is happening. His partner says he is missing most of the report.
c7_geo_ch02.prompt: What should Ravi actually record for that morning?

options.text: Temperature, how dry or moist the air feels, wind speed and direction, and cloud cover — weather is the combined state of all these elements at that moment, and a calm clear morning is still a weather condition.
options.outcome: This treats weather as the full set of atmospheric elements, not just rain or storms, which is what a weather diary is meant to track.

options.text: Ravi is right — weather only counts when it rains or storms, so the entry can stay blank until something changes.
options.outcome: Leaving it blank loses the data: clear skies, low wind and dry cold air are themselves weather elements that explain later changes.

options.text: He should copy yesterday's entries, because weather stays roughly the same from one day to the next.
options.outcome: Weather is dynamic and can shift within hours — copying yesterday assumes a stability the real atmosphere does not have.

c7_geo_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_geo_ch03.scenario: After five straight days of unseasonal March rain in Jaisalmer, a local headline declares 'Thar is no longer a desert — its climate has permanently changed.' A classmate asks whether the headline is right.
c7_geo_ch03.prompt: What is the correct geographical reading of those five days?

options.text: The rain is a weather anomaly — climate is the average pattern over about 30 years, so five wet days cannot reclassify the desert. Only a sustained shift in long-term averages would count.
options.outcome: This separates a single short-term event from the decades of data that define a climate, which is exactly what the headline confuses.

options.text: The headline is right — five days of heavy rain is real data, so the desert classification should be updated immediately.
options.outcome: One wet spell is far too short; climate classifications rest on roughly 30-year normals, not single events.

options.text: Weather and climate are the same thing here, so the question cannot be answered either way.
options.outcome: They differ precisely by timescale: weather is day-to-day, climate is the long-term average — that difference is what resolves the question.

c7_geo_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_geo_ch04.scenario: A family in the dry rain-shadow part of the Deccan plateau visits relatives in Punjab and returns inspired. They announce they will flood their fields and grow the same water-hungry paddy, because 'farming is farming anywhere in India.'
c7_geo_ch04.prompt: What is wrong with their plan, and what would suit their land better?

options.text: Their farm sits where hills block monsoon winds, so rainfall is low and water is scarce; agriculture there suits tank irrigation and drought-resistant crops, not paddy. Farming choices must match local soil, terrain and water, not copy another region.
options.outcome: This respects the core principle: Indian agriculture is shaped by physical geography — relief, soil and water — so practices cannot be transplanted unchanged.

options.text: The plan is fine — with enough tractors and chemical fertiliser, climate and rainfall no longer matter to farming.
options.outcome: Machinery and fertiliser cannot manufacture water; groundwater recharge and soil moisture still depend on the monsoon, so paddy would fail or exhaust the water table.

options.text: They should simply work harder — differences between Indian farms come down to effort, not geography.
options.outcome: Effort cannot replace physical conditions: a rain-shadow field and a Punjab alluvial plain differ in water and soil no matter how hard anyone works.

c7_geo_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c7_geo_ch05.scenario: In a map quiz, Sohail argues that Sri Lanka and the Maldives are 'not really neighbours' of India because a person cannot walk across to them — only countries sharing a land border count.
c7_geo_ch05.prompt: How should the class judge his claim?

options.text: Reject it: neighbours include maritime ones — Sri Lanka lies just across the narrow Palk Strait and shares India's oceanic space, monsoon systems and sea routes, so proximity across water still makes a neighbour.
options.outcome: This uses the full geographical definition: regional proximity and shared physical systems, not only shared land, define a neighbour.

options.text: Accept it — a border you cannot walk across is not a real boundary, so island nations are foreigners in every sense.
options.outcome: This ignores maritime geography; the Indian Ocean connects rather than isolates, and Sri Lanka and the Maldives share climate and waters with India.

options.text: Accept it, because political borders are arbitrary lines anyway and physical features like seas and mountains do not decide them.
options.outcome: Most of India's borders follow real landforms — Himalayan crests, river courses — and seas define maritime neighbours, so physical geography is central, not arbitrary.

c7_hist_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch01.scenario: Watching a documentary, Nikhil hears a narrator say that towns grew in the Gangetic plains around 600 BCE 'because ambitious kings ordered walls to be built.' His sister asks whether that is really how cities appear.
c7_hist_ch01.prompt: What actually made those towns possible, and where does the king's order fit in?

options.text: Iron axes and ploughshares let farmers clear forests and till heavy Gangetic soil, producing grain surpluses that fed full-time potters, smiths and traders — towns grew from that surplus, and kings could only fortify places the economy already sustained.
options.outcome: This puts causes in the right order: technology drives surplus, surplus feeds specialists and markets, and political walls follow rather than create urban life.

options.text: The narrator is right — a royal decree to build walls is what turns a village into a city, so the economy is irrelevant.
options.outcome: Walls without food surplus cannot house craftspersons or merchants; the decree explains fortification, not urbanisation.

options.text: Those towns were simply Harappan cities like Mohenjo-daro that kept running continuously into the Gangetic plains.
options.outcome: The Harappan cities in the Indus basin had declined over a thousand years earlier; the Gangetic towns were a fresh, second wave in a different region.

c7_hist_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch02.scenario: In a class debate, Arjun argues that an empire is 'just a kingdom whose army won a few extra battles — nothing else changes.' His opponent needs to show what really separates a mahajanapada from an empire.
c7_hist_ch02.prompt: What is the strongest counter to Arjun's claim?

options.text: Winning battles gives only temporary dominance; an empire needs a permanent standing army, centralised tax collection through royal officials, uniform administration and control over distant, diverse regions — all funded by agricultural surplus and trade revenue, not just bravery.
options.outcome: This distinguishes short-term conquest from imperial structure: institutions and economic foundations are what turn a kingdom into an empire.

options.text: Arjun is right — once you defeat neighbouring kings, the bigger territory automatically runs itself the same way a small kingdom did.
options.outcome: Larger, diverse territories cannot be run by personal rule and local chiefs alone; without bureaucracy and standing forces, conquered lands break away.

options.text: The real difference is that emperors had better titles — the actual administration stayed identical to a small janapada.
options.outcome: Titles signalled sovereignty, but the substance changed too: salaried officials, centralised revenue and permanent armies replaced direct local collection.

c7_hist_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch03.scenario: After learning that the Mauryan Empire broke apart, Tara tells her study group: 'So obviously India went into a dark age — trade died, towns emptied, and culture collapsed until the next big empire.'
c7_hist_ch03.prompt: How should the group correct her?

options.text: Fragmentation is not collapse: regional dynasties like the Shungas and Satavahanas competed to attract merchants, minted their own artistic coins, patronised craft guilds, and trade with Rome and Central Asia via the Silk Route actually boomed.
options.outcome: This replaces the 'empire or darkness' assumption with the evidence: decentralised rival states fostered commerce and cultural blending.

options.text: Tara is right — without one emperor, there was no one to protect traders, so all exchange must have stopped.
options.outcome: Regional rulers depended on commercial taxes and actively protected routes and guilds; rival kingdoms made travel more competitive, not impossible.

options.text: The real reason the period mattered is that foreign invaders like the Kushanas completely replaced Indian culture with their own.
options.outcome: Foreign groups assimilated into local religions and produced hybrid art like the Gandhara school — synthesis, not replacement.

c7_hist_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch04.scenario: For a class presentation, Dev plans to say: 'The Gupta Empire appeared overnight when one mighty conqueror swept across India in a single campaign.' His teacher asks him to check the titles on early Gupta inscriptions and coins first.
c7_hist_ch04.prompt: What will the evidence actually show Dev?

options.text: The first Guptas, Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha, used the modest title Maharaja as local chiefs; only generations later did Chandragupta I take the imperial title Maharajadhiraja after marrying the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi — so the empire was built gradually through Magadha's fertile base, alliances and rising titles, not one battle.
options.outcome: This reads the sources correctly: title changes and joint royal coins trace a slow consolidation from local chieftains to sovereigns.

options.text: Dev's version stands — inscriptions exaggerate, so a single conquest story is close enough for a school presentation.
options.outcome: Coins and inscriptions are primary evidence; they record generations of subordinate Maharajas before any imperial title, directly contradicting overnight conquest.

options.text: The coins will show the Guptas began as outsiders who seized power in a desert region far from Magadha.
options.outcome: The dynasty rose inside Magadha — the same fertile Ganga basin with iron resources that had earlier sustained the Mauryas — so geography, not foreign invasion, was the base.

c7_hist_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch05.scenario: On a trip to Haridwar, Kavya watches thousands gather at the Ganga for aarti. Her cousin shrugs: 'The river is only called holy because some priest wrote it in a book long ago — otherwise it is just water.'
c7_hist_ch05.prompt: How should Kavya explain why the river became sacred?

options.text: Communities depended on the river for water, fertile silt and travel; gratitude and awe produced rituals and stories over generations, turning a physical lifeline into shared sacred geography that now binds distant pilgrims together.
options.outcome: This traces sacredness from everyday survival dependence to cultural tradition — it grew from people's lives, not from a single decree or text.

options.text: The cousin is right — sacredness is just a rule imposed from above, so the crowd is only following an old instruction.
options.outcome: Reverence for life-giving rivers existed among ordinary farming communities long before texts codified it; the rituals express dependence, not obedience.

options.text: The river matters purely as a water supply — calling it sacred adds nothing to understanding its history.
options.outcome: Sacred status created pilgrimage networks that linked people across rival kingdoms into a shared cultural identity — far more than a water utility.

c7_hist_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch06.scenario: A king in 7th-century India, short on coins as long-distance trade shrinks, starts paying his military officers with villages — each officer may collect the land revenue himself and keep his own armed men. A student predicts this will strengthen the kingdom.
c7_hist_ch06.prompt: What is the land-grant policy actually setting in motion?

options.text: It hands each officer independent control of revenue and soldiers; as these samantas grow wealthy and armed, they stop sending tribute and declare their own kingdoms — the policy fragments the realm, which is exactly how post-Gupta India splintered.
options.outcome: This follows the causal chain: scarce coinage leads to land payment, land payment builds autonomous local power, and autonomy breaks the centre.

options.text: The prediction is right — paid-in-land officers will stay loyal, because land is worth more than coins and gratitude guarantees obedience.
options.outcome: Loyalty fails precisely because the grant makes the officer self-sufficient; once he controls revenue and troops locally, he no longer needs the emperor.

options.text: It will trigger a total dark age — once the empire fragments, all culture, temples and learning will disappear too.
options.outcome: Fragmentation moved power to regional courts that patronised temples, regional languages and local economies — political disunity is not civilisational collapse.

c7_hist_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch07.scenario: Two friends argue about the 12th-century battles of Tarain. One says: 'The Indian kings lost only because their soldiers were cowards — elephants and huge armies should have crushed any invader on open ground.'

options.text: It was a tactical mismatch, not cowardice: Turkic horse archers struck fast, flanked and withdrew before slow infantry could respond, while war elephants could panic when hurt — and rival regional kingdoms, divided by feuds, never fielded a united defence.
options.outcome: This identifies the real mechanisms — cavalry mobility against elephant-heavy formations, plus political disunity — rather than blaming morale.

options.text: The friend is right — with bigger armies and more elephants, bravery alone decides battles, so losing can only mean cowardice.
options.outcome: Size and courage cannot offset mobility; fast cavalry dictated the pace of battle and fragmented kingdoms could not coordinate, whatever their soldiers' bravery.

options.text: The invasions mattered because Mahmud of Ghazni settled down and ruled the Gangetic plains like a Mughal emperor.
options.outcome: Mahmud's raids a century earlier aimed at plundering temple wealth, not permanent rule; conflating raiding with empire-building misreads the period.

c7_hist_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c7_hist_ch08.scenario: In a discussion on India's past, Rehan says: 'Everyone who ever came to India from outside arrived as an invader — foreigners always came to conquer.' A classmate mentions Parsis, Jewish traders on the Malabar coast and Arab merchants.
c7_hist_ch08.prompt: How should the group evaluate Rehan's claim?

options.text: Reject it: most arrivals were traders drawn by monsoon sea routes and rich markets, or refugees fleeing persecution — like the Zoroastrians — whom local rulers welcomed with land and freedoms; they settled, married locally and enriched India's culture without conquering anyone.
options.outcome: This separates peaceful mercantile and refugee migration from military invasion, matching the historical record of plural, welcomed communities.

options.text: Rehan is right — crossing the sea or a mountain pass to reach India is itself an act of conquest, whatever the newcomers intended.
options.outcome: Intent and record matter: merchant guilds and refugee groups arrived with royal permission and integrated into local economies, leaving no conquest behind.

options.text: The migrants did come peacefully, but they had to erase their own languages, foods and faiths completely to be accepted.
options.outcome: Integration was two-way synthesis, not erasure: migrants kept distinct practices while adopting local customs, adding crafts, cuisines and traditions to the mosaic.

c7_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch01.scenario: Comparing two phone prices, Chintu announces that ₹3,99,900 must cost more than ₹4,08,200 'because 9 is a bigger digit than 4, and this number is full of nines.'
c7_math_ch01.prompt: Where does his comparison go wrong?

options.text: Price comparison starts from the leftmost, highest place: 3,99,900 has 3 in the lakh place while 4,08,200 has 4, and 4 lakh beats 3 lakh no matter what digits follow — so ₹4,08,200 is actually larger.
options.outcome: This uses place value correctly: digits are weighed by their column, and the lakh column outranks every smaller column combined.

options.text: Chintu is right — the number with the largest single digit anywhere is the bigger number.
options.outcome: A 9 in the hundreds place is worth 900 while a 4 in the lakh place is worth 4,00,000; digit size cannot beat place value.

options.text: Actually they are equal, because both have six digits and six-digit numbers all count as lakhs.
options.outcome: Same digit count means compare column by column from the left — 4 lakh is one full lakh more than 3 lakh, so they differ by ₹8,300.

c7_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch02.scenario: Riya buys 4 notebooks at ₹30 each and 3 pens at ₹15 each, with a ₹20 discount at the counter. She writes the bill as 4 × 30 + 3 × 15 − 20. Her little brother insists the expression has six separate terms: 4, 30, 3, 15, 20 'and the multiplications.'
c7_math_ch02.prompt: How many terms does the bill really have, and what does it total?

options.text: Three terms — 4 × 30, 3 × 15 and 20 — because × and ÷ glue numbers into one term while + and − are the walls between them; the bill is 120 + 45 − 20 = ₹145.
options.outcome: This applies term structure correctly: multiplication binds each item's quantity and price into a single term before the addition and subtraction walls are counted.

options.text: The brother is right — every number separated by any symbol is its own term, so there are five or six terms to add up in order.
options.outcome: Splitting at × signs breaks the price-per-item blocks; the expression would be mangled into meaningless additions and multiplications in sequence.

options.text: There are two terms: everything before the minus sign is one big term, so it is (4 × 30 + 3 × 15) and then just 20.
options.outcome: A + sign is a wall too — it splits the notebook cost and the pen cost into separate terms, which matters the moment brackets or further operations enter.

c7_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch03.scenario: Measuring a table for a school project, Asha finds the edge lands between 84 cm and 85 cm. Her partner writes '84 cm' and says, 'Whole numbers are good enough — just pick the nearer mark.'
c7_math_ch03.prompt: Is whole-number precision acceptable here, and what should they record?

options.text: No — the gap between 84 and 85 cm is real length, so divide that centimetre into 10 equal parts; if the edge sits at the 3rd mark, the true measure is 84 and 3/10 cm (84.3 cm), and the small marks exist exactly for this.
options.outcome: This recognises that measurement is continuous: tenths are smaller units that capture what whole numbers leave out.

options.text: The partner is right — measurements must always be whole numbers, so rounding to 84 is the only correct answer.
options.outcome: Whole numbers leave gaps between consecutive integers; rounding throws away real information, which is why rulers carry subdivisions.

options.text: They should write 84.3 as '84 cm and 3 whole centimetres extra', since 0.3 means three more full units.
options.outcome: The digit after the decimal is three-tenths of one centimetre, not three whole centimetres — smaller units are parts of a whole, not new wholes.

c7_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch04.scenario: The canteen charges ₹15 per samosa, so Karan writes the cost as 15y where y is the number of samosas. His friend objects: 'You can't leave a letter in a maths answer — y has to be one fixed number, so tell me what y equals.'
c7_math_ch04.prompt: Who understands what the letter is doing?

options.text: Karan does — y is a variable, a placeholder for however many samosas someone buys; the expression 15y works for 1, 7 or 40 samosas, which is exactly why it is more powerful than writing 15 × 5 for one fixed case.
options.outcome: This treats the letter as a number-in-disguise that can take many values — the core purpose of a variable.

options.text: The friend is right — every letter in algebra hides one secret correct value, and the job is to guess it.
options.outcome: That confuses a variable with a puzzle answer; unless an equation pins it down, a variable ranges over many possible values.

options.text: Neither — the y is just an abbreviation for 'samosas', so 15y means '15 samosas' and no maths is involved.
options.outcome: Letters stand for counts, not objects: y is the number of samosas, so 15y is fifteen times that number — a cost, not a label.

c7_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch05.scenario: Sketching a rangoli with two straight chalk lines crossing, Farid tells his teammate: 'Make the lines cross at two spots so the junction looks stable.' Meanwhile another student says the X they drew makes only two angles.
c7_math_ch05.prompt: What does the geometry of two straight lines actually allow?

options.text: Two distinct straight lines can cross at exactly one point — a second crossing would force a line to bend — and that single point of intersection always creates four angles around it, even when all four are right angles.
options.outcome: This applies both facts correctly: one intersection point per pair of straight lines, and four angles formed there.

options.text: Farid is right — long straight lines can dip back and cross again, giving two points of intersection.
options.outcome: If a line crossed the same straight line twice it would have to curve between the points, which means it was never straight.

options.text: The second student is right — an X is two strokes, so only two angles exist at the crossing.
options.outcome: Count the regions, not the strokes: four rays leave the point and bound four angles — a right-angled cross makes four 90-degree angles, not two.

c7_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch06.scenario: Vasu tracks a potted plant's weekly height: 2 cm, 6 cm, 18 cm, 54 cm. Seeing the first jump of 4, he predicts next week will be 54 + 4 = 58 cm and enters it in the school science log.
c7_math_ch06.prompt: What should he check before locking in that prediction?

options.text: Check the other jumps: 6−2=4 but 18−6=12 and 54−18=36 — the differences are not constant. The heights multiply by 3 each week, so the next reading is about 162 cm, not 58.
options.outcome: This tests the rule on every consecutive pair instead of trusting the first one — addition failed, multiplication by 3 fits, which changes the prediction completely.

options.text: The prediction is fine — the first gap of 4 fixes the rule, and later jumps can be ignored.
options.outcome: A rule must work for every step; the second and third gaps already disprove 'add 4', so 58 contradicts the given data.

options.text: Since the numbers grow fast, the next one should just be the biggest round number he can write, like 100.
options.outcome: Sequences follow a fixed rule, not guesses; testing differences and ratios is what reveals it.

c7_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch07.scenario: For a craft model of a triangular warning sign labelled P, Q and R, Simran's teammate says: 'The side opposite corner Q is QR, and to edge the sign we need to cover 4 border pieces, one per corner plus the frame.'
c7_math_ch07.prompt: Which parts of his statement need fixing?

options.text: Both: the side opposite vertex Q is the one that does not touch it — PR — and edging a triangle covers its 3 sides, since a triangle has exactly 3 vertices, 3 sides and 3 angles.
options.outcome: This applies the definitions precisely: a side is named by the two vertices it joins, 'opposite' means across from the vertex, and the boundary is 3 sides.

options.text: Only the count is wrong — the opposite side to Q really is QR because it shares the letter Q.
options.outcome: Sharing the letter is exactly why QR is adjacent to Q, not opposite; the opposite side never touches that vertex.

options.text: Only the naming is wrong — a triangle has 4 border pieces if you count the corner points as separate pieces.
options.outcome: Vertices are points, not border pieces; the perimeter is made of the 3 sides alone, so 4 strips would have nothing to cover.

c7_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch08.scenario: After the school fair, 3/4 of a big cake is left. Didi tells Mehul he may take home 1/2 of the leftover. Mehul announces, 'Half is half — I get half the whole cake,' and reaches for the knife.
c7_math_ch08.prompt: How much of the original cake is he actually owed?

options.text: Half of the leftover, not half of the whole: 'of' means multiply, so 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8 of the original cake — a piece smaller than either fraction because multiplying proper fractions takes a part of a part.
options.outcome: This multiplies numerators and denominators straight across and reads 'fraction of a fraction' correctly — the product shrinks, it cannot give him half the original.

options.text: Mehul is right — multiplying by 1/2 still leaves him half the original cake, since multiplication always makes things bigger or equal.
options.outcome: Multiplication by a fraction under 1 shrinks the amount; 'always bigger' is a whole-number habit that fails for proper fractions.

options.text: He gets 1/2 + 3/4 = 5/4 of the cake, because combining shares means adding the fractions.
options.outcome: He is taking a portion of the leftover, not combining two shares — 'of' signals multiplication, and 5/4 would exceed the whole cake anyway.

c7_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch09.scenario: A photo studio prints the same picture as a passport photo and a big wall poster. Leela tells the shopkeeper the two prints are 'congruent' because the picture looks identical on both.
c7_math_ch09.prompt: Is she using the word correctly?

options.text: No — congruent means same shape AND same size, so one figure could be laid exactly over the other. The photo and poster have the same shape but different sizes: they are similar, not congruent.
options.outcome: This separates congruence from similarity — matching angles alone never guarantees matching size.

options.text: Yes — since every angle and proportion matches, the two prints are congruent regardless of scale.
options.outcome: Identical angles with different side lengths is similarity; congruence fails the moment one print cannot cover the other.

options.text: They cannot be compared at all, because congruence only applies to triangles drawn in geometry class.
options.outcome: Congruence applies to any figures — rectangles, stars, photos — the test is always exact match of shape and size.

c7_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch10.scenario: A weather app shows Leh at −15°C and Kufri at −5°C. Planning a trip, Amaan says, 'Fifteen is bigger than five, so −15°C is the warmer place — let us go to Leh and pack light.'
c7_math_ch10.prompt: Where does his reasoning break down?

options.text: On a number line, −15 sits further left of zero than −5, so it is the lower value — Leh at −15°C is colder, and he needs the heavy jackets, not light packing.
options.outcome: This reads signed numbers by position: among negatives, the bigger digit means a deeper deficit below zero, i.e. a smaller temperature.

options.text: Amaan is right — 15 beats 5, so −15°C must be warmer than −5°C.
options.outcome: The minus sign reverses the ordering: −15 is further below zero, meaning colder, not warmer.

options.text: Both towns are below zero, so they are equally cold and the digits do not matter.
options.outcome: Negative values still have order — a −15 night can freeze what −5 cannot, so the digits matter a great deal.

c7_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch11.scenario: For a school stall, Neha must pack 42 cookies and 70 chocolates into identical gift boxes with nothing left over. Her teammate suggests making 36 boxes 'because 36 is a nice common number for both.'
c7_math_ch11.prompt: What actually decides the possible number of boxes?

options.text: The box count must divide both 42 and 70 exactly — a common factor. The common factors of 42 and 70 are 1, 2, 7 and 14, so she can make 2, 7 or 14 boxes (more than one), but never 36.
options.outcome: This turns equal distribution into a common-factor problem and verifies each candidate by division — 36 cannot divide 42 at all.

options.text: The teammate is right — any number that feels like it belongs to both lists works, and 36 is close to both numbers.
options.outcome: Feelings aside, a factor must divide with zero remainder: 42 ÷ 36 does not come out even, so 36 fails outright.

options.text: She should use a multiple like 210 boxes, since multiples are the numbers both 42 and 70 share.
options.outcome: That reverses factors and multiples: 210 is a common multiple (both numbers divide into it), but you cannot make more boxes than items.

c7_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch12.scenario: A sports-day timer prints three 100 m times: Tara 14.2 s, Zoya 14.05 s, Isha 14.125 s. Handing out medals, a volunteer announces Zoya ran the slowest 'because .05 is the smallest decimal bit — only 5.'
c7_math_ch12.prompt: How should the times really be ordered?

options.text: Pad to thousandths: 14.200, 14.050, 14.125 — so Zoya (14.05) is fastest, then Isha, then Tara. The decimal part is not a whole number; .2 means 2 tenths, i.e. 200 thousandths, far more than 50.
options.outcome: This equalises decimal places before comparing, which is the only reliable way to order decimals of different lengths.

options.text: The volunteer is right — with fewer digits after the point, 14.05 is plainly the smallest number and the slowest time.
options.outcome: That compares 5 to 200 to 125 as if the digits were whole numbers; the tenths place decides first, and 14.05 has the smallest tenth-digit block.

options.text: Since all three are 'fourteen point something', the times are tied and medals should be shared equally.
options.outcome: The fractional parts differ by hundredths of a second — exactly what a sprint timer exists to distinguish.

c7_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch13.scenario: For a statistics project, Reema drafts two survey questions: 'How many students are in Class 7B right now?' and 'How many hours of sleep did each Class 7B student get last night?' She claims both are equally good data questions.
c7_math_ch13.prompt: Which question is genuinely statistical, and why?

options.text: Only the sleep question — it expects a different answer from every student, so it studies variability. The head-count question has one fixed answer; everyone asked gives the same number, so nothing varies to analyse.
options.outcome: This applies the variability test: a statistical question anticipates a spread of answers across a group, not a single lookup.

options.text: Both are statistical — any question whose answer is a number produces data for statistics.
options.outcome: A number answer alone is not enough; with zero variation across responses there is no distribution to study.

options.text: Neither is statistical — real statistical questions must ask for an average or a percentage, not a plain count.
options.outcome: Summaries like averages come later; what makes a question statistical is the variable data it gathers, not the statistic computed afterward.

c7_math_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch14.scenario: In a constructions worksheet, Madhav must copy segment AB onto a fresh line. He reads '6.2 cm' off his ruler and draws from the 0 mark to 6.2 on the new line, then wonders why his later arcs do not intersect symmetrically — his compass hinge slipped mid-way.
c7_math_ch14.prompt: What does proper construction require instead?

options.text: Set the compass span directly from A to B and transfer it without changing the width — the compass carries the exact distance, so no numbers are needed and the copy cannot drift; also hold the compass by its top knob so the hinge cannot slip.
options.outcome: This is the Euclidean method: a fixed compass width guarantees equal radii and equal lengths, avoiding ruler-reading errors and mid-arc slipping.

options.text: His method was already a perfect construction — reading the scale and redrawing is exactly what the tools are for.
options.outcome: That is measurement, not construction; scale markings invite parallax and worn-edge errors, and the compass exists precisely to transfer length without numbers.

options.text: The fix is to squeeze the compass legs tighter and press harder on the paper so the width cannot change.
options.outcome: Gripping the legs is what makes the hinge slip; the correct habit is holding the top knob and re-checking the span before each new arc.

c7_math_ch15.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch15.scenario: Homework says: 'A vendor puts x kg of potatoes plus 3 kg of onions on one pan, and it balances 18 kg of weights.' Binita writes 4x + 3 and tries to 'solve it for x.' Her friend claims x = 5 already solves the equation 4x + 3 = 18.
c7_math_ch15.prompt: What is wrong with both claims?

options.text: The situation is x + 3 = 18 — an equation needs an equals sign, and 'x kg of potatoes' is just x, not 4x. And testing x = 5 in 4x + 3 gives 23, not 18, so it fails the balance check anyway.
options.outcome: This separates expressions from equations and verifies solutions by substitution — both fixes are grounded in what the equals sign means.

options.text: Binita is close enough — any string with a letter can be solved, so 4x + 3 can be set to zero to find x.
options.outcome: An expression has no balance condition, so there is nothing to solve; inventing '= 0' answers a different problem entirely.

options.text: The friend is right — x = 5 must work because the number was chosen sensibly, and substitution is only for checking your own answers.
options.outcome: Substitution checks any claimed solution: LHS at x = 5 is 23 while RHS is 18, so the claim collapses on testing.

c7_physics_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch01.scenario: In a classroom demo, a flat sheet of paper and the same-size sheet crumpled into a ball are dropped together — the ball lands first. Aryan declares, 'Science already told us: heavy things fall faster,' and closes the question.
c7_physics_ch01.prompt: What would a scientific next step look like?

options.text: Treat his claim as a hypothesis and test it: the two sheets have identical mass, so mass cannot explain the result — vary the shape while keeping mass fixed (or repeat with different objects) and record fall times to isolate air resistance as the cause.
options.outcome: This is the scientific process: question, identify the real variable, control the others, and let evidence — not a remembered slogan — decide.

options.text: Aryan is right to stop — once a result matches a familiar rule, no experiment is needed.
options.outcome: The observation actually contradicts the rule: equal masses fell differently, so the slogan fails and a new variable must be tested.

options.text: The experiment failed because it disproved the guess, so they should drop the whole thing and pick an easier topic.
options.outcome: A result that disproves a hypothesis is still a success — it rules out a wrong explanation and points at the better question to ask.

c7_physics_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch02.scenario: On a winter evening, Sameer plugs a room heater and a water geyser into the same wall socket to save time, saying 'electricity is electricity — the socket will manage.' His mother reaches for the plug board.
c7_physics_ch02.prompt: Who is right about the risk?

options.text: His mother — both are high-power heating appliances that draw heavy current together, which can overheat the wiring and cause a short circuit or fire; the socket's limit is about total load, not about whether the switch is on.
options.outcome: This recognises that appliances convert electrical energy to heat and that simultaneous heavy loads exceed safe current limits.

options.text: Sameer is right — a live socket supplies whatever is plugged in, so two heaters are no different from one.
options.outcome: Wiring is rated for a limited current; doubling high-power heating loads overheats conductors regardless of the switch position.

options.text: The real danger is that electricity gets 'used up' and disappears inside the heater, so running two wastes it faster.
options.outcome: Energy is not consumed into nothing — it converts to heat, light or motion; the issue here is excess current load, not depletion.

c7_physics_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch03.scenario: At a school picnic, Gopi warns everyone: 'Don't stand near that big tub of warm bath water — the tiny steel glass of boiling tea in my hand has way more heat, so it's harmless compared to the tub.'
c7_physics_ch03.prompt: Has he got heat and temperature straight?

options.text: No — the tea has the higher temperature (faster average particle motion, so it scalds on contact), but the huge tub holds vastly more water molecules and therefore far more total thermal energy; temperature is hotness, heat is total energy — they are different quantities.
options.outcome: This keeps the two concepts separate: temperature decides burn intensity and the direction of heat flow, while total heat depends on mass as well.

options.text: He is right — whatever is hotter contains more heat, so the cup outweighs the tub in heat.
options.outcome: Heat content scales with the number of particles; a lukewarm swimming pool stores far more joules than a boiling cup.

options.text: He is half right — the tub has more heat, so it must also be at a higher temperature than the tea.
options.outcome: More total energy does not mean higher temperature; the tub's energy is spread over far more particles, so each particle moves slower than in the tea.

c7_physics_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch04.scenario: For a history-cum-science exhibit, a class builds a sundial and a bottle water clock. On the day of the fair the sky is overcast, and the water clock seems to run fast when freshly filled. A visitor asks why both are 'failing.'
c7_physics_ch04.prompt: How should the students explain the behaviour?

options.text: The sundial needs direct sunlight travelling in straight lines to cast the gnomon's shadow, so clouds blind it; the water clock runs fast when full because a higher water level means higher pressure and a faster drip — neither device is broken, both are hostage to their physical inputs.
options.outcome: This ties each limitation to its mechanism — blocked light for the sundial, level-dependent flow for the water clock — which is exactly why later clocks needed regulation.

options.text: Both clocks are just poorly built — a properly made sundial and water clock keep perfect time in all weathers.
options.outcome: No craftsmanship removes the dependence: shadows need sunlight, and a draining vessel's flow slows as its level falls, so calibration is always needed.

options.text: The sundial is failing because cold cloudy air slows down shadow movement, and the water clock speeds up because warm water drips faster — it's all about temperature.
options.outcome: Clouds block light rather than slow shadows, and while temperature does change water flow, the fast start here comes from water pressure at high level, not warmth.

c7_physics_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch05.scenario: On a night cycling trip, Chotu's red rear reflector blazes whenever a car headlight hits it. He tells his sister, 'My reflector is a light source, just like the moon — they both shine in the dark.'
c7_physics_ch05.prompt: Are the reflector and the moon really light sources?

options.text: Neither — a source must emit its own light. The reflector only bounces back headlight beams, and the moon only returns sunlight; put both in true darkness with nothing shining on them and they go black. A firefly or a bulb genuinely emits light.
options.outcome: This applies the emit-versus-reflect test: visibility alone does not make a source, only self-generated light does.

options.text: Chotu is right — anything that shines brightly in the dark is a light source by definition.
options.outcome: Shining by reflected light is being a mirror, not a source; the test is whether it glows when no outside light falls on it.

options.text: The moon is a natural light source because it is huge and in the sky, but the reflector is not because humans made it.
options.outcome: Natural-versus-artificial is about origin, but source-versus-reflector is about emission: the moon emits nothing, whatever its size or pedigree.

c7_physics_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch06.scenario: During a video call at lunchtime, Vani's cousin in America says it is midnight there. Vani's little brother objects: 'The sun must have moved under the Earth to reach them — that is where it goes at night.'
c7_physics_ch06.prompt: What actually explains the noon-midnight split?

options.text: The sun stays put; Earth spins west to east on its axis, so the half facing the sun has day while the opposite half sits in Earth's own shadow — as India rotates into the light, the other side rotates out of it. One rotation takes about 24 hours.
options.outcome: This swaps apparent motion for real motion: the daily cycle is Earth's spin carrying us in and out of sunlight, not the sun travelling around us.

options.text: The brother is right — every night the sun slips underneath the Earth and re-emerges in the east by morning.
options.outcome: That is a geocentric picture; the spinning-chair illusion makes a stationary sun seem to move, but it is our rotation that carries us away from it.

options.text: They are both partly right — it is midnight in America because clouds there are blocking the sun, and it will clear by their morning.
options.outcome: Night is not weather cover; it is the geometric shadow cast by an opaque, rotating Earth — half the planet is always dark.

c7_physics_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c7_physics_ch07.scenario: Sorting three unlabelled kitchen liquids — lemon juice, sugar water and soap solution — Farida's partner suggests the fastest method: 'Sip a drop of each; sour means acid, bitter and soapy means base.'
