c7_physics_ch07.prompt: What is the safe and correct way to classify them?

options.text: Never taste unknown liquids — touch-test is risky too. Use an indicator instead: red litmus turning blue marks the basic soap solution, blue litmus turning red marks the acidic lemon juice, and no change marks the neutral sugar water.
options.outcome: This uses the defining colour-change behaviour of indicators, which is exactly why scientists test with litmus or turmeric rather than their senses.

options.text: The partner is right — taste is the official test, and since lemon juice is safe, any sour liquid is just a harmless food acid.
options.outcome: Taste-testing unknown liquids is dangerous because strong acids and bases corrode tissue; and 'all sour things are safe' forgets that corrosive mineral acids are also acidic.

options.text: Just smell each bottle — strong smells are always bases, mild smells always acids, and no special paper is needed.
options.outcome: Odour does not map to acid or base at all; classification rests on indicator reactions and properties like soapy feel, not on how something smells.

c8_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_bio_ch01.scenario: At a science exhibition, a poster says: 'Robert Hooke discovered living cells swimming around in cork, and Leeuwenhoek invented the multi-lens compound microscope.' A visitor asks the student presenter if the poster is accurate.

options.text: Swap both claims: Hooke saw only dead, empty box-like walls in cork bark — he named them 'cells' after monks' rooms — while Leeuwenhoek used a single finely ground lens to watch living microbes moving in pond water.
options.outcome: This assigns each scientist his real contribution: dead plant walls versus living animalcules, compound versus simple high-power lens.

options.text: The poster is right — the man who named cells must have seen them alive, and more lenses always means a better microscope.
options.outcome: Cork cells were dead walls with nothing living inside, and Leeuwenhoek's single hand-ground lenses out-magnified the blurry compound scopes of the day.

options.text: Neither matters — both men proved the full cell theory that all organisms are made of cells, so the details are interchangeable.
options.outcome: Hooke only saw empty walls and cell theory took two more centuries of work; crediting either man with the finished theory skips the entire history.

c8_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_bio_ch02.scenario: A classmate tops every exam, never falls sick and jogs daily, but lately he eats lunch alone, snaps at friends and says he feels constantly tense. He insists, 'I am perfectly healthy — look at my report card and my stamina.'
c8_bio_ch02.prompt: Is he healthy by the full definition?

options.text: Not fully — health means complete physical, mental and social well-being together. His body is fine, but the tension (mental) and isolation and conflict (social) mean a dimension is failing, and a strong report card does not patch it.
options.outcome: This applies the three-dimension definition: no-disease-plus-fitness is only one third of health.

options.text: He is right — health is a medical state, and since he has no disease and good stamina, nothing else counts.
options.outcome: That is the narrow view the definition rejects; mental strain and broken social ties are health problems even with a perfect body.

options.text: He is unhealthy only if the stress gives him a fever — until a physical symptom appears, mental and social issues are separate matters.
options.outcome: Waiting for a fever confuses dimensions with symptoms; anxiety and loneliness already impair the mental and social dimensions directly.

c8_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_chem_ch02.scenario: At lunch, Diya stirs two spoons of salt into a full glass of water. The salt disappears and the water level barely rises. Her brother concludes, 'The salt is gone — it merged into the water.'
c8_chem_ch02.prompt: What really happened to the salt?

options.text: It broke into countless invisible particles that slipped into the empty spaces between water particles — which is why the level hardly rose and the water tastes uniformly salty. The salt is still there, just dispersed.
options.outcome: This uses the particulate model correctly: matter is made of discrete particles with gaps between them, so dissolving spreads rather than destroys.

options.text: The brother is right — once it disappears from sight, the salt has fused into water as a single continuous material.
options.outcome: Matter is not a continuous sheet; the salt's particles are intact and recoverable by evaporation — disappearance is dispersion, not fusion.

options.text: The salt turned into water molecules, which is why the volume did not increase.
options.outcome: No chemical change happened — the particles are still salt, sitting in the gaps between water particles; boiling water does not even break H2O into atoms, let alone salt.

c8_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_chem_ch03.scenario: In the school lab, Kabir stirs grey iron filings with yellow sulfur powder and gets a speckled blend. His partner writes 'new compound formed' in the record book because two elements are now touching.

options.text: No — it is a mixture: no chemical reaction occurred, the proportions were arbitrary, and dragging a magnet through the blend pulls the iron out unchanged, proving each part kept its own properties. Only heating it would make the compound iron sulfide.
options.outcome: This applies the mixture test: components that keep their properties and separate physically never bonded chemically.

options.text: The partner is right — whenever two elements share a container, a compound with new properties results.
options.outcome: Compounds need chemical bonding in fixed proportions; a magnet still lifts the iron out, so no new substance exists here.

options.text: It cannot be a mixture because mixtures are only liquids like salt water — two solids together must be a compound.
options.outcome: Mixtures can be solid-solid too, like bhel or this powder blend; the test is retained properties and physical separability, not state.

c8_civ_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_civ_ch01.scenario: A housing society holds elections for its committee. The chairman proposes: 'Members who pay higher maintenance fees get three votes; ordinary members get one. Also, tenants who don't own flats may not vote.'
c8_civ_ch01.prompt: Does this fit the democratic principle of universal adult franchise?

options.text: No — franchise means one person, one vote of equal value for every adult citizen, with no weighting by wealth and no exclusion by property status; fees buy services, not extra political power.
options.outcome: This recognises that the equal value of each vote is the heart of the principle — letting money multiply votes recreates the old restricted-franchise systems democracy abolished.

options.text: It is fair — those who pay more have more at stake, so heavier votes reflect their bigger contribution.
options.outcome: That argument was exactly what property-based franchise used to justify; democracy counts heads, not wallets, because political equality cannot be purchased.

options.text: Only the tenant ban is wrong — excluding non-owners breaks the rule, but weighted votes for payers are acceptable.
options.outcome: Both clauses fail the same test: 'universal' bars exclusions and 'one vote of equal value' bars weighting; fixing only one still leaves unequal votes.

c8_civ_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_civ_ch02.scenario: During a mock-parliament club session, a student says: 'Indians vote directly for the Prime Minister, and once chosen he rules for a fixed term no matter what MPs do — just like a president.'
c8_civ_ch02.prompt: What is the correct picture of India's system?

options.text: Citizens elect MPs; the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha picks the Prime Minister from among them. The executive sits inside the legislature and survives only while it keeps the house's confidence — MPs can question ministers daily and a lost majority vote brings the government down.
options.outcome: This captures the defining feature of a parliamentary system: the executive is drawn from the legislature and continuously accountable to it.

options.text: The student is right — the PM is chosen in a separate national ballot and cannot be removed mid-term.
options.outcome: That describes a presidential system; India has no direct executive ballot, and a no-confidence motion can end a government any day.

options.text: Neither — the President appoints anyone he likes as Prime Minister, so the legislature plays no role at all.
options.outcome: The President appoints whoever commands the Lok Sabha majority; the choice flows from the elected house, not personal preference.

c8_civ_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_civ_ch03.scenario: In a school, one boy keeps grabbing all the cricket gear at recess. The sports committee debates two fixes: suspending him for a week, or writing a fair-turns roster so every class gets the kit.
c8_civ_ch03.prompt: Which response is closer to the full idea of justice?

options.text: The roster — justice is not only punishing wrongdoing after it happens but building fair rules that prevent it; the Preamble promises social, economic and political justice, meaning equal access and dignity, not just penalties.
options.outcome: This widens justice from punishment to fairness-by-design: a system where no one can monopolise a shared resource in the first place.

options.text: Suspension alone — justice is complete only when a wrongdoer is punished hard enough to scare others.
options.outcome: Punishment is one slice of justice; without changing the unfair arrangement, the same grabbing starts again next term.

options.text: Neither — it is just playground squabbling, and justice is a court-and-police word that does not apply to schools.
options.outcome: Justice applies wherever fairness is at stake; a classroom injustice is the small-scale version of the same principle the Constitution promises.

c8_civ_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_civ_ch04.scenario: A foreign businessman who has lived in Pune for six years, pays all local taxes and employs fifty people demands a voter ID: 'I pay my share and live here — that makes me a citizen.'
c8_civ_ch04.prompt: Does residence plus taxes make him an Indian citizen?

options.text: No — citizenship is a legal membership defined by the Constitution and law (birth, descent, naturalisation), carrying political rights like voting and office. He is a resident with civil protections, and paying taxes does not purchase political membership.
options.outcome: This separates legal membership from mere presence and contribution — the exact distinction Articles 5-11 and citizenship law draw.

options.text: Yes — anyone who lives in a country long enough and pays taxes has earned the vote automatically.
options.outcome: Residency and tax-paying are obligations of anyone present, not membership; without naturalisation he remains a foreign national however long he stays.

options.text: Yes, but only if he also owns property — property plus residence together complete the requirements.
options.outcome: Neither taxes nor property figure in the constitutional routes to citizenship; adding a property clause invents a rule that does not exist.

c8_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_eco_ch01.scenario: For an economics poster, Tara photographs a car factory and captions it 'production.' Her partner says their mother's hair salon cannot appear on the poster 'because no goods roll off an assembly line there.'
c8_eco_ch01.prompt: Should the salon be on the poster?

options.text: Yes — production is any process combining inputs into outputs that satisfy wants. The salon uses scissors, shampoo, electricity and the stylist's labour (inputs) and transforms them into haircuts and styling services (outputs); services count just as much as factory goods.
options.outcome: This applies the input-transformation-output definition broadly, recognising that value creation is not limited to manufacturing.

options.text: The partner is right — production means factories and machines, so a salon is just a service, not production.
options.outcome: That restricts production to physical goods and erases the service economy; a haircut is an output created from real inputs and labour.

options.text: Only if the salon also sells shampoo bottles — a service alone is never an output because you cannot hold it.
options.outcome: Outputs can be intangible; software and haircuts satisfy wants without being holdable, so the haircut already qualifies.

c8_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_eco_ch02.scenario: Two districts each hold 100,000 people. District A records 2,500 births and 500 deaths a year; District B records 1,000 births and 1,200 deaths. A planner says, 'Same population, same budget needs — copy the plan across both.'

options.text: No — demography is about change, not a static count. District A grows by 2,000 a year and will need far more primary schools as its babies age in; District B is actually shrinking by 200 a year, so copying the plan wastes resources.
options.outcome: This applies births, deaths and migration as the drivers of population change, and shows why structure — not just size — shapes demand.

options.text: Yes — planning is about the total headcount, and since both totals match today, the needs match too.
options.outcome: The totals hide opposite trajectories: A is adding 2,500 children annually while B loses people, so their school and clinic needs diverge within a few years.

options.text: District B needs more schools — shrinking places always need extra facilities to attract people back.
options.outcome: B's low birth rate means fewer children arriving, so expanding schools there serves a cohort that is not growing; need follows the age structure, not the wish.

c8_eco_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_eco_ch03.scenario: A village of 8,000 people gets concrete roads, 4G towers and a new mall, while 80% of its workers still farm wheat and its homes spread over 25 sq km. Its sarpanch declares it is now officially a city.
c8_eco_ch03.prompt: Does the Census definition back him up?

options.text: No — urban classification needs all three criteria together: at least 5,000 people, density of 400 per sq km, and 75% of male main workers in non-farm jobs. This village passes only the population test; 8,000 over 25 sq km is 320 per sq km, and 80% farming fails the occupation test.
options.outcome: This applies the conjunctive criteria rather than judging by modern looks — amenities do not reclassify a settlement.

options.text: Yes — paved roads, malls and smartphones are what make a place urban; paperwork thresholds are outdated.
options.outcome: Urban status is structural, not cosmetic: it is defined by how densely people live and how they earn their living, and this village's economy is still agricultural.

options.text: Yes — with 8,000 people it clears the population bar, and the Census only requires one of the three criteria.
options.outcome: The three criteria must hold simultaneously; meeting population while failing density and occupation still leaves it rural.

c8_engl_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_engl_ch01.scenario: A class performs a skit where Tenali Ramakrishna marches up to King Krishnadeva Raya and shouts, 'You are wrong, Your Majesty!' in front of the whole court. The teacher asks whether the scene is believable for its setting.
c8_engl_ch01.prompt: What does the setting demand instead?

options.text: Indirect wit — a 16th-century royal court ran on strict protocol and the king's absolute power, so plain contradiction could mean banishment or worse; the setting is exactly why Tenali wraps criticism in humour and riddles.
options.outcome: This treats setting as more than a painted backdrop: time period, place and social rules together dictate how a character may speak.

options.text: The skit is fine — honest people speak their mind in every era, and setting is just scenery behind the dialogue.
options.outcome: That flattens setting into location only; the Vijayanagara court's hierarchy made direct defiance dangerous, so the scene breaks its own rules.

options.text: Tenali should simply stay silent and say nothing at all, since courts tolerated no opinions.
options.outcome: Courtiers did influence kings — the point is how: clever indirection, not muteness, is what the setting makes necessary and what makes Tenali's role possible.

c8_engl_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_engl_ch02.scenario: A friend summarises a chapter on 1947: 'India launched Operation Gulmarg to grab Kashmir, sent troops in first, and the Maharaja signed papers later to make it legal.' Another student frowns at the sequence.
c8_engl_ch02.prompt: What does the correct order of events show?

options.text: The invasion came first — tribesmen reached Baramulla by 24 October; the Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October; only then did Indian troops land at Srinagar airport on 27 October. Gulmarg began as an emergency defence of the valley's only air lifeline, not a land grab.
options.outcome: This keeps the sequence straight and shows why accession had to precede deployment — Indian entry was legally impossible before it.

options.text: The friend's version works — the paperwork is just a formality that could follow the troops.
options.outcome: Reversing accession and troop landing turns a defensive response into an invasion; the legal accession is what made the deployment possible at all.

options.text: The Maharaja invited Indian troops weeks earlier as part of a pre-planned offensive to take the whole region.
options.outcome: He had actually delayed choosing either country, hoping to stay independent; only the tribal invasion forced his hand — nothing about it was pre-planned expansion.

c8_engl_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_engl_ch03.scenario: In a book-club discussion, a classmate says Encyclopedia Brown cracks cases because 'he's just the smartest person in town — smarter than every adult.' A teammate wants to argue the real reason is something else entirely.
c8_engl_ch03.prompt: What actually makes the boy detective effective?

options.text: His childlike perspective — he questions the assumptions adults take for granted and spots the small, mundane details they dismiss, like a stopped clock contradicting a suspect's alibi. His repeatable method is observation, not luck or superior book knowledge.
options.outcome: This links trait to theme correctly: his age gives him fresh eyes, which is precisely what lets him see what experience-blinded adults miss.

options.text: The first classmate is right — reading that many books simply makes him smarter than the grown-ups, including the police chief.
options.outcome: The stories show him beating adults at noticing, not knowing; his edge is a viewpoint free of adult assumptions, not a bigger memory.

options.text: It is mostly luck — he happens to glance at the right detail at the right moment in each case.
options.outcome: Luck is not repeatable, but his method is: he deliberately checks statements against physical evidence every single time.

c8_engl_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_engl_ch04.scenario: Summarising 'The Cherry Tree' for homework, a student writes: 'Setting: Mussoorie. The story is just about a boy and his grandfather, so the place doesn't matter — it could be anywhere.'
c8_engl_ch04.prompt: What does the Mussoorie setting actually contribute?

options.text: It is an active force — stony soil, icy winds, steep slopes, grazing goats and monsoon downpours are the obstacles the seedling must survive; strip them away and the tree's survival is no longer an earned triumph of resilience.
options.outcome: This shows setting driving the conflict: the Himalayan environment creates the struggle that gives the story its meaning.

options.text: The student is right — naming the town completes the setting analysis, and the plot would unfold identically on a warm farm in the plains.
options.outcome: On soft fertile soil a seed's survival is routine, not miraculous; the harsh terrain is what turns a small tree into the story's achievement.

options.text: The setting matters only for mood — it makes the story feel cold and quiet but changes nothing that happens.
options.outcome: Mood is only half of it; the cold snaps, slopes and goats directly threaten the sapling and shape what the characters must do.

c8_engl_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c8_engl_ch05.scenario: A student rewriting 'Feathered Friend' moves the story to a deep underground bunker on Earth 'because it's still isolated and has artificial air — same thing.' His editor asks if anything essential is lost.
c8_engl_ch05.prompt: Does the swap preserve what the setting does?

options.text: No — a bunker keeps normal gravity, so the canary's effortless slow-motion loops that endear her to the crew vanish; and the station's isolation is absolute, thousands of miles from help, which is what makes depending on a bird — after expensive sensors fail — so ironic and so tense.
options.outcome: This evaluates setting element by element: low gravity and unreachable isolation are load-bearing parts of the plot, not interchangeable décor.

options.text: The swap works — sealed air and isolation are the whole setting, so nothing important changes.
options.outcome: That misses the zero-gravity behaviour that makes the bird special and the spatial isolation that raises the stakes; two of the setting's jobs disappear.

options.text: It actually improves the story — on Earth the crew could just open a window for fresh air whenever oxygen ran low.
options.outcome: Opening a window erases the central survival constraint; the crew's total dependence on machines is precisely what the canary's warning had to overcome.

c8_geo_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_geo_ch01.scenario: A geologist reports rich iron ore 5 km under a forest. Digging would cost ₹10,000 per tonne while ore sells at ₹4,000. A local official declares, 'Iron is useful, so this deposit is already a resource — start mining.'
c8_geo_ch01.prompt: Is the deposit a resource yet?

options.text: Not yet — a substance becomes a resource only when it is useful, technologically reachable, economically feasible AND culturally acceptable. Useful it is, and reachable barely, but extraction costs more than the ore is worth, so it stays a potential resource.
options.outcome: This applies all four criteria rather than stopping at usefulness — physical existence alone never makes a resource.

options.text: The official is right — anything useful found in nature is automatically a resource we can use.
options.outcome: That confuses a natural deposit with a resource; the same logic would call ancient sunlight a power plant before solar technology existed.

options.text: It fails only because mining technology is lacking — with better drills the price problem disappears.
options.outcome: Even with perfect drills the economics fail: paying ₹10,000 to recover ₹4,000 of ore is unfeasible regardless of the machinery used.

c8_geo_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_geo_ch02.scenario: A school globe looks perfectly round, so a classmate insists Earth is an exact sphere. He adds that since the flattening is 'only 42 km,' printing the globe onto flat paper should lose nothing at all.
c8_geo_ch02.prompt: Which parts of his claim need correcting?

options.text: Both parts: Earth is an oblate spheroid — spinning pushes material outward fastest at the equator, bulging it (~12,756 km) relative to the poles (~12,714 km). And no curved 3D surface, however slightly flattened, lies flat on paper without stretching or squeezing shapes — that is why map projections always distort something.
options.outcome: This links the rotation-causes-bulge mechanism to the unavoidable map-distortion consequence.

options.text: He is right on both counts — the globe looks round, and a 42 km difference is too tiny to matter for maps.
options.outcome: Looks deceive: the bulge is only ~0.33% of the diameter, invisible to the eye but real — and the flattening is not what distorts maps; flattening any sphere onto a plane does.

options.text: The bulge exists, but it is caused by gravity pulling harder at the equator, piling matter outward there.
options.outcome: Gravity pulls inward everywhere; the equator bulges because it is farthest from the rotation axis and spins fastest, so outward centrifugal effect peaks there.

c8_hist_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_hist_ch01.scenario: For a history debate, Ravi argues: 'Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghori did the same thing — both invaded to build an empire in Delhi, and both beat the Rajputs because Rajputs were cowards.'
c8_hist_ch01.prompt: Which parts of his argument fail the evidence?

options.text: Both parts. Mahmud raided for temple wealth to fund his Ghazni empire and never tried to govern the Gangetic plain; Ghori, 150 years later, annexed territory and left governors behind — leading to the Delhi Sultanate. And the Rajputs were famously brave: they lost to mobile horse archers with stirrups outmanoeuvring war elephants, plus rival kingdoms that never united.
options.outcome: This separates plunder from conquest and replaces a 'bravery' story with structural causes — technology and political fragmentation.

options.text: Ravi is right — an invader is an invader, and whichever side loses a battle was simply less brave.
options.outcome: That erases the raid-versus-conquest distinction and ignores that the Rajputs actually defeated Ghori at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191 — courage was not the deficit; coordination and cavalry tactics were.

options.text: The motives differed, but the Rajputs did lose because elephants are useless animals in any battle.
options.outcome: Elephants had won Indian battles for centuries; the failure was tactical — fast horse archers circling and panicking them — not the animals being inherently useless.

c8_hist_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_hist_ch02.scenario: A classmate insists the Marathas 'appeared out of nowhere in the 1600s when Shivaji created them as a warrior caste.' A friend points to the older Wari pilgrimage, where farmers have sung Marathi abhangas together for centuries.
c8_hist_ch02.prompt: Whose account does the evidence support?

options.text: The friend's — Maratha identity grew for centuries before Shivaji: Kunbi cultivators served as seasonal cavalry and rose into Maratha status, while the Marathi language and Bhakti saints like Dnyaneshwar welded farmers and warriors into one regional community long before any coronation.
options.outcome: This credits the deep linguistic and cultural groundwork instead of crediting one ruler with inventing a people.

options.text: The first classmate is right — a political identity begins only when a king proclaims it, so 'Maratha' started with Shivaji.
options.outcome: Identity is built by shared language and custom, not proclamation; the Bhakti movement and Sultanate service had fused that community by the 16th century.

options.text: Both are partly wrong — Kunbis and Marathas were always two sealed, unrelated castes with no overlap.
options.outcome: Records show the same families farmed in peace and rode as militia in war; it was a fluid continuum, not two fixed castes.

c8_hist_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_hist_ch03.scenario: A student writes in her notebook: 'Colonialism began at Plassey in 1757 when the British government invaded India — just another foreign conquest like the Mughals before them.' Her teacher asks her to check two claims against the record.

options.text: Both claims need repair: Europeans had been in India since 1498 and moved in stages — trade, then fortified coastal enclaves, then political control — and Plassey was a turning point, not a start. Unlike the Mughals, who settled and reinvested revenue locally, the Company drained India's wealth to a distant state — that extraction is what makes it colonialism.
options.outcome: This places Plassey inside a 250-year multi-power process and draws the key structural line between settled conquerors and absentee exploiters.

options.text: Her note is correct — 1757 is the founding moment, and all foreign rulers are basically the same.
options.outcome: That compresses two and a half centuries of Portuguese, Dutch, French and English rivalry into one date and misses that Mughals lived off and spent within India while the Company shipped surplus home.

options.text: Only the date is wrong — colonialism began in 1498 the day Vasco da Gama landed, because arrival equals conquest.
options.outcome: Arrival was trade, not rule; for over two centuries Europeans held only fortified coastal posts, and conquest came much later through specific 18th-century contingencies.

c8_hist_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_hist_ch04.scenario: A museum caption reads: 'Before 1857, India slept — the only sparks were a few sepoy mutinies over religious insults.' A student who has read about the Sanyasi, Paika, Kol and Santhal risings challenges the caption.
c8_hist_ch04.prompt: What does the record actually show about early resistance?

options.text: The caption is wrong on both counts: dozens of uprisings flared between 1757 and 1857, and most were peasant and tribal movements driven by land revenue, lost customary rights and exploitation — led by local chiefs and figures like Jayi Rajguru, not soldiers. They failed mainly because each stayed local, restoring its own grievances rather than joining a shared cause.
options.outcome: This corrects the 'sepoys only' picture and gives the structural reason the risings were crushed one at a time.

options.text: The caption is fair — the countryside stayed quiet because only sepoys had grievances worth fighting over.
options.outcome: The archive says otherwise: famines, resumed jagirs, doubled taxes and moneylender seizure pushed peasants and tribals into repeated armed revolts decades before 1857.

options.text: The uprisings were real but failed simply because Indians lacked muskets and drill — weapons were the whole story.
options.outcome: Technology mattered, but the deeper cause was fragmentation: isolated risings defending local privileges could be suppressed piecemeal regardless of weaponry.

c8_hist_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c8_hist_ch05.scenario: On a heritage walk, a guide claims: 'Temple builders kept using post-and-lintel beams even after arches arrived because they simply did not know the new technique — Indian engineering only started when outsiders brought the arch.'
c8_hist_ch05.prompt: How should a student of Indian architecture respond?

options.text: Push back — the lintel choice was deliberate: the horizontal beam carried ritual meaning as the threshold between worlds, and arches were meanwhile being used in secular and water structures. Indian masons had centuries of stone innovation (corbelling, interlocking, polished Mauryan shafts) — the arch was absorbed, not the beginning.
options.outcome: This separates technological ignorance from cultural choice and recognises India's continuous engineering tradition.

options.text: The guide is right — a technique unused must be a technique unknown.
options.outcome: Builders used arches where they wanted them; temple form followed symbolic grammar, so choosing not to arch a shrine was a decision, not a gap in skill.

options.text: Both are wrong — architecture is pure art, so debating construction technique misses the point of the monuments.
options.outcome: The tradition never split art from engineering; every carvings-and-load decision was both aesthetic and structural at once.

c8_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch01.scenario: Tiling a square classroom floor 6 m by 6 m with 1-metre tiles, Bunty writes '6² = 6 × 2 = 12 tiles.' His partner recounts the rows and disagrees.

options.text: The partner — 6² means 6 × 6, giving 36 tiles: six rows of six unit squares. The little 2 means 'multiply the number by itself', the area of a square of side 6 — not 'times 2', which would describe a 6-by-2 rectangle.
options.outcome: This ties the exponent to the area model: n² counts the unit squares inside an n-by-n square.

options.text: Bunty is right — the superscript 2 tells you to multiply the number by 2.
options.outcome: That reading would make 5² = 10, but a 5-by-5 grid plainly holds 25 tiles; the 2 marks two equal factors, not a second addend.

options.text: Both are wrong — 6² means 2 multiplied by itself 6 times, so the floor needs 64 tiles.
options.outcome: That swaps base and exponent; 2⁶ is a different quantity entirely, and the floor would overflow long before 64 tiles fit.

c8_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch02.scenario: For a paper-art project, Leela folds a sheet in half repeatedly to build thickness. After 2 folds she counts 4 layers and predicts '10 layers at the 5th fold — two more each time.'
c8_math_ch02.prompt: How many layers will the 5th fold actually give?

options.text: 32 — every fold doubles all the layers already there: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Her rule 'add 2' only matched the first step by coincidence; the pattern multiplies by 2, it does not add.
options.outcome: This separates multiplicative growth from additive growth — the constant is the factor ×2, not the amount +2.

options.text: Her prediction stands — the count went 2, 4, so the rule is clearly +2 and the 5th fold gives 10.
options.outcome: The third fold already breaks the rule — it gives 8, not 6; trusting the first two terms misreads doubling as adding.

options.text: The 5th fold gives 25 layers, because fold number times itself — squaring the count of folds.
options.outcome: Squaring the fold number is a different pattern; layers track the previous layer count, not the fold count — each fold only sees 'how many layers exist now' and doubles it.

c8_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch03.scenario: In a skit about early humans, a student plays a herder with no number words who must check whether all 40 goats returned at dusk. He suggests: 'I'll just look at the herd and remember what it looked like.'
c8_math_ch03.prompt: What method would actually work without numbers?

options.text: Pair each goat with one pebble in a bag in the morning, then match returning goats against the pebbles at dusk — leftover pebbles mean missing goats. This one-to-one matching is exactly how pre-numeric peoples counted before number words existed.
options.outcome: This shows counting's origin: external one-to-one records solve 'how many' when memory and eyesight fail at scale.

options.text: His plan works fine — humans can spot a missing goat by looking, which is why numbers were never really needed.
options.outcome: Instant recognition collapses beyond a handful of items; at 40 goats a missing one is invisible, which is precisely the problem that invented counting.

options.text: He should shout 'forty' at the sky each morning — even without written symbols, number words work.
options.outcome: The scene has no number words at all; the historical fix was physical matching — tallies, pebbles, knots — with symbols and words arriving only later.

c8_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch04.scenario: Surveying a plot for a school garden, students measure three corners as 100°, 110° and 70°. Without measuring, the teacher asks the fourth angle. A student objects: 'The plot isn't a neat rectangle, so the 360° rule may not apply.'
c8_math_ch04.prompt: Does the angle-sum rule still hold?

options.text: Yes — any quadrilateral, however irregular, splits along a diagonal into two triangles, so its interior angles total 2 × 180° = 360°; the missing corner is 360 − (100+110+70) = 80°.
options.outcome: This applies the proof behind the rule — two triangles — which works for every four-sided closed figure, even concave ones.

options.text: The student is right — the 360° total only holds for rectangles and squares where all angles look equal.
options.outcome: The rule depends on having four sides, not on looking regular; a lopsided or even a dented concave quadrilateral still sums to 360°.

options.text: The rule gives 180°, not 360° — quadrilaterals follow the same angle sum as triangles.
options.outcome: A quadrilateral contains two triangles' worth of angles, so the total doubles the triangle's 180°.

c8_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch05.scenario: In a number-game round, the host says: 'Pick any four consecutive whole numbers — your sum will always be a multiple of 4, because there are four terms.' A contestant hesitates before playing along.
c8_math_ch05.prompt: Is the host's claim safe to rely on?

options.text: No — test 1+2+3+4 = 10, which is not a multiple of 4. Four consecutive numbers sum to 4n+6 = 2×(odd), always even but never divisible by 4. The three-number trick works only because an odd count has a middle number acting as the average.
options.outcome: This tests the pattern instead of assuming it — 'as many terms' does not mean 'divisible by that many' when the count is even.

options.text: The claim holds — k terms always give a multiple of k, and three consecutive numbers prove the pattern.
options.outcome: The three-term case works because its sum is 3×(middle term); with an even count the average is a half-integer, so the divisibility quietly breaks.

options.text: It fails but in the other direction — four consecutive numbers always give an odd sum.
options.outcome: Check 1+2+3+4 = 10: even, not odd; the real rule is 'always even, never a multiple of 4.'

c8_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch06.scenario: Pricing 5 class kits where each kit needs a ₹12 notebook and an ₹8 pen, a student computes 5 × (12 + 8) but expands it as '5 × 12 + 8 = 68.' The bill looks suspiciously cheap to the treasurer.
c8_math_ch06.prompt: Where did the arithmetic go wrong?

options.text: The 5 must reach both terms inside the bracket: 5 × 12 + 5 × 8 = 60 + 40 = ₹100. He multiplied only the first item — the classic incomplete distribution — leaving the pens almost free.
options.outcome: This applies a(b+c) = ab+ac correctly: the outside multiplier hits every term inside, which is why both methods of pricing the kits must agree.

options.text: The calculation is right — brackets mean multiply by the first term and then add the rest.
options.outcome: Brackets mean the outside factor multiplies the whole sum; touching only the 12 undercounts every kit by ₹32 across five kits.

options.text: It should be 5 + 12 + 8 = 25, since expanding a bracket means adding all the numbers together.
options.outcome: That drops the multiplication entirely — the total must scale with 5 kits, so a sum of the prices cannot describe the bill.

c8_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch07.scenario: Amma's sherbet recipe mixes 1 cup syrup with 4 cups water for 5 glasses. For a family gathering needing double, cousin Ajay suggests 'just add 1 cup of each — same increase for both, so the taste stays identical.'
c8_math_ch07.prompt: Will Ajay's batch taste the same?

options.text: No — keeping the taste means keeping the 1:4 ratio, and only multiplying both parts preserves it: 2 cups syrup + 8 cups water. Ajay's '+1 each' gives 2:5, which is a weaker syrup fraction — noticeably more watery.
options.outcome: This is the core of proportional change: equal additions break ratios; only equal factors keep them.

options.text: Ajay is right — adding the same amount to both ingredients is the fairest way to scale up.
options.outcome: Fair-feeling but mathematically wrong: 2/5 is not 1/4, so the ratio shifts and the flavour dilutes.

options.text: Neither works — you can never double a recipe because larger batches always concentrate differently.
options.outcome: Doubling is exactly what proportions allow: 2:8 keeps every sip identical; the failure belongs to the additive method, not to scaling itself.

c8_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch08.scenario: Sana scored 36 out of 50 on a quiz; her friend in another section scored 40 out of 80. Comparing mark sheets, Sana converts hers: '36/50 = 0.72, so I got 0.72% — my friend must have done far better.'
c8_math_ch08.prompt: Where does her comparison go wrong?

options.text: 0.72 is a decimal, not a percentage — % means 'per hundred', so she must rescale to 72/100 = 72%. Her friend's 40/80 = 50/100 = 50%. On the common base of 100, Sana actually scored far higher.
options.outcome: This applies the definition of % as a shared denominator of 100 — the whole point of percentages is comparing different wholes fairly.

options.text: Sana is right — a decimal answer like 0.72 can be written straight as 0.72% since they are the same number.
options.outcome: 0.72% means 0.72/100, a hundred times smaller than 0.72; sticking % on a decimal shrinks it by two places.

options.text: Neither score can be compared at all — percentages only work when both tests are already out of 100.
options.outcome: Comparing unlike totals is exactly what percentages are for: rescaling any fraction to 100 makes 36/50 and 40/80 comparable.

c8_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch09.scenario: Re-enacting an ancient Sulba-Sutra task on the school field, a team must mark a square altar with exactly double the area of a 10 m square, using only rope and stakes. One member suggests: 'Easy — double the side to 20 m.'
c8_math_ch09.prompt: Does doubling the side double the area?

options.text: No — a 20 m square has 400 m², four times the original 100 m². The Sulba-Sutra trick is to use the original square's diagonal as the new side: the square on the diagonal holds exactly two of the original squares, giving exactly 200 m².
options.outcome: This distinguishes linear from area scaling and recovers the rope-geometry insight — the diagonal is the side that doubles area.

options.text: The suggestion works — twice the side is twice everything, including the area.
options.outcome: Area scales with the square of the side; doubling the side quadruples the ground covered — the field would run out of rope and space.

options.text: Instead multiply the side by 1.5 — since 1.5² = 2.25, close enough to double.
options.outcome: Ritual construction demanded exactness, and 2.25 overshoots by 12.5%; the diagonal method is exact because the diagonal squared equals precisely twice the area.

c8_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch10.scenario: A scooter covers 180 km on 12 litres of petrol. To find fuel needed for 270 km, Nikhil sets up 180/12 = 270/x, then multiplies numerators and denominators: 180 × 270 = 12x, getting x = 4,050 litres.

options.text: Cross-multiplication pairs each numerator with the opposite denominator: 180 × x = 12 × 270, so x = 18 litres. He paired numerator with numerator, producing a physically absurd answer that a sanity check — 270 km cannot need 4,050 litres — would have caught.
options.outcome: This restores the diagonal pattern of extremes and means and shows why checking reasonableness matters after the mechanics.

options.text: His method was correct; the error is only arithmetic — 4,050 should be 4.05 litres.
options.outcome: The pairing itself was wrong, not just the arithmetic; multiplying the same-position terms is not cross-multiplication at all.

options.text: The proportion cannot be solved at all while x sits in the denominator — he should have given up.
options.outcome: An unknown in the denominator is routine: clearing it by cross-multiplication isolates x normally once the correct pairs are multiplied.

c8_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch11.scenario: For a nature-geometry display, Ira pins up a fern photo, a tree photo and a Konkan coastline photo, calling them 'symmetric fractals.' A visitor asks whether symmetry is really the point.

options.text: Self-similarity across scales — each fern leaflet is a miniature of the frond, each branch echoes the whole tree, and the coastline stays equally jagged whether you view it from a satellite or standing on the beach. It is a scale match, not a mirror match.
options.outcome: This names the defining feature correctly — parts resemble the whole at smaller scales, which is different from left-right symmetry.

options.text: The label is right — a shape whose two halves mirror each other is exactly what fractal means.
options.outcome: That is bilateral symmetry; a fern is not even mirror-symmetric, yet each leaflet still miniatures the whole — the relationship is scaling, not reflection.

options.text: They are fractals because the same pattern repeats side by side, like identical tiles in a row.
options.outcome: Wallpaper repeats at the same size; fractal self-similarity repeats the pattern shrunk — a part resembling the whole at a smaller scale.

c8_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch12.scenario: Five friends' marble counts are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, with mean 6. Planning a redistribution game, a student argues the mean is 'just the middle number' and any central number balances the group the same way.
c8_math_ch12.prompt: What makes the mean a true balance point?

options.text: Distances below and above it must cancel: 2 sits 4 below the mean and 4 sits 2 below (total 6 below); 8 sits 2 above and 10 sits 4 above (total 6 above). Only the mean makes the two sides equal; shift it and the balance breaks.
options.outcome: This uses the defining property — signed deviations from the mean always sum to zero — so '6' is provably the pivot, not merely 'the middle.'

options.text: He is right — the mean is whichever number sits in the middle, so 4, 6 or 8 all balance equally well.
options.outcome: Try 4: the below-side is only 2 while the above-side sums to 14 — wildly unbalanced; centrality-by-position is not the balancing property.

options.text: The mean balances only when data is symmetric like this set; in general the deviations need not cancel.
options.outcome: The cancellation holds for every data set by definition of the mean — symmetry is not required, only that total below-distance equals total above-distance.

c8_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch13.scenario: At a fair, a magician calls: 'Think of a number, multiply by 5, add 15, divide by 5, subtract your number — the answer is always 15!' A student in the crowd whispers that the answer is not 15 at all.

options.text: Let x be the number: 5x + 15 over 5 is x + 3, and subtracting x leaves 3 — not 15. The trick works because x cancels, but the added 15 got divided by 5 along the way, shrinking it to 3.
options.outcome: This tracks each operation on the expression instead of fixating on the big number — division acts on the sum, not just on x.

options.text: The magician is right — whatever number you add becomes the final answer, so 15 it is.
options.outcome: The add-15 step is followed by a divide-by-5 step that cuts it to 3; ignoring later steps misreads the trick.

options.text: The whisperer is wrong too — the answer keeps changing with the starting number, so nothing can be predicted.
options.outcome: The construction guarantees cancellation: the subtract-x step removes the variable entirely, leaving a fixed constant every time.

c8_math_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch14.scenario: Ordering a banner for the school gate, Rohan measures the space as 5 m long and 300 cm tall. He calculates the area as 5 × 300 = 1,500 m² and emails the printer for a quote on fifteen hundred square metres of vinyl.
c8_math_ch14.prompt: What mistake is in the order?

options.text: He multiplied metres by centimetres — both sides must share a unit first. Converting 300 cm to 3 m gives 5 × 3 = 15 m²; his figure is a hundred times too big and would buy a small wall's worth of vinyl for the price of a billboard.
options.outcome: This enforces unit consistency before multiplying — area is only meaningful when length and width are in the same unit.

options.text: The order is fine — multiplication works on any units since area is just length times width.
options.outcome: The formula needs compatible units; '5 m × 300 cm' does not produce m², and 1,500 m² would cover a parking lot.

options.text: The error is using the area formula at all — banners are measured by perimeter, so he needed 5 + 300 = 305 m.
options.outcome: Covering a surface is an area problem; and perimeter too requires matching units — it would be 5 + 3 = 8 m either way.

c8_physics_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch01.scenario: For the science fair, Javed wants to study 'why pressure cookers whistle.' His mentor asks him to narrow it to something measurable in the school lab.
c8_physics_ch01.prompt: Which rewrite turns his curiosity into a focused question?

options.text: 'How does the heat level of the stove affect the time between whistles?' — it names what will be changed (heat, the independent variable), what will be measured (time between whistles, the dependent variable), and implies keeping water amount and cooker size constant.
options.outcome: A focused question pins down the relationship between variables that can be changed and measured — 'why does it whistle' gives nothing to vary or time.

options.text: 'What makes a pressure cooker whistle?' — adding the words 'what makes' already sharpens the question enough.
options.outcome: It still asks for a general explanation with no identified variables; nothing in it can be changed or measured in a fair test.

options.text: 'Do all pressure cookers whistle?' — a yes-or-no question is the most focused kind because it has a single answer.
options.outcome: A yes/no classification tests no relationship between variables; focus means isolating one change against one measurement, not shrinking to a single fact.

c8_physics_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch02.scenario: Rebuilding Oersted's demo on a desk, a student rests a compass near a wire, closes the switch and watches the needle swing. His lab partner concludes, 'The wire must have turned into a permanent magnet — it will attract iron pins even with the switch off.'
c8_physics_ch02.prompt: Is that what the needle's deflection shows?

options.text: No — the needle deflects only while the circuit is closed and springs back to north-south when it opens, so the magnetic field exists only while current flows; the wire never becomes a permanent magnet, and reversing the battery flips the deflection.
options.outcome: This reads the evidence correctly: current produces a field, and the field lives and dies with the current.

options.text: The partner is right — once a wire carries current it stays magnetised, which is why the needle moved.
options.outcome: Then the needle would stay deflected with the switch open; it does not, so the effect belongs to the flowing current, not a magnetised wire.

options.text: The needle moves because current flows through the compass itself — the wire and needle are part of one circuit.
options.outcome: The needle is a free magnet outside the circuit; it is the wire's magnetic field, acting at a distance, that turns it.

c8_physics_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch03.scenario: At lunch, Pia squeezes her rubber stress ball flat and it stays in her fist, unmoving. Her friend says, 'No force was involved — nothing moved.' Pia squeezes again and watches it deform.
c8_physics_ch03.prompt: Did a force act on the ball?

options.text: Yes — force is a push or pull, and its effects include changing shape, not just motion; her squeeze is a compressive force that deformed the ball even though it stayed in place. Its SI unit is the newton.
options.outcome: This keeps the definition complete: speed change, direction change, and shape change are all effects of force.

options.text: The friend is right — force only exists when an object moves, so a still, squashed ball proves no force acted.
options.outcome: That limits force to motion; deformation without displacement is still the work of a force — the ball's changed shape is the evidence.

options.text: The ball 'has force stored in it' from the squeeze, which is what deformed it.
options.outcome: Force is not a possession an object stores; it is an interaction — Pia's hand pushing on the ball.

c8_physics_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch04.scenario: Chopping vegetables, Mira finds the blunt knife only mashes the tomato while the sharp one slices it cleanly — same hand, same push. Her brother insists, 'Same force means same pressure; the sharp knife just looks better.'
c8_physics_ch04.prompt: Why does the sharp knife really cut?

options.text: Pressure is force per unit area — the sharp edge concentrates the identical push onto a tiny contact area, producing pressure high enough to break the skin, while the blunt edge spreads it over a larger area and only crushes.
options.outcome: This applies P = F/A directly: the same force on a smaller area means greater pressure — that is the physics of every pin and knife.

options.text: The brother is right — pressure is just another name for force, so equal pushes give equal results.
options.outcome: Force and pressure are different quantities; ignoring area predicts both knives should behave identically, which the tomato disproves.

options.text: The sharp knife works because doubling the contact area doubles the pressure it delivers.
options.outcome: That inverts the relationship — larger area at the same force means less pressure, which is exactly why the blunt edge fails.

c8_physics_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch05.scenario: Mixing nimbu pani for guests, Tara dissolves 20 g of sugar in 100 g of water. Her cousin labels the diagram: 'Sugar is the solvent because it is the solid; water is the solute because it is the liquid.'

options.text: No — solvent and solute are decided by amount, not state: water at 100 g is the larger component, so water is the solvent and sugar the solute. The mixture is a true solution because the sugar particles are uniformly spread at molecular level and never settle out.
options.outcome: This uses the amount-based definition and the homogeneity test rather than judging by which ingredient started solid.

options.text: The cousin is right — the solid ingredient is always the solvent and the liquid always the solute.
options.outcome: State does not assign the roles; quantity does — the bigger share is always the solvent, whatever phase it is.

options.text: Neither is right — nimbu pani is not a solution at all because you can still taste the sugar.
options.outcome: Taste proves the sugar's properties survived, which is normal for mixtures; a solution is defined by uniform molecular distribution, which this clear liquid has.

c8_physics_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch06.scenario: Playing with a steel spoon at dinner, Esha sees her face magnified on the inner side but small and upright on the outer side. Her uncle says, 'Same spoon, same curve — the images should match.'
c8_physics_ch06.prompt: Why do the two sides of one spoon behave differently?

options.text: Each side acts as a different spherical mirror: the inner, caved-in surface is concave (it can magnify or invert depending on distance) while the outer, bulging surface is convex (always upright and diminished). The mirror type is named by which surface reflects, not by the spoon's shape.
options.outcome: This uses the real definition — reflecting surface, not object shape — to explain both images from one piece of steel.

options.text: The uncle is right — one object means one mirror type, so both sides must be convex since the spoon is curved.
options.outcome: A spherical shell has two faces; 'concave' and 'convex' describe which face does the reflecting, so one spoon hosts both mirror types.

options.text: The difference is just dirt or lighting on one side — mirrors of any shape always give identical images.
options.outcome: Curvature direction, not cleanliness, controls the image; concave and convex surfaces bend light oppositely.

c8_physics_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch07.scenario: Watching the moon shrink from full to a thin crescent over two weeks, Dev's sister says, 'Earth's shadow is slowly covering the moon — that's why it changes shape every night.'

options.text: No — the sun always lights half the moon; as the moon orbits Earth we simply see different fractions of that lit half, and the dark part is the moon's own night side. Earth's shadow produces a lunar eclipse only on rare full-moon nights, roughly twice a year — not a monthly cycle.
options.outcome: This separates the two phenomena: phases are viewing geometry on a half-lit sphere; eclipses are shadow events.

options.text: His sister is right — anything that darkens part of the moon is a shadow, and Earth's is the only one around.
options.outcome: If a shadow caused phases, every night would be an eclipse; the moon's unlit half is its own night, visible in different proportions as it orbits.

options.text: Neither — the moon makes its own light and dims it on a schedule, like a lamp being turned down.
options.outcome: The moon emits no light; it reflects sunlight, and phases come from how much of the sunlit half faces us.

c8_physics_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch08.scenario: For a habitat poster, a group lists 'fish, frogs, water plants' under 'parts of a pond habitat' and writes 'water, sunlight, mud' under 'just background — not really part of it.'
c8_physics_ch08.prompt: Does the second column belong in the habitat?

options.text: Absolutely — a habitat is biotic plus abiotic components together: the water, dissolved oxygen, sunlight and muddy bottom are what let the fish and plants live. Remove the 'background' and the living column collapses with it.
options.outcome: This recognises that non-living factors are not scenery — they are the survival conditions every organism in the habitat depends on.

options.text: The split is correct — only living things make a habitat; the rest is setting, like furniture in a room.
options.outcome: Without water and dissolved oxygen there are no fish at all; abiotic components are habitat members, not furniture.

options.text: The abiotic items matter only for plants, since animals like fish do not use sunlight or soil.
options.outcome: Fish depend on plants and algae driven by sunlight and on oxygen dissolved from air and photosynthesis — the abiotic web feeds everything.

c8_physics_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch09.scenario: In a quiz, a team argues Earth supports life 'simply because it is at the right distance from the Sun.' The opposing team points out the Moon sits at essentially the same distance, yet swings between 127°C and −173°C.
c8_physics_ch09.prompt: What does the Moon comparison prove?

options.text: That distance alone cannot explain habitability — Earth stays temperate because its atmosphere traps heat and holds breathable gases, its gravity retains that atmosphere, and its magnetic field shields it from solar wind; life needs all these conditions at once, not just a good orbit.
options.outcome: This replaces the single-factor answer with the real bundle of conditions — the Moon shares the orbit but lacks the atmosphere.

options.text: Nothing — the Moon is small and dead anyway, so the team's original point about distance stands.
options.outcome: The Moon is the perfect control case: same sunlight, no atmosphere, extreme temperatures — showing atmosphere, not distance, moderates heat.

options.text: It proves Venus is a better comparison, since being nearer the Sun is the real reason it is hot — so distance is still the main factor.
options.outcome: Venus is only modestly closer in solar terms; its 464°C comes from a runaway greenhouse of dense CO2 — again an atmosphere story, not a distance story.

c9_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_bio_ch01.scenario: Preparing a science-museum label, a student drafts: 'In 1665 Hooke peered at cork and saw living cells at work — the moment we discovered the living unit of life.' The curator asks him to check it against what each pioneer actually saw.

options.text: Split the credit: Hooke saw only the dead, empty walls of cork cells — the rooms, not the occupants — and coined the word 'cell'; it was Leeuwenhoek's sharper single lens that later revealed living, moving animalcules, and only together did the two pictures become the living cell idea.
options.outcome: This assigns structure to Hooke and life to Leeuwenhoek — the distinction the history of cell theory rests on.

options.text: The draft is fine — whoever coined 'cell' must have seen a living cell, since dead tissue has no cells.
options.outcome: Cork is dead tissue made of cells: the walls remained after the living contents decayed, so Hooke catalogued architecture, not life.

options.text: Give Leeuwenhoek all the credit and remove Hooke — living things are what matter, so his discovery alone counts.
options.outcome: Erasing Hooke loses the structural concept; the cell idea needed both the named compartment and the living creature inside it.

c9_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_bio_ch02.scenario: Cattle graze the tip off a young wheat plant. Watching it later, a farmer's son predicts: 'Height growth is over, but it may still thicken at the stem — not every growing cell lives at the tip.'
c9_bio_ch02.prompt: Does his tissue-level reasoning hold up?

options.text: Yes — the grazed tip was the apical meristem that drives lengthening, but meristems are not only apical: the lateral meristem (cambium) keeps dividing to add girth. Meristematic cells are the thin-walled, densely cytoplasmic dividers; the thick-walled storage and transport cells are permanent tissue.
options.outcome: This applies the meristem-versus-permanent split and correctly locates which growing zone survives the grazing.

options.text: No — meristem means the tip, so losing the tip ends all growth everywhere in the plant.
options.outcome: Meristematic tissue also sits at grass nodes and in the woody cambium; 'dividing cells' is a tissue type, not a single spot.

options.text: It will regrow from the tip anyway, because all plant cells can divide whenever needed.
options.outcome: Permanent cells have differentiated past division — thick walls and big vacuoles are for their jobs, not for splitting; only meristems divide.

c9_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_bio_ch03.scenario: Watching mould bloom over forgotten monsoon-season bread, a student says, 'Each fuzzy patch must have come from two parent moulds mating — complex organisms always need two parents, so this can't be asexual.'
c9_bio_ch03.prompt: What does asexual reproduction actually require?

options.text: Just one parent and mitosis — no gametes, no fusion. Spores landing on bread divide into identical clones. And it is not limited to microbes: Hydra buds, Planaria regenerates, and a flowering potato plant still propagates asexually through its tubers.
options.outcome: This keys on the defining mechanism — single parent, mitotic division, genetically identical offspring — rather than the organism's complexity.

options.text: The student is right — anything beyond bacteria and yeast must reproduce sexually, so mould needed two parents.
options.outcome: That boundary does not exist; moulds spread by spores, and even starfish and flowering plants reproduce asexually alongside their other modes.

options.text: It is asexual, but only because the patches look identical — clones are defined by appearance.
options.outcome: Clones are defined by identical DNA from mitotic copying, not by looking alike — appearance can mislead where genotype does not.

c9_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c9_bio_ch04.scenario: A farmer boasts his new field of a single high-yield wheat variety holds 'maximum biodiversity — thousands of living plants.' Next season a rust disease sweeps it while the neighbouring mixed plot survives.

options.text: Biodiversity is variety at three levels — genetic, species and ecosystem — not a headcount. One wheat genotype across thousands of plants means near-zero genetic diversity: no resistant variants to buffer the rust, plus lost species diversity, so the field had no resilience.
options.outcome: This uses the three-level definition to explain why a big monoculture is fragile — numbers of individuals are not diversity.

options.text: The farmer is right — biodiversity counts living things, and his field held more life than the wild hedgerow.
options.outcome: Ten thousand identical plants are one species and one genotype; the diversity that resists shocks lives in variety, not volume.

options.text: The field failed only because it lacked pesticide — biodiversity would not have changed the outcome.
options.outcome: A mixed, genetically varied field gives the pathogen fewer compatible hosts — resilience is a property of diversity itself, not of spraying.

c9_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_chem_ch01.scenario: Setting up for a class demo, a student holds a glass of clear lime water and a glass of chalk-water: 'Both look uniform enough to me — call both homogeneous.' A torch beam, though, scatters visibly through one and not the other.

options.text: The lime water — its dissolved particles are below a nanometre, form one phase, never settle, and do not scatter the beam. The chalk particles are thousands of times larger, make a second phase, scatter light and settle — a heterogeneous suspension, whatever it looks like.
options.outcome: This classifies by the real criteria — particle size, phase uniformity, Tyndall effect — instead of trusting a quick glance.

options.text: The student is right — if you cannot see separate parts, a mixture is homogeneous by definition.
options.outcome: Looks can deceive: milk looks uniform yet is a heterogeneous colloid; the test is particle size and light scattering, not appearance.

options.text: Both are heterogeneous — water mixtures always contain visible dirt at some level.
options.outcome: That throws out true solutions entirely; dissolved ions are molecular-scale and genuinely form one uniform phase.

c9_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_chem_ch02.scenario: Building an atom model for an exhibition, a student writes labels: 'Proton — positive, 1 u, in nucleus. Electron — negative, same mass as proton, orbiting. Neutron — neutral, so massless.'

options.text: Two of them: the electron's mass is only about 1/1837 of a proton's — nearly nothing — and the neutron, though uncharged, still weighs about 1 u, matching the proton. No charge never meant no mass.
options.outcome: This separates the two independent properties — charge and mass — that the labels tangled together.

options.text: All three labels are fine — orbiting like a planet gives the electron real mass, and neutral means weightless.
options.outcome: The solar-system picture misleads: deflection experiments show electrons curve sharply precisely because they are almost massless, and mass number counts protons plus neutrons.

options.text: Only the neutron label is wrong — neutrons have mass, but the electron genuinely equals the proton in mass.
options.outcome: Half right, but electron and proton differ by a factor of 1837; equal charge does not imply equal mass.

c9_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_chem_ch03.scenario: Repeating Lavoisier's experiment for the school lab, a group heats magnesium ribbon in an open crucible: 2.4 g in, 4.0 g of white ash out. 'Mass increased — the conservation law is broken!' one declares.
c9_chem_ch03.prompt: What actually happened to the extra mass?

options.text: Nothing was created — the open crucible let oxygen atoms from the air bond with the magnesium, and that borrowed 1.6 g is the gain. The law holds only in a closed system; seal the vessel as Lavoisier did and the total stays constant.
options.outcome: This redraws the system boundary correctly — the reactants included invisible oxygen, which has mass.

options.text: The student is right — a heavier product means mass was created, and laws have exceptions.
options.outcome: The exception is the weighing, not the law: counting only the solid reactant while air streamed in is an incomplete ledger.

options.text: The gain is just trapped heat, since energy registers as mass on a balance.
options.outcome: A school balance cannot register heat; the extra grams are real oxygen atoms that joined the reaction from the air.

c9_civ_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_civ_ch01.scenario: A news item describes a country that votes every five years — yet opposition leaders sit in jail, the media is censored, and courts never rule against the government. A classmate shrugs: 'They hold elections, so it's a democracy.'
c9_civ_ch01.prompt: Does voting alone settle the question?

options.text: No — elections are only the procedure. Substantive democracy also needs political freedom (speech, fair contest), rule of law with independent courts, and rulers accountable to the ruled; India writes these into Articles 19, 14 and 326 precisely so that a ballot cannot coexist with jail cells for critics.
options.outcome: This separates procedural from substantive democracy — the full system is continuous constraints on power, not a single voting day.

options.text: The classmate is right — a government that won an election carries the people's mandate and can govern as it likes.
options.outcome: A mandate is limited authority, not a blank cheque; constitutional rights and courts exist exactly to stop a majority from becoming a tyranny.

options.text: It fails as a democracy only because its elections might be rigged — fair counting would fix everything.
options.outcome: Even honest counting would leave jailed opponents and censored media untouched; the missing pieces are rights and accountability, not arithmetic.

c9_civ_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_civ_ch02.scenario: After record turnout in a general election, a columnist declares, 'With this many voters queueing, our democracy is fully functioning — the case is closed.' A student who read about vote share, media fairness and between-elections accountability wants to disagree.
c9_civ_ch02.prompt: What does turnout alone fail to prove?

options.text: Turnout proves only that people voted — the procedure ran. It says nothing about whether the contest was fair (free media, level funding field) or whether the government answers citizens between elections; a 55% seat win on 37% of votes can be legal yet thin on broad consent.
options.outcome: This distinguishes electoral ritual from substantive legitimacy — elections must be free, fair and consequential, not merely crowded.

options.text: The columnist is right — queues at booths are the definition of a working democracy.
options.outcome: Crowded booths can coexist with manipulated media, money power and unresponsive rule; the ritual can be full while the substance is hollow.

options.text: Turnout actually proves the opposite — real democracies should let citizens protest instead of voting.
options.outcome: Protests supplement but cannot install or remove governments; the election is the binding mechanism — its quality, not its existence, is the issue.

c9_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_eco_ch01.scenario: Scrolling a rich celebrity's interview, Rohan scoffs: 'Scarcity is a poor family's problem — a billionaire faces none.' Yet the same billionaire must choose which of three rival projects to fund, and still has only 24 hours a day.

options.text: Scarcity is universal, not a poverty symptom — it exists whenever wants outrun resources, and every budget, from ₹500 of pocket money to a ₹45 lakh crore national budget, must still answer what to produce, how, and for whom.
options.outcome: This keeps the two-sided definition — unlimited wants against limited means — which holds at every income level.

options.text: Rohan is right — once you can afford everything you want, scarcity disappears.
options.outcome: Wants expand with means, and some resources — time, land, attention — stay fixed for everyone; even a billionaire's choices sacrifice alternatives.

options.text: Both miss it — scarcity is just a shortage, solved whenever shops restock the shelves.
options.outcome: A shortage is a temporary gap at a price; scarcity is the permanent condition that wants exceed resources — restocking never ends it.

c9_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_eco_ch02.scenario: A Class 9 student 'demands' a ₹50,000 phone, telling his father 'demand means desire.' Weeks later, when the milk price rises from ₹60 to ₹70, the family buys less — and the student reports their 'demand for milk has fallen.'
c9_eco_ch02.prompt: How should both statements be corrected?

options.text: Demand needs willingness AND ability to pay — a phone you cannot afford is a desire, not demand. And the milk case is a fall in quantity demanded (moving along the curve as price rose), not a fall in demand — the curve itself shifts only when a non-price factor like income or taste changes.
options.outcome: This applies both board-level distinctions — want versus demand, and movement along versus shift of the curve.

options.text: Both statements were correct — demand is whatever you want, and buying less means demand fell.
options.outcome: Wanting without the power to pay is not demand, and a price change alone moves along the existing curve rather than shifting it.

options.text: Only the milk point is wrong — the phone claim holds because strong desire creates demand in a market.
options.outcome: Markets respond to effective demand — desire backed by money; without ability to pay, want registers nothing to a seller.

c9_geo_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_geo_ch01.scenario: Labelling a cutaway of Earth for the science room, a student colours the whole mantle bright orange and captions it 'a 2,900 km ocean of liquid magma — that's where lava comes from.'
c9_geo_ch01.prompt: Is the caption right about the mantle?

options.text: No — the mantle is solid rock that creeps viscously over geological time; only the outer core is liquid, proven by S-waves vanishing beyond ~103° since they cannot cross liquid. Magma forms by partial melting of solid mantle at plate boundaries — the mantle is not a magma sea.
options.outcome: This applies the seismic evidence and separates 'ductile solid' from 'liquid' — the diagram's colour fooled him.

options.text: The caption is right — volcanoes erupt molten rock, so the layer below must be molten too.
options.outcome: Eruptions need only local partial melting; S-waves cross the mantle fine but die at the outer core, locating the liquid layer deeper down.

options.text: The mantle is liquid AND the inner core is liquid too, since deeper always means hotter and more melted.
options.outcome: The inner core is hotter yet solid — immense pressure raises its melting point above its temperature; depth does not simply mean liquid.

c9_geo_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_geo_ch02.scenario: Filling in an atmosphere pie chart, Meera writes: 'Air is basically all oxygen — that's what we breathe — and CO₂ at 0.04% is so tiny it cannot matter for climate.'
c9_geo_ch02.prompt: What does the real composition show?

options.text: Nitrogen dominates at ~78%, oxygen is ~21%, argon ~0.93% — oxygen is not even half of air. And 0.04% is not insignificant: CO₂ absorbs infrared where water vapour is transparent, so a trace gas steers the whole climate. Water vapour, meanwhile, is the variable gas driving weather.
options.outcome: This replaces 'we breathe it so it's most of air' with the measured percentages, and shows trace does not mean trivial.

options.text: Meera is right — since we breathe oxygen, air must be mostly oxygen; filler gases like nitrogen don't count.
options.outcome: Breathing uses a minority gas; nitrogen's bulk is not filler — it dilutes oxygen enough to prevent runaway combustion and feeds the soil's nitrogen cycle.

options.text: Water vapour is the biggest gas since it drives all weather — permanent gases are the minor part.
options.outcome: Water vapour tops out near 4% and swings with place and season; the weather-maker is a variable trace, while nitrogen quietly forms four-fifths of the air.

c9_engl_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch01.scenario: For homework, a student must summarise 'How I Taught My Grandmother to Read' in 120 words. His draft opens: 'This inspiring story proves education matters and everyone should respect elders.'
c9_engl_ch01.prompt: What does a proper summary need instead?

options.text: Plot, not praise: Krishtakka, a 62-year-old in a North Karnataka village, depended on her granddaughter for the weekly Kashi Yatre serial; left alone for a week, she resolved to learn, set a Saraswati Puja deadline, practised daily, read independently, and honoured her granddaughter with guru dakshina — in order, without opinion.
options.outcome: This supplies protagonist, conflict, sequenced events and resolution — exactly what a summary is, minus the moralising.

options.text: His opening is right — a summary's job is to state the lesson the story teaches, and 'inspiring' earns marks for insight.
options.outcome: Opinion is not summary; examiners want the ordered events and resolution, and 'it is inspiring' proves nothing was read.

options.text: A better summary lists every scene — the wedding, the meals, each practice day — so nothing the author wrote is left out.
options.outcome: Exhaustive retelling is not summary either; the skill is selecting only the events that carry the conflict to its resolution.

c9_engl_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch02.scenario: Asked to summarise 'Sentila's Pursuit of Pot Making,' a student writes: 'Sentila wants to make pots. Her mother says no. She practices secretly. There is a fair. Her pots win. Mother is happy.'
c9_engl_ch02.prompt: What is missing from this summary?

options.text: The substance: the Naga village setting, why Arenla objects — she sees a government job as security and pottery as an uncertain craft — the grandfather's legacy behind Sentila's passion, and the exhibition where public admiration finally turns the mother. Plot points without stakes are not a summary.
options.outcome: This restores the conflict's reasons and the cultural context that make the resolution meaningful — the difference between a gist and a board-level summary.

options.text: Nothing — it is short, in order, and hits every event, which is all a summary requires.
options.outcome: It omits the setting, the mother's actual reasoning and the craft's significance; brevity without the conflict's cause is just a chopped plot list.

options.text: The summary fails only because it never says whether pottery or education was the better choice.
options.outcome: A summary does not adjudicate; it reports the conflict and its resolution — the verdict belongs to the story, not the student.

c9_engl_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch03.scenario: Summarising 'Evolution of the Pankha,' a student writes: 'There were leaf fans, bamboo fans, cloth fans and electric fans.' For order, he puts the Mughal jewelled pankha before the medieval woven one 'because it sounds more impressive.'
c9_engl_ch03.prompt: What two things does this summary get wrong?

options.text: It lists stages with no development — 'as weaving improved, bamboo replaced leaves; later courts turned the fan ceremonial' shows how each stage produced the next — and it scrambles the timeline, which in an evolutionary text destroys the logic itself.
options.outcome: This fixes both faults: causal connectors between stages and strict chronology are what make it an evolution, not a catalogue.

options.text: Only the wording is weak — any order is fine as long as every stage gets mentioned.
