options.outcome: In a text about change over time, order is the argument; a jumbled 'evolution' proves nothing evolved.

options.text: The summary needs more detail, not less — adding the colours and patterns of each fan would fix it.
options.outcome: Detail without sequence or causation makes the warehouse bigger, not the summary better; selection and timeline are the skills being tested.

c9_engl_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch04.scenario: Summarising 'Grandpa's Memory Challenges,' a student writes: 'Grandpa forgets Ravi's name. He wanders off. A policeman brings him home. Vidya cries. They buy labelled jars. Grandpa becomes happy.'
c9_engl_ch04.prompt: Why would examiners call this a list rather than a summary?

options.text: Because the events float loose of each other: the wandering is the crisis that triggers the care-home discussion, and the 'Vitamin-M' routine — colour-coded jars, fixed walks — is the compromise that restores Grandpa's independence. The causal chain is the summary; bare events are just a travel log.
options.outcome: This supplies the cause-and-effect spine — conflict driving each event — which is what a board-level summary must demonstrate.

options.text: They would not — all the main events are present, and summary means writing what happened in order.
options.outcome: Events without linkage hide the story's engine: safety versus independence. Two sentences with 'as a result' would show comprehension the list cannot.

options.text: The draft only needs a moral ending like 'we must respect our elders' to become a full summary.
options.outcome: A moral is interpretation, not plot; the missing piece is how each event causes the next, not a lesson pasted on top.

c9_engl_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch05.scenario: Summarising the chapter on the Paralympics and Dr. Deepa Malik, a student writes only: 'Deepa got a spinal tumour at 29, survived three surgeries paralysed waist-down, and won silver at Rio 2016.'
c9_engl_ch05.prompt: Why does this cost marks despite being accurate?

options.text: The text runs on two rails — the Paralympic movement's history (Rome 1960, India's 1968 debut) and Deepa's personal arc — and the summary must braid both, ending by linking her medal to the chapter's title about limitless possibilities; a person-only sketch drops the institutional half.
options.outcome: This mirrors the text's dual architecture — board summaries must condense the whole text, not just its hero.

options.text: It costs nothing — the Paralympic dates are background decoration, and Deepa's story is the real chapter.
options.outcome: The institutional history is the frame that gives her medal its meaning — first Indian woman on a Paralympic podium — and omitting it is omitting the text's design.

options.text: The fix is emotional language — 'bravely fought a tragic fate' — since the facts are already there.
options.outcome: Board summaries want factual reporting — diagnosed at 29, three surgeries, Rio 2016 silver — not inspirational adjectives; feeling belongs to personal response.

c9_engl_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch06.scenario: Writing a summary of the play 'Twin Melodies,' a student lists: 'Act 1: Shruti hears a violin. Act 2: she practises secretly. Act 3: father finds out, they argue. Act 4: they perform together.'
c9_engl_ch06.prompt: What does a play summary need beyond the act list?

options.text: The conflict that drives it: Shruti's fascination with the violin collides with her guru-father's view of music as a sacred lineage, so the secret practice is resistance, the discovery forces confrontation, and the fusion finale is a negotiated space — not a tidy win. Frame each event as a choice under that pressure.
options.outcome: This converts the event list into a dramatic arc — conflict, escalation, climax, negotiated resolution — which is what a play summary must show.

options.text: Nothing more — naming each act in order is exactly what a summary of a play is.
options.outcome: That is a table of contents; drama is structured around choices under pressure, and without the tradition-versus-voice conflict the events have no engine.

options.text: The summary should end by declaring that father and daughter fully reconcile — audiences want a clean ending.
options.outcome: The play deliberately leaves tension — the father's 'the raga remains, even if the vehicle changes' is qualified acceptance, and calling it full reconciliation misreads the resolution.

c9_engl_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch07.scenario: Summarising 'Khetaram, the Gramin Dak Sewak,' a student writes: 'Khetaram is a very brave man walking in the hot desert. I feel sad for him in the sandstorms. The story teaches us to work hard.'
c9_engl_ch07.prompt: What rules of summary does this break?

options.text: Two at once: 'I feel sad' is a personal reaction and 'teaches us to work hard' is a moral — both interpretation, not plot. A summary reports objectively: a Gramin Dak Sewak crossing the Thar by bicycle and on foot through 50°C heat so isolated villages get letters, pensions and government notices.
options.outcome: This swaps evaluation for evidence — the factual who-where-what of the route and its stakes, which is all a summary is permitted to carry.

options.text: None — feelings and morals show the student understood the story deeply, which examiners reward.
options.outcome: Emotional response is a different question type entirely; inside a summary it is ruled out, and 'work hard' replaces the story's actual content.

options.text: The only fix needed is naming every village on Khetaram's route, since thoroughness makes a summary complete.
options.outcome: A travelogue of every stop violates conciseness; a summary selects representative detail — it is a map, not a photograph.

c9_engl_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c9_engl_ch08.scenario: Summarising a mother's letter to her daughter about chasing a dream, a student writes: 'First she says she loves her daughter. Then she talks about her own dance dream. Then she warns about shortcuts. It was heartfelt and I felt inspired.'
c9_engl_ch08.prompt: How should this reflective letter be summarised instead?

options.text: As an argument, not an event list: 'The mother urges her daughter to pursue her dream with conviction; her own abandoned dance ambition shows that unfulfilled dreams get rechoreographed into new purpose, she warns against shortcuts, and closes by affirming family support' — claim, evidence, warning, reassurance, reported without 'I felt.'
options.outcome: This maps the letter's logic — the anecdote supports the advice — and keeps the summary objective, which is what epistolary summarising demands.

options.text: The draft stands — a letter is a small story, so 'first… then… then' plus a reaction is a fair summary.
options.outcome: A reflective letter is persuasive, not narrative; sequencing its paragraphs like scenes misses that each part serves the advice, and 'I felt inspired' belongs to a personal response.

options.text: Fix it by naming the emotion properly — call the tone 'heartfelt and touching' since the letter is emotional.
options.outcome: Describing tone is fine, but only objectively — 'encouraging yet realistic'; adjectives of your own feeling are your response, not her letter.

c9_hist_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_hist_ch01.scenario: Debating whether history counts as a real science, a student argues: 'A chemist can rerun an experiment, but nobody can rerun the Battle of Panipat — so history is just storytelling, not science.'
c9_hist_ch01.prompt: Is the experiment test the right yardstick?

options.text: No — social sciences are systematic but interpretive: the past cannot be rerun, so historians build explanations from surviving traces — documents, artefacts, revenue records — tested by logic and critique. Science means disciplined use of evidence, not necessarily repeatable experiments.
options.outcome: This defends the right criterion — rigour with fragmentary evidence — rather than letting the laboratory define all science.

options.text: The student is right — no lab, no science; history is opinion dressed up as fact.
options.outcome: Interpretive is not arbitrary: claims about the past are still constrained by evidence and open to falsification — different method, not less rigour.

options.text: History would be a science if historians simply made predictions, like physicists do.
options.outcome: Human agents react to being studied, so deterministic prediction is impossible — social science explains patterns instead of forecasting dates.

c9_hist_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_hist_ch02.scenario: At the Bhimbetka rock shelters, a visitor sneers at the 30,000-year-old hunting paintings: 'These people barely survived — starving, sick, always on the edge. Farming finally rescued them.'
c9_hist_ch02.prompt: Does the evidence support the sneer?

options.text: Mostly not — ethnographic parallels like the !Kung San show foragers worked 15–20 hours a week, ate dozens of plant species, shared equally and stayed healthy; early farmers in fact worked harder, ate narrower diets and built hierarchies. 'Primitive' is a progress myth, not a finding.
options.outcome: This confronts the progress narrative with the actual evidence — foraging was often healthier and more equal than early farming.

options.text: The visitor is right — without farms or cities, life was unrelieved misery, which is why humans invented agriculture.
options.outcome: Skeletal evidence shows foragers were taller and better-toothed than early farmers; agriculture was adopted for other pressures, not because foraging failed.

options.text: Half right — hunter-gatherers were healthy only because there were so few people; hardship arrived purely from population growth.
options.outcome: The record shows active advantages — diverse diet, short work, egalitarian sharing — not merely the absence of crowding; the sneer still misreads the evidence.

c9_hist_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_hist_ch03.scenario: A quiz question asks what changed between the Rigvedic and Later Vedic periods. A contestant answers: 'Nothing much — same people, same rigid four-caste system from day one, just new addresses.'
c9_hist_ch03.prompt: What did the transition actually involve?

options.text: A society remade: eastward migration from the Punjab to the Ganga doab, iron axes and ploughshares turning forest into farmland, surplus funding chiefs who became territorial kings — and varna hardening from a fluid occupational order into birth-based hierarchy. Even the Rigveda's caste verse is a late hymn, not day-one reality.
options.outcome: This traces the real causal chain — iron → surplus → janapadas → stratification — instead of projecting a later rigidity backward.

options.text: The contestant is right — the Purusha Sukta is in the Rigveda, so the rigid caste order existed from the start.
options.outcome: The Purusha Sukta belongs to the late tenth mandala; earlier hymns show occupational fluidity — the poet's father a physician, his mother grinding corn.

options.text: The only real change was religious — bigger sacrifices for bigger gods; economy and society stayed pastoral.
options.outcome: Ritual elaboration rode on a material shift: cattle camps became ploughed villages, and tribal janas became taxed territorial kingdoms.

c9_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch01.scenario: Marking seating spots on graph paper for a school drill, the PE teacher reads '(3, 5): three right, five up from the origin.' A student plots it as three up and five right, arguing '3 and 5 are 3 and 5 — same point either way.'
c9_math_ch01.prompt: Does the order inside the pair matter?

options.text: Completely — (3, 5) means 3 units from the vertical axis then 5 from the horizontal one; (5, 3) is a different square entirely. The pair is ordered by convention — horizontal first, vertical second — and only the line y = x is where a swap coincidentally lands on the same spot.
options.outcome: This applies the fixed convention that makes coordinates unambiguous — shared language, not personal preference.

options.text: The student is right — the pair is just the two numbers, and the point exists wherever you place them.
options.outcome: Coordinates are signed distances from specific axes; swapping them moves the point, which is why the convention exists.

options.text: Neither is standard — teachers let each student choose which number goes horizontal.
options.outcome: The convention is universal: x first, y second; letting everyone choose would make every shared map meaningless.

c9_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch02.scenario: Sorting expressions on a worksheet, Priya circles 1/x + 2, x² + 3x, and 0x + 4 as 'all linear polynomials — I can see an x in each one.'
c9_math_ch02.prompt: Which of her picks actually qualify?

options.text: None of them. A linear polynomial is ax + b with a ≠ 0 and x only to the first power: 1/x puts x in a denominator, x² raises it to power 2, and 0x + 4 collapses to the constant 4. Seeing an x is not the test — the power and the coefficient are.
options.outcome: This applies the real criteria — degree 1 and non-zero coefficient — instead of scanning for the letter x.

options.text: All three qualify — any expression containing x is a linear polynomial by definition.
options.outcome: That test would make √x and 1/x 'linear'; the definition restricts x to power 1 with a non-zero coefficient.

options.text: Only 0x + 4 counts, because it already looks like ax + b written out.
options.outcome: It only looks the part — with a = 0 the variable vanishes and what remains is a constant, not a linear expression.

c9_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch03.scenario: Filling a number-system chart, a student writes 'natural numbers start at 0' and reasons: 'since 0 leaves numbers alone in addition, dividing by 0 should give the number back too — division is just the inverse of multiplication.'
c9_math_ch03.prompt: Which of the two claims needs correction?

options.text: Both: ℕ starts at 1 while whole numbers W add the 0. And zero's calm in addition (a + 0 = a) hides its violence in multiplication (a × 0 = 0 for every a) — which is exactly why division by zero is undefined: a ÷ 0 would need an answer that 0 × anything can never produce.
options.outcome: This separates the sets correctly and traces 'cannot divide by zero' to zero's own properties, not an arbitrary rule.

options.text: Both claims are fine — zero counts and dividing by it just returns the same number.
options.outcome: Zero is a whole number but not a natural number, and 5 ÷ 0 would demand a number whose product with 0 is 5 — impossible when 0 annihilates everything.

options.text: Only the first is wrong — natural numbers start at 1 — but the division logic is sound.
options.outcome: The inverse argument fails precisely at 0: because 0 × x = 0 always, '5 ÷ 0' has no candidate answer and '0 ÷ 0' has infinitely many — neither can be a number.

c9_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch04.scenario: Computing (103)² mentally for a puzzle, Kavya writes 'square each part: 100² + 3² = 10,009.' Her friend recomputes on paper and gets a different answer.

options.text: Squaring a sum does not split: (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b², so 103² = 10,000 + 600 + 9 = 10,609 — she dropped the middle term 2ab = 600, the piece the distributive expansion always produces.
options.outcome: This restores the missing cross-term that separates (a+b)² from a² + b² — checkable instantly: 5² = 25 but 2² + 3² = 13.

options.text: Kavya is right — the square of a sum is the sum of the squares; exponents distribute like multiplication.
options.outcome: Exponents do not distribute over addition: (2+3)² = 25 while 2² + 3² = 13; the cross-term 2ab is where the extra 12 went.

options.text: Both are wrong — (a+b)² equals a² − 2ab + b², so the answer should be 9,409.
options.outcome: That is the difference identity; for a sum the middle term is positive, giving 10,609.

c9_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch05.scenario: Labelling a diagram of a circle, a student marks a chord that misses the centre as 'diameter — it crosses the circle,' and calls a 10 cm chord in a 10 cm-radius circle 'a radius, since it is 10 cm long.'
c9_math_ch05.prompt: What do the definitions actually require?

options.text: Endpoints, not lengths: a radius runs centre-to-boundary and a diameter is a chord that passes through the centre. A chord joining two boundary points is never a radius, and a chord that skips the centre is never a diameter — no matter how long it is.
options.outcome: This checks the defining conditions — which endpoints and whether the centre lies on the segment — rather than matching lengths.

options.text: The labels are fine — any segment inside a circle touching the boundary is a diameter, and any 10 cm line is a radius here.
options.outcome: That ignores where the segment starts: radii must touch the centre, diameters must pass through it — position, not length, is the test.

options.text: Half right — the chord is not a diameter, but a 10 cm chord does count as a radius because the lengths match.
options.outcome: Equal length is a coincidence, not the definition: a chord's endpoints are both on the boundary, while a radius must end at the centre.

c9_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch06.scenario: Fencing a rectangular garden 12 m by 8 m, a student tells the hardware shop: 'Perimeter is 12 + 8 = 20 metres, so 20 m of wire at ₹45 a metre.' His uncle counts the corners and frowns.
c9_math_ch06.prompt: How much wire is actually needed?

options.text: 40 m — perimeter is the whole boundary, and a rectangle's two lengths and two breadths give 2(l + b) = 2(20) = 40 m, costing ₹1,800. The student priced only half the fence — the semi-perimeter — and would come home short.
options.outcome: This applies the full-boundary definition and shows why the distributive 2 must reach both dimensions.

options.text: The student is right — one length plus one breadth is the perimeter of any rectangle.
options.outcome: That measures only two of the four sides; wire must close the loop, which doubles the 20 m to 40 m.

options.text: Neither — the real figure is 12 × 8 = 96 m, since fencing covers the area inside.
options.outcome: Area and perimeter are different measures: wire runs around the edge (metres), while 96 m² is the grass inside it.

c9_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch07.scenario: An app shows 'rain tomorrow: 0.8.' Neha packs for a picnic anyway, and her friend warns, 'Point eight is basically one — it will definitely rain.' Neha counters with a coin argument.

options.text: An 80% chance — likely but not certain; probability 1 alone means certainty, and 0.8 leaves a live 20% for a dry day. It measures likelihood, it does not guarantee an outcome — a fair coin's two sides are equally likely precisely because symmetry justifies it.
options.outcome: This reads probability as quantified uncertainty — a number in [0,1] — rather than a disguised prediction.

options.text: The friend is right — any probability above a half means the event will happen.
options.outcome: Then '80% chance of rain' would wrongly forbid the 20% dry outcome; below 1, the complement always stays possible.

options.text: Neha's coin logic misfires — every coin toss has three outcomes since it could land on its edge, so nothing is ever 50-50.
options.outcome: The edge outcome is vanishingly rare and excluded from the idealised model; 'equally likely' covers the model's outcomes, not every physical possibility.

c9_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch08.scenario: A puzzle shows the start of two saving plans: Plan A deposits 2, 4, 8, 16 rupees; Plan B deposits 2, 4, 6, 8 rupees. A friend calls them 'the same sequence — both just grow.'

options.text: Their rules: Plan A multiplies by 2 each term (a doubling rule: 2,4,8,16,32…) while Plan B adds 2 (2,4,6,8,10…) — identical openings, different generating rules, and by the fifth term A is already more than triple B.
options.outcome: This treats a sequence as a position-indexed rule, not a lookalike list — the rule, not the first two terms, is the identity.

options.text: The friend is right — matching first terms mean the sequences are the same pattern continuing.
options.outcome: Two different rules can share an opening; the third term (8 vs 6) already proves the generators differ.

options.text: Neither is a sequence at all — a real sequence must follow an obvious arithmetic step like +2.
options.outcome: A sequence is any ordered list with a rule assigning a term to each position n — doubling qualifies as fully as adding.

c9_physics_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch01.scenario: A WhatsApp forward announces: 'NASA confirms — rubbing lemon on the forehead cures migraine instantly.' A student who has seen his grandmother's remedies 'work many times' calls it scientific because someone observed it.
c9_physics_ch01.prompt: Does observation alone make the claim scientific?

options.text: No — systematic science demands more than watching: a falsifiable, measurable claim, controlled comparison (placebo, dosage), reproducibility by independent testers, and peer review. 'It worked for grandma' is observation without controls; a forward citing NASA is authority without method.
options.outcome: This applies the communal, testable-evidence criteria that separate science from anecdote — personal observation is necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

options.text: It counts as scientific — repeated observation is exactly how science collects its facts.
options.outcome: Repeated uncontrolled observation cannot rule out placebo or natural recovery; science starts only when the claim is structured so evidence could prove it false.

options.text: It is scientific because NASA said so — trusted institutions make a claim reliable.
options.outcome: That is appeal to authority: no study, no mechanism, no replication is cited — an institution's name is not a method.

c9_physics_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch02.scenario: On a school hike, a group walks 3 km north to a stream, then 4 km east to a camp. Tallying the day, a student writes 'we are 7 km from where we started — same as the distance we walked.'

options.text: No — 7 km is the distance, the scalar total of path walked. Displacement is the vector start-to-finish: √(3² + 4²) = 5 km northeast. Distance collects every step; displacement cares only about endpoints.
options.outcome: This applies the scalar-versus-vector split and the Pythagorean straight line between the two positions.

options.text: The tally is right — distance and displacement are two words for the same measurement.
options.outcome: They diverge the moment the path bends: distance adds legs (3 + 4), displacement draws the straight line between ends (5).

options.text: Displacement is 7 − 5 = 2 km, the difference between the two legs.
options.outcome: Subtracting legs measures nothing here; the net change is the hypotenuse of the 3-4 right triangle, 5 km.

c9_physics_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch03.scenario: On a bus that brakes suddenly, Kabir lurches forward into the seat ahead. Explaining it later he says, 'a force threw me forward — motion needs force to keep going, so when the bus's force stopped, mine pushed me on.'
c9_physics_ch03.prompt: What does Newton's first law say instead?

options.text: No forward force existed — Kabir and the bus shared a velocity; braking acted on the bus, not directly on him, so his inertia kept him moving while the bus slowed. Force changes motion; it is not needed to maintain it — things only 'stop on their own' because hidden friction does the changing.
options.outcome: This replaces the phantom forward push with inertia of motion — the law's actual content.

options.text: Kabir is right — a moving body needs continuous force, and losing it is what flung him ahead.
options.outcome: That is the pre-Newtonian error: a force is required to change velocity, not to sustain it — in frictionless space he would coast forever.

options.text: He lurched because braking created a backward force on the bus that bounced off him.
options.outcome: Nothing bounced: the seat and floor simply decelerated while his body, left unforced, continued at the old speed.

c9_physics_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch04.scenario: Helping at a bookstall, Asha holds a 20 N bag of stock at shoulder height for five long minutes, arms aching. She reports to her teacher: 'I did hundreds of joules of work — I was exhausted.'
c9_physics_ch04.prompt: How much physics work did she do on the bag?

options.text: Zero joules — work needs force AND displacement in the force's direction; the bag never moved, so W = 20 N × 0 m = 0 J. Her tired muscles spent energy internally, but no work was done on the bag.
options.outcome: This separates the physics quantity from the feeling of effort — exhaustion is not evidence of displacement.

options.text: She is right — effort times time is work, so five minutes of holding counts.
options.outcome: Work is force times displacement, not force times duration; a motionless hold, however tiring, transfers no energy to the bag.

options.text: Work was done but negative, since the bag's weight pulled opposite to her lift.
options.outcome: Negative work still needs displacement — with zero movement, the product is simply zero, whatever the direction of the forces.

c9_physics_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch05.scenario: In music period, a student plucks a stretched rubber band and hears a twang. He clamps it still with his palm — silence — yet insists 'the band is still stretched tight, so the sound should continue.'

options.text: Sound needs vibration, not tension — his palm damped the oscillation, so no compressions and rarefactions formed in the air. Tautness is the setup; the to-and-fro motion is the source, which is why every instrument — string, membrane, air column, plate — is a vibrator.
options.outcome: This ties the sound to the motion itself rather than to the stretched condition — damp the vibration, kill the sound.

options.text: The sound should continue — a stretched object stores sound the way a battery stores charge.
options.outcome: Nothing stores sound; the air disturbance exists only while the source oscillates — stop the vibration and nothing is left to radiate.

options.text: It stopped because his palm blocked the sound waves from escaping — the vibration is still going inside.
options.outcome: His palm stopped the vibration itself; blocking the air path would muffle, but the deeper point is that a non-vibrating band produces nothing at all.

c9_physics_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch06.scenario: Reading that Earth is closest to the Sun in January, a student concludes: 'So Delhi's January should be its warmest month — less distance, more heat. The tilt idea is a myth.'

options.text: Geometry, not distance: Earth's 23.5° tilt makes the Sun's rays strike the northern hemisphere at a slant in January, spreading the same beam over more area and shortening the day — that is why it is winter while Earth is near perihelion. The distance change is only a few per cent; the angle change is the dominant term.
options.outcome: This applies the cosine-of-zenith-angle idea — slanted light is diluted light — and correctly ranks tilt above orbital distance.

options.text: The student is right — nearer the Sun always means hotter, so the calendar confirms it.
options.outcome: The orbit is nearly circular — perihelion changes sunlight by only ~7% — while tilted incidence and day length swing heating far more; the Southern Hemisphere is in summer at the same moment.

options.text: Neither matters — seasons come from ocean currents carrying warm and cold water around the globe.
options.outcome: Currents redistribute heat but cannot create the global winter-summer pattern; the input is uneven insolation set by tilt and solar angle.
